en: The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara:
The Section on the Religious Student (Brahmacārikāṇḍa)
The Section on the Investigation of Sacred Fords (*Tīrthavivecanakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara;
the Auspicious Invocation (*Maṅgalācaraṇa*).
The dwellings of the immortals, whose peaks are like Dharma’s stainless golden jars, possess as their friends an innumerable assembly of mendicant seekers of liberation;
and at sacred fords, their scales proclaim the likeness of the gates of the City of Dharma.
In the eighth chapter, Lakṣmīdhara elaborates upon the examination of sacred fords (tīrthas).
The promise was made in this eighth section on sacred sites (*tīrthakāṇḍa*): first, the procedure for pilgrimage to sacred sites;
then the majesty of Vārāṇasī, and after that, that of Prayāga.
Furthermore, [he recounted] the majesty of the Gaṅgā and the majesty of Gayā,
as well as the majesty of Kurukṣetra and that of Pṛthūdaka.
And likewise the majesty of Puṣkara and Madhurā,
as well as that of Ujjayinī, the Narmadā, and Kubjāmraka.
The greatness of Śūkara and likewise of Kokāmukha;
the greatness of Badaryāśrama and likewise of Mandāra.
[2] The majesty of Śālagrāma, and likewise the praise of the Lord,
the majesty of Dvārakā, and also that of Lohārgala.
Beyond this, the various sacred sites of Kedāra and Naimiṣa,
as well as the pilgrimage to Mahāpatha, have been proclaimed in detail.
Twenty-four joints have been established in the section on the sacred sites (tīrthakāṇḍa).
Now follows the procedure for pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrāvidhi*),
as stated therein in the *Mahābhārata*: "The sages have described the sacrificial rites (*kratu*) here according to their sequence in the Vedas."
And likewise, the fruit and the reality [of all things] in every respect, both here and after death.
O lord of the earth, those sacrifices cannot be attained by a poor man;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
These are attained by these kings or by men who are prosperous; they are never attained by those deficient in wealth, by the lowly, by those who are solitary, or by those who are not united.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn of that rite which even the poor are able to perform, which is equal to the meritorious fruits of sacrifices, and which leads to lordship over the gods.
O best of the Bharatas, this supreme secret of the seers—
that the meritorious pilgrimage to sacred fords excels even sacrifices— is hereby declared.
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, one is born indeed as a poor man.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which is gained by visiting sacred fords (tīrtha).

“By those without attendants” means by those lacking companions such as oxen; “by those who are single-minded” means by those without wives; “by those who are unassociated” means by those lacking assistants such as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Likewise: “He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained...”
Possessing knowledge, austerity, and fame, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

“His hands are restrained” by abstaining from taking what is not given and so forth; his feet as well by abstaining from visiting improper places; and his mind too by abstaining from formative intentions (*saṃkalpa*). “Knowledge” is the understanding of the qualities of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like. “Austerity” is characterized by dwelling at sacred fords, fasting, and so on. “Fame” is renown for virtuous conduct and the like. Likewise:
“He has turned away from accepting gifts and is content with whatever he may have.”
And being liberated from the sense of ego, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
He who is free from conceptual construction, free from worldly undertakings, moderate in diet, and has conquered his senses— he,
being liberated from all attachments, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

[5] “Free from conceptual construction” (*akalpaka*) means devoid of deceit. “Without undertaking” (*nirārambha*) here means free from activities such as the acquisition of wealth. “With all attachments” (*sarvasaṅgaiḥ*); here, attachment refers to unordained clinging.
Likewise: “O Indra among kings, he is free from anger, truthful, and firm in his vows.”
And he who treats all beings as himself enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
“And [treating] beings as like oneself” means being intent on the welfare of all beings. Śaṅkha says:
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained...
Through knowledge, austerity, and fame, one enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

And this restraint of the hands and so forth is an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of pilgrimage (*tīrthayātrā*), because it is stated in the *Mahābhārata* after introducing the subject of pilgrimage. Furthermore, it is an ancillary part of rites such as bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha-snāna*), because Śaṅkha, without even mentioning the section on pilgrimage, gives a general statement: "He enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The hero, full of faith and concentrated, while visiting the sacred fords..."
Even one who has committed evil would be purified, how much more so one who performs pure deeds?
He shall not go to the womb of an animal, nor be born in an evil land;
indeed, the brahmin attains heaven and finds the means to liberation.

[6] The one lacking faith, the evil-minded, the nihilist, the one whose doubts are not severed, and the one who relies solely on worldly causes— these five do not partake in the fruit of the sacred fords.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who dwells at a sacred ford after having conquered desire, anger, and greed—
there is nothing that he would not have attained by visiting such sacred fords."
But those wise men who wander among the sacred fords according to the prescribed rule, enduring all pairs of opposites, go to heaven.
“Enduring all dualities” means being patient with hardships such as cold and heat.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen, O sinless one, as I speak of the mental sacred fords (tīrthas) according to my own understanding.
By bathing properly in these, a person attains the supreme goal.
Truth is a sacred ford, forgiveness is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford;
compassion toward all beings is a sacred ford, and straightforwardness indeed is a sacred ford.
Generosity is a sacred ford, self-restraint is a sacred ford, contentment is said to be a sacred ford;
celibacy is the supreme sacred ford, and pleasant speech is also a sacred ford.
Knowledge is said to be a sacred ford, fortitude is a sacred ford, and austerity is declared to be a sacred ford;
yet that which is the sacred ford even among sacred fords is the supreme purity of mind.
[7] Bathing is not said to be for one whose body is merely drenched with water;
he is truly bathed who has bathed in self-restraint, being pure and cleansed of the impurities of the mind.
He who is greedy, malicious, cruel, hypocritical,
and devoted to sensual objects remains defiled and sinful, even if he has bathed in all the sacred fords.
A person does not become stainless merely by discarding the impurities of the body;
rather, when the impurities of the mind are abandoned, one becomes perfectly pure within.
Leeches are born and die in the waters alone;
yet they do not go to heaven, for their minds are defiled by the impurity of passion.
Excessive attachment toward sense objects is called the mental impurity; indeed, detachment from those very same objects is declared to be its purity.
A mind that is corrupt within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
it remains as impure as a liquor jar washed a hundred times in water.
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, purity, visiting sacred fords, and likewise sacred learning—
all these are not true sacred fords if one's inner disposition is not stainless.
Wherever a man dwells who has withdrawn the collection of his senses,
there indeed is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and the Puṣkara lakes.
He who bathes in the mental sacred ford, purified by knowledge and filled with the water of meditation that removes the stains of passion and hatred, attains the supreme goal.
This, O King, has been told to you regarding the characteristics of mental sacred sites (tīrtha). Now hear the reason for the merit even of terrestrial sacred sites.
Just as certain parts of the body are remembered as most sacred,
so too certain regions on earth are remembered as most sacred.
[8] The sanctity of sacred fords (tīrtha) is traditionally held to arise from the miraculous power of the earth, the brilliance of the water, and the acceptance of them by sages.
Therefore, he who constantly bathes in both terrestrial and mental sacred fords attains the supreme goal.
"By the power of the water" means by the efficacy of the water;
[as stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "completely with all the water of the Gaṅgā."
Furthermore, we declare that one whose mind is corrupted will not become pure, even if they are constantly devoted to ritual bathing from birth until death, like a mountain of clay.
Fish dwell constantly at holy fords such as the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds dwell in temples; yet,
being devoid of spiritual realization, they do not obtain the fruit [of those places].
And from a crossing, and from a principal temple of the gods.
Then, having placed one's being within the lotus of the heart, one should, with a concentrated mind, visit the sacred fords—
that pilgrimage which has been described by the lords of sages.
Whether performed, undertaken, or even rejoiced in.
A student, being well-restrained and commissioned by his teacher, performs that rite according to the rule;
or else, O King, even when all his possessions have been lost.
Having placed the virtuous Brahmins at the very forefront.
[9] Or, even when his entitlement to perform sacrifices has ceased, a Brahmin may wander among sacred fords (tīrthas),
because the fruit of sacrifice is fully attained at sacred fords.
Thus it was proclaimed by the lords of sages, whose natures are stainless.
For one who has the qualification for the iṣṭi sacrifices, his excellent house and all its domestic duties [are fulfilled].
Thus, for one established in the householder stage of life,
visiting sacred fords was prohibited by those of old;
indeed, all sacred fords are [equivalent to] the Agnihotra.
We say that they are by no means equal.
Whoever should go on a pilgrimage to sacred fords,
being well-restrained, having first observed a fast at his own home, pure and vigilant;
One should worship Gaṇeśa, bowing with devotion.
Having diligently honored the gods, the ancestors, the Brahmins, the virtuous, and the formidable ancestors according to one's wealth and power,
he likewise returned once again.
One should also worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins.
For one who acts in this way, there is the fruit of the water from sacred fords and the like; therefore, there is no doubt in this matter.

“Bhāva” refers to a pure mental disposition. Regarding the phrase “gods and ancestors,” for one intending to perform a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrtha-yātrā*), the worship of gods, ancestors, and Brahmins is mandatory. Furthermore, by the statement “ancestors according to the power of one’s wealth,” it is specifically enjoined that the worship of the ancestors must be performed by those possessing wealth.
In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
“At sacred sites, one should never examine a Brahmin in any way whatsoever.”
Manu declared that food should be given to one who has arrived seeking food.
The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) with roasted flour (saktu), with groats (saṃyāva), with milk-rice (pāyasa),
with honey-mixtures (eṣāka), and with molasses (guḍa) is prescribed by the sages.
Sesame oil-cakes should always be offered by devoted men;
however, the Śrāddha ceremony there must be performed without the ritual invocation (anvāvāhana).
That śrāddha which is not seen by dogs, crows, vultures, or ravens is declared to be "tīrthika," bringing satisfaction to the ancestors.

Whether out of season or at the proper time, when men have reached a sacred site (tīrtha), they must always perform the Śrāddha rite; likewise, the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) must be performed.
The offering of the piṇḍa is indeed praised and is exceedingly dear to the ancestors;
one must not delay at all, nor should one create any obstacle.
[11] Śaṅkha says: Having reached a sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform a bath at that ford as a secondary consequence;
one obtains the fruit born of bathing, but not the fruit of a pilgrimage to the sacred ford.
Likewise:
"For men who have committed sins, there may be a destruction of sin at a sacred ford;
however, for men of pure soul, the sacred ford yields the fruit as it has been described."
Paiṭhīnasi says: "He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part [of the merit];
he who goes by way of association obtains half of the fruit of the sacred site."
One should immerse an image made of kusha grass in the waters of a sacred ford;
whoever one has in mind when performing this immersion, that person shall receive an eighth part of the merit.

Since authoritative texts prohibit the use of vehicles when traveling to holy sites other than Prayāga, there is no restriction against using a vehicle to go to other such sites. Furthermore, fasting at a holy site is for the sake of a specific fruit;

for Devala states: "Having approached a holy site, one who is engaged in vows, fasts, and observances, bathing there for three days and staying for three nights, is liberated from all sins and becomes possessed of well-being. Thus, even on a single day, if one reaches various specific holy sites, many *śrāddhas* should be performed.
Whether it be out of season or in season, when men have arrived at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
they must always perform the śrāddha rite and the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa).
Thus, according to the statement in the Devīpurāṇa.
Now, regarding the majesty of Vārāṇasī,
it is stated therein in the Matsya Purāṇa:
Īśvara said—
O Daughter of the Mountain King, here in Vārāṇasī— my beautiful city, which is the very essence of the three worlds— is there always;
even those who have committed various misdeeds come here.
Through the destruction of evil, mortals appear free from passion.
Thus, O Goddess, this field— forever dear to me and ever-remembered— is filled with various trees, shrubs, creepers, and beautiful flowers;
embodied beings who die here attain the supreme state.
It is indeed called liberation; there is no doubt about this, even regarding the mind.
Likewise: "This most secret field, Vārāṇasī, is always mine;
it is at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings."
In this place, O Goddess, the perfected ones (siddhas), always established in my vow,
practice the supreme yoga with disciplined minds and conquered senses.
[13] “Wearing various marks” means those belonging to the four stages of life (*āśrama*) who bear such marks as the girdle and the deerskin.
Likewise:
“With his mind fixed on Me, My devotee, and one who has dedicated all his actions to Me.”
Just as one attains liberation here, it cannot be attained anywhere else in such a manner.
Likewise:
"Because it has not been abandoned by me, nor will it ever be abandoned,
this great field is therefore remembered as 'Avimukta' (the Unabandoned)."
For liberation is not attained merely by bathing or by frequenting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, Gaṅgādvāra, or Puṣkara.
Because liberation is attained here, this place is superior; O beloved, whether it be at Prayāga or at Mahākāla, one may find release.
Likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka, or similarly at Kāyāvarohaṇa,
at Kālañjara, O fortunate one, or here on earth through my favor.
This very place is remembered as even greater than Prayāga, the foremost of sacred fords (tīrtha).
By the statement, "This very place is remembered as great," it is meant that liberation is attained here with little effort. Likewise:
As I meditate there constantly, the fire of yoga blazes intensely;
I attain the supreme state of liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Liberation, which is difficult to attain anywhere else at any time, is attained here by sages whose outward signs are unmanifest and who know all philosophical systems.
And to them I grant unsurpassed mastery in yoga,
as well as union with my own self and the desired state.
The great yakṣa Kubera, having likewise dedicated all his actions to him,
indeed attained the status of a lord of the Gaṇas simply through the service of that sacred field.
And whoever is devoted to me in every way,
O Goddess, having worshipped me right here, he too shall attain unsurpassed perfection.
The son of Parāśara, the yogi, the seer Vyāsa of great asceticism,
endowed with righteousness, shall be the one who establishes the foundation of the Vedas for the future.
O lotus-eyed one, that bull among sages shall also dwell in this field,
as will Brahmā together with the divine seers, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, and Divākara.
Śakra, the king of the gods, as well as other inhabitants of the third heaven—
all these high-souled ones of excellent vows attend upon me here.
And other yogis and perfected ones, their forms concealed under the great vow,
always worship me here with undistracted minds.
And by my grace, Alarka shall regain this city;
and he, having restored it as before, filled with the four castes and the four stages of life.
Having enjoyed this prosperous land filled with people for a very long time, the king,
having surrendered all his life-breaths to me, will thus attain me alone.
From that time forward, O lady of beautiful limbs, even those residing in this field—
whether householders or ascetics— who are my devotees and devoted to me, [shall attain liberation].
By my grace, even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects and who has abandoned delight in the Dharma shall attain liberation, which is most difficult to obtain.
[15] Even one who dies here in this field shall not enter saṃsāra again—
those, moreover, who are free from the sense of "mine," steadfast, established in being, and have conquered their senses.
All those observers of vows who are free from worldly undertakings have been absorbed in me;
having reached the dissolution of the body, they shine forth, liberated from all attachment.
By my grace, those of excellent vows have indeed attained supreme liberation—
that which a yogi might reach after practicing for thousands of future births.
Right here, even before death, he attains supreme liberation.
This, O Goddess, is the great fruit of this sacred field in brief.
I have declared this supreme secret to you for one who is not yet liberated; the phrase "in this very life" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Likewise:
In Avimukta is the supreme accomplishment; in Avimukta is the supreme goal.
Whatever is chanted, given, offered in sacrifice, performed as ritual action, or whatever austerity is practiced—[all that bears fruit there].
All acts of giving and study shall become inexhaustible;
likewise, whatever sin has been previously accumulated over thousands of lifetimes [shall be destroyed].
For one who has entered Avimukta, all that goes to destruction,
like cotton placed in a fire consumed by the fire of Avimukta.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes; as well as worms, Mlecchas, and others who are of mixed origin and born of sinful wombs.
Insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be—
listen, my dear, they too meet their end through time in Avimukta.
O Goddess, all those men who are born there in my city, O Śivā, become ones who wear the crescent moon as a crest, who have an eye on the forehead, and who have the bull as their emblem.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, even if born among the animals,
one who gives up their life in my world while unliberated is glorified.
When, at some point in the course of time, one goes to Avimukta,
one shall pierce one's feet with a stone and meet one's death right there.
Likewise:
"The sacred fords (tīrthas) renowned throughout the three worlds are heard to be eternally present at the feet of Avimukta."
Likewise:
"Whoever does not abandon that sacred field until the fall of the body shall have properly performed sacrifices with the vows of celibacy."
Likewise: "The brahmin who dwells there with self-restraint and concentrated mind should always be as if subsisting on air, even while eating three times a day."
For he who possesses devotion even for a mere moment toward Avimukta,
being endowed with celibacy, shall attain supreme austerity.
There the hero should dwell for a month, eating light food and with his senses subdued;
by that, the great and divine Pāśupata vow has been perfectly performed.
Having crossed over the fear of death in this world, he attains the supreme goal;
he shall enjoy the meritorious state of ultimate liberation as well as the state of Yoga.
Indeed, the state of yoga cannot be attained even in hundreds of other births;
it is obtained through the greatness of the sacred field and by the power of Śaṅkara.
[17] “The path leading to the highest good” (*naiḥśreyasī gatiḥ*) refers to the attainment of a distinguished body that is conducive to liberation. However,
if a killer of a Brahmin should ever go to Avimukta,
his sin of killing a Brahmin is removed by the greatness of that sacred field.
For one who does not leave that sacred field until the fall of the body,
not only the sin of killing a Brahmin but even ordinary worldly attachments cease to exist.
“Having attained the Lord Viśveśvara, that being is not born again.
“Prākṛta” refers to the bondage of saṃsāra.
He who, having become single-minded, does not abandon Avimukta—
The God is always pleased with him and grants all his desires.
That which is the gateway for those of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—therein dwells the Lord;
for the God becomes possessed of attributes out of compassion for his devotees.
Avimukta is the supreme field; in Avimukta is the supreme goal;
in Avimukta is the supreme accomplishment; in Avimukta is the supreme state.
A wise man who desires no further rebirth for himself should dwell in Avimukta, which is frequented by hosts of celestial sages.
The qualities of Mount Meru can be described, and likewise those of the continents and all the oceans; but they cannot be described in the case of Avimukta.
At the time of death, when the vital points of human beings are being severed and they are driven by the wind, no memory whatsoever arises.
For at the time of death, the Lord himself bestows the whispered instruction into the ear upon his devotees who are being driven away by their past actions at the point of liberation.
Impelled by the Lord, one attains that which is difficult for those of unrefined self to reach;
knowing this human condition to be impermanent and fraught with many sins.
[18] One should resort to Avimukta, which grants liberation from the fear of saṃsāra,
bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is divine, and destroys manifold sins.
He who, even when being agitated by obstacles, does not abandon the Unreleased,
does not abandon this impermanent cycle of birth, old age, and death.
But through faith in Avimukta, one shall attain union with Śiva. Likewise:
"Whether he be a sinner, a corpse-like wretch, or a righteous man,"
One is liberated from all sins if one goes to Avimukta.
Likewise: "O lady of beautiful hips, blessed are those twice-born ones, my devotees, who have entered this most secret, supreme, auspicious, and most beloved abode of mine."
Those men who are eternally devoted solely to me and do not worship others,
having cast off their lives in this place, go to the supreme goal.
A person who remains established in Avimukta always sacrifices through the great sacrificial session (sattra), always bestows gifts, and is always an ascetic.
O beloved, I am always pleased with him who constantly worships me;
he who gives all gifts and is initiated into all sacrifices [is likewise pleased].
O Goddess, those who, being firmly resolved, always go to Avimukta, shall attain me here, having received the consecration of all sacred fords.
O lady of beautiful hips, those devotees of mine remain here in heaven;
by my grace, O goddess of auspicious eyes, they shine with splendor.
[19] They become invincible, difficult to restrain, and free from all feverish distress. Likewise:
"My devotees, firm in their resolve, perform sacrifice in Avimukta."
For them, there is no returning again, even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Likewise,
those men who have gone to Avimukta and have performed great meritorious deeds indeed become imperishable, ageless, and invincible.
O lady of excellent hips, by my grace they enter into me alone—
those who subsist on vegetables and leaves, those who are self-controlled, those who cleanse themselves thoroughly, and those who drink only rays of light.
There are those who use their teeth as a mortar, and others who grind with stones;
there are the "Samprakshalas," who wash [their bowls] immediately after eating and are free from food for the following day;
and those who, month by month, taste water only with the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Some have their dwellings at the roots of trees, while others likewise sleep upon rocks.
All possessed bodies as radiant as the sun; they had conquered anger and subdued their senses, having likewise observed various other vows elsewhere.
Even those who practice asceticism elsewhere while eating at all three times of the day do not merit even a sixteenth part of those who dwell in Avimukta.
Those who dwell here in liberation enter into heaven;
there is no man equal to me, nor among women is there one equal to you.
A field equal to Avimukta has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
for in Avimukta is the supreme yoga, and in Avimukta is the supreme goal.
In Avimukta there is the supreme liberation; no other field is like it.
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall declare the supreme secret according to its true nature.
O Goddess, if this yoga is obtained, then that which was indeed enjoyed by me previously in hundreds of other births within the great field of Avimukta is [realized].
Liberation may or may not be obtained after a hundred thousand births;
however, O Goddess, my devotee who is firm in resolve shall dwell in Avimukta.
Even he attains both yoga and liberation in a single birth. Likewise:
"O beloved, Dharma is always embodied in that field; it is ever present there."
For all four castes, however, this is remembered as the supreme goal.
Likewise:
"O lady with eyes as long as a cow's ear, he who gives a milch cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a cloth around her neck in Vārāṇasī..."
O lady of excellent limbs, by giving a cow to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, his lineage up to the seventh generation is purified; of this there is no doubt.
O lady of beautiful countenance, whoever should give gold, silver, clothing, or an abundance of food and drink to a brahmin in that sacred field;
[21] And that which is situated there, O fair-eyed one, is indeed imperishable and undecaying.
Listen to the true nature of this sacred ford’s majesty and its ultimate fruit.
Having bathed there, O illustrious lady, people become free from passion;
they obtain whatever fruit would result from ten horse-sacrifices.
O fair-faced one, that righteous-souled person who, having bathed there,
gives even a very small gift to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, attains that [fruit].
He attains an auspicious rebirth and shines like fire. Likewise,
the man who, having observed a fast, gratifies the Brahmins [attains the same].
That person obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
But he who remains for a month eating only once a day, O fair-faced one,
destroys in that single month the sin committed throughout his entire life.
Those people who, according to the prescribed rite, enter the fire at Avimukta,
shall happily enter into me and shall not be born again.
But those devotees of mine who, having made a firm resolve, practice fasting unto death—
for them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I shall declare the merit that a human being attains by worshipping me in Avimukta.
Listen now to the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice obtained by one who offers ten *sauvarṇikas* of incense at the Avimukta [temple], as well as the merit from the gift of fragrances.
[22] The fruit of the gift of land is remembered as equal to that; the fruit of giving a cow is equal to that.
For sweeping, the merit is five hundredfold; for anointing, it is a thousandfold.
With hundreds of thousands of garlands and infinite song and instrumental music,
I have created this sacred field, a holy site that removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
This is a cremation ground—blessings be upon you, O lady of excellent complexion—and it is my boon;
having become Time, I destroy and create this entire world.
O Goddess of gods, this place is the most beloved of all secrets to me;
my devotees as well as the devotees of Viṣṇu go there.
O Goddess, those who are devotees of Bhāskara, the Lord of the World, the Maker of Day—
whoever casts off the body while staying here shall enter into me alone.
Likewise:
"The destination ordained by the virtuous for those who have established themselves in knowledge and desire supreme bliss— that same destination belongs to one who dies in Avimukta."
Indeed, the joy of existence in Avimukta is incomparable and peerless;
for there the fruit is incalculable and one's destination shall be imperishable.
That which is declared the supreme secret, known by the name "the cremation ground," namely Avimukta— those men who do not frequent it are deceived on this earth.
By being touched by the meritorious dust raised by the wind from those who dwell in Avimukta,
even those who have performed evil deeds shall go to the supreme destination.
Indeed, even by gods, dānavas, and humans, it is impossible to describe its unliberated qualities, for they are immeasurable; therein Bhava himself resides.
Whether one has not maintained the sacred fires, has not performed sacrifices, is impure, or even a thief—
whoever should dwell in Avimukta, he shall dwell in the abode of the Lord.
No one there incurs demerit, whether by ignorance or by knowledge, whether it be a woman or a man, solely due to the power of the Lord.
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by means of human intellect,
all of it shall be reduced to ashes for one who has entered Avimukta.
Likewise: "Having seen these wretched and miserable sinners who have committed evil deeds,
the Lord, out of compassion, swiftly leads them all to the supreme goal."
The Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, leads even those born as animals to that place where the performer of sacrifices does not go.
Likewise: "That destination which is ordained for men dwelling in Avimukta is not attained at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Puṣkara."
Even those beings born in the animal realm who have not yet established themselves in liberation,
when they meet their end in due time, go to the supreme destination.
Even a heap of evil karma as vast as Mount Meru or Mandara,
upon reaching Avimukta, perishes in that very instant.
That which is renowned as the cremation ground is the unmanifested abode of Śiva;
it is the home of the God of gods, it is the sacred ford, and it is the grove of asceticism.
There, the gods headed by Brahmā and led by Nārāyaṇa,
as well as the yogins and the Sādhyas, [worshipped] the eternal Blessed One.
My devotees, who are intent on me, worship Śiva with devotion;
they attain that goal which belongs to those of knowledge and austerity, and that goal which belongs to those who perform sacrifices and yoga.
For those who die in Avimukta, that auspicious goal has been ordained. Likewise:
"By performing the worship of the Sun, Brahmins have attained immortality."
There are also other phonemes there which are devoted to existence and are concentrated.
Those who are liberated in Avimukta shall go to the supreme goal;
for eight months, there should be a dwelling for ascetics of restrained self.
One may dwell for four months and another half-month in one place;
however, for those who have entered Avimukta, there is no such thing as a temporary residence.
No fault shall overcome one there; this is seen in the ancient scriptures.
There, liberation is indeed certain even for one who has met his death.
Those women who are devoted to their husbands, who are devotees of Bhava, and who are composed in mind,
shall be liberated in Avimukta and go to the supreme goal.
Other women who act according to their own desires and are devoted to sensual enjoyments also attain the supreme goal when they meet their end in due time.
Having reached Avimukta, where both yoga and liberation— difficult for men to attain— are found,
one should not go to any other forest of asceticism.
For all living beings, austerity and truth are the supreme goal; of this there is no doubt. But that man who should dwell in Avimukta would become equal to me.
Since it was not released by me, it is therefore remembered as "Avimukta" (the Unreleased). Those deluded men who are dominated by darkness do not resort to Avimukta.
[25] They dwell again and again in the midst of feces, urine, and semen;
[possessed by] desire, anger, excessive greed, hypocrisy, arrogance, and extreme envy.
Sleep, drowsiness, as well as laziness and malice— these ten obstacles,
established by Śakra himself, reside in Avimukta.
And the affliction of Vināyaka shall constantly remain upon his head;
may all this merit accrue through compassion for the devotees.
Knowing this to be the supreme secret,
it was then proclaimed by the gods of gods and by the sages who perceive reality, in accordance with the sacred scriptures.
The earth, overwhelmed by ignorance and devoid of liberation,
became entirely purified when protected by Mahādeva.
By that, the wise also perform the consecration of the ground here.
“Stambhaḥ” means pride; “atimatsaraḥ” means extreme envy; “paiśunyam” means that which brings about the faults of others. Likewise:
having reached that auspicious Mahādeva, who is inhabited by Īśvara...
One should perceive oneself as having accomplished the goal, thinking, "I am liberated."
Avimukta is frequented by hosts of sages, gods, and asuras devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, as well as by ascetics seeking liberation.
No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell;
for all those favored by the Lord attain the supreme goal.
[26] Likewise: "By its power, Avimukta surpasses all the sacred sites (tīrthas) that exist on the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven."
But those who, having attained meditative absorption, with disciplined minds and concentrated attention,
restrain the entire collection of their senses and chant the Śatarudriya;
Those twice-born ones who dwell constantly in Avimukta have accomplished their purpose;
likewise, the wise man who dwells there, even while being struck by hundreds of obstacles, [is successful].
He goes to the supreme state, having gone to which he does not grieve.
Endowed with [the transcendence of] birth, death, and old age, he goes to the supreme abode of Śiva—
that destination of those who desire liberation and never die again.
Having attained which one would have accomplished all that was to be done; thus do the wise consider it.
Likewise: "Neither by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices,
nor even by knowledge is that desired goal attained which is indeed obtained in Avimukta."
There were Caṇḍālas of various complexions and discolored, who were loathsome,
their bodies filled with sins as well as with the most heinous crimes.
The wise know that for them, the Unreleased is the supreme medicine;
whoever should die in the Unreleased throughout thousands of other births.
One who is constantly devoted to the Lord of the Universe is not born again;
whatever is performed here—whether sacrificed, offered as an oblation, given in charity, or whatever austerity is practiced—is [efficacious].
Everything in this Avimukta is imperishable; of this there is no doubt.
Through time, one reaches cessation and the imperishable union with existence (bhava-sāyujya).
Having committed thousands of sins,
he who later falls into remorse and does not release what was unreleased attains the supreme goal.
One should not distinguish between the northern or southern solstice;
for whoever dies in Avimukta, every time there is auspicious.
In that matter, the time need not be deliberated upon, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,
due to the majesty of that deity Sthāṇu, whose deeds are wondrous.
[This is] indeed for all [beings], by the Lord himself, and for all [beings], by the All-pervading One himself.
Likewise: "For liberation is not attained on earth by human beings without yoga."
But for those dwelling in Avimukta, both yoga and liberation are accomplished.
By this very birth, the supreme goal is attained right here;
such is the power of this sacred field, O Supreme Goddess.
O Goddess, by dwelling in Avimukta, Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor shall attain unsurpassed liberation in a single birth.
Having wandered about with great effort, he did not obtain any alms at all;
then, overcome by hunger and filled with rage, he thought of an ultimate curse.
“May there be no learning for three generations; may there be no wealth for three generations; may there be no kingdom for three generations—thus did Vyāsa curse Vārāṇasī.”
"For those people of meritorious deeds who dwell here without being liberated,
I create obstacles for them all, so that no success is found."
Then, having perceived Vyāsa’s mind, the God of gods, the Lord of Umā,
assumed a human form and granted his vision to Vyāsa.
"Come, come, O Blessed One! O virtuous one, accept alms, O Best of Beings!
O Great Sage, you have never before come to our home."
Having heard this, his mind filled with joy, he prepared to receive alms;
and having given Vyāsa alms consisting of the six flavors, which were like nectar, [he offered them].
That [food], never tasted before, was then consumed by the sage;
having eaten that alms-food, Vyāsa reflected with a joyful mind.
O lotus-petal-eyed one, Vyāsa spoke these words:
"The god, the goddess, the river Gaṅgā, sweet food, and auspicious intelligence."
"O large-eyed one, who would not find pleasure in dwelling in Vārāṇasī?
Having spoken thus, Vyāsa then gazed upon the city.
And as he contemplated that alms-food which brought joy to his heart,
he then beheld before him the God and the Goddess, the Daughter of the Mountain.
To Vyāsa, who was standing in the courtyard of his house, the God of gods spoke this:
"O great sage, you must not dwell here in this sacred field; you are prone to anger."
Having thus entered into this agreement, Vyāsa spoke these words to the god:
Vyāsa said:
"On the fourteenth and likewise on the eighth day, you ought to grant me entrance."
Having granted permission by saying, "So be it," he vanished right there.
Neither that house, nor that queen, nor that god was known anywhere;
thus it was in the past with Vyāsa, the great ascetic, world-renowned throughout the three realms.
Having understood all the virtues of that field, he remained right by its side;
thus, knowing Vyāsa to be stationed there, the wise praise the field.
Likewise: whatever austerities are recited, whatever vows and observances there are,
the bathing at all sacred fords, and the fruits of all acts of giving— [all these are attained].
Whatever merit exists in all sacrifices, one shall obtain that in Avimukta,
whether through knowledge or even through ignorance, and whether it belongs to the past or the present.
And whatever sin he has, it perishes upon seeing that field;
as do whatever austerities have been performed by those who are peaceful and self-controlled, and whatever is designated as Dharma.
A man who has conquered his senses attains all of this in Avimukta;
having reached Avimukta, he worships the Liṅga.
Even after hundreds of millions of eons, there is no further rebirth for him;
indeed, being immortal and free from activity, he sports in the vicinity of existence.

The sacred field is undoubtedly the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of all holy places (*tīrtha*); the meaning of "the secret doctrine of holy places" is that this is the esoteric essence of all sacred sites. Indeed, in Avimukta, they worship and praise Mahādeva.
But those who are liberated from all evil remain free from old age and death;
whereas those sacrifices that fulfill every desire are remembered as leading to rebirth.
All those who die in Avimukta are indeed non-returners;
for the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, there is fear of falling due to time.
For those who die in Avimukta, there shall be no falling away,
even for thousands of millions of eons or hundreds of millions of eons.
There is no returning again for those who have died in that supreme field,
even though they were wandering through the terrible ocean of saṃsāra by the turn of time.
Having reached Avimukta, they go to the supreme goal, knowing that the terrible Kali age has become senseless and filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!"
Those men on earth who have accomplished their purpose do not leave Avimukta;
for if one who has entered Avimukta should depart from there again, [he would lose its benefit].
Then all beings laugh at those men on earth who are seized by lust, anger, and greed, clapping their hands against one another.
O Goddess, men go forth deluded by the leader of punishment;
likewise,
the qualities of Avimukta have been described here merely in outline.
The expansion of the Unreleased One is like that of the jewels in the ocean.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*,
Brahmā said:
"And that ancient abode of yours is indeed Avimukta."
The sacred ford known as Kapālamocana shall exist at each of those locations.
I and you shall remain there, and Viṣṇu will also go;
by the sight of you there, even those who are great sinners [shall be purified].
They too enjoy their wealth in my pure abode;
Varaṇā and Asi are two rivers beloved by the gods.
In the interval between those two, one's field shall never enter the earth anywhere.
This is the foremost of all holy fords (tīrthas), the foremost of all sacred fields (kṣetras). Those men who serve this field until the fall of their bodies—
Having died, they go to the divine realm by means of a swan-vehicle, free from all fear;
moreover, a sacred field measuring five krośas has been granted to you by me.
O Rudra, when the Gaṅgā flows through the middle of the field toward the lord of rivers, by that act this city shall become a great and meritorious one.
The Gaṅgā is meritorious when flowing northward, as is the Sarasvatī when flowing eastward;
the river Jāhnavī flows northward for two yojanas.
There all those gods, together with me and their kinsmen, will come to dwell; release the skull right there.
Having gone to that sacred ford, they shall indeed satisfy their ancestors with offerings of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and funeral rites (śrāddha); for them, there shall be an imperishable world in heaven.

Having bathed at the great sacred ford (mahātīrtha) of Vārāṇasī, a person is liberated; indeed, by merely going there, one is released from the sins committed in seven lifetimes. That sacred ford is proclaimed to be the most excellent of all sacred fords.
Likewise, those living beings who, being self-restrained, give up their lives there, [attain that goal].
Having approached you who are like Rudra, they rejoice together with you;
and whatever gift, even if as small as an atom, is given there by those whose souls are devoted to Rudra.
And for those of purified self who perform repairs on what is broken or cracked there, it yields great fruit.
Having reached the world of Rudra, they rejoice there, ever happy;
for there, worship, recitation, and fire-offerings have been performed by those embodied beings.
All these yield infinite fruit for those endowed with devotion to Rudra;
therein, by the offering of a lamp, one attains the suprasensory eye of knowledge.
By the offering of incense, one attains the abode frequented by Rudra—
a place that is brilliantly white, youthful, serene, beautiful, and filled with fragrance.
[32] Furthermore, he who releases animals goes to the supreme destination;
together with his ancestors, he attains liberation—of this there is no doubt.
Now, what is the use of saying more? Whatever gift is given by men with a view toward virtue, pleasure, or wealth, that shall yield infinite fruit.
For that is indeed the most excellent sacred site on earth, the cause of both heaven and liberation;
for bathing, recitation, and likewise fire-offerings performed there are the means for attaining infinite fruit.
He who goes to the sacred ford of Vārāṇasī and performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, and he who meets his death there, attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers,
and the Ādityas are likewise ordained as their great-grandfathers.
O sinless one, I have explained the procedure for the threefold offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa);
humans who have arrived here should always perform the offering of the piṇḍa and other rites.
And there itself, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) should be performed with devotion by good sons;
for good sons bring happiness to their ancestors.
O Bhava, let this Āditīrtha grant liberation through the sight of you;
one who has bathed there in its waters is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
"Released from the sin of killing a Brahmin, stay at your ease, O Rudra;
remain here together with your wife in this Avimukta granted by me."
In the Liṅga Purāṇa, the Lord said:
"Furthermore, I shall declare to you another means for attaining the knowledge of the [proper] methods."
Those sacred sites which were previously described by me in the Vyomatantra—
Among them, O Great Sage, Avimukta is the most preeminent holy site;
indeed, all holy sites have been established by me in that place.
O Sage, I have never abandoned this place,
which is eternally meritorious, composed of all sacred fords, and the greatest secret among secrets.
O best of sages, Maheśvara is the primordial source of all sacred places,
where the seers attained supreme perfection.
With this very body, one attains supreme nirvāṇa;
and having been born right there, a human being attains gnosis.
Likewise:
"Go quickly to Vārāṇasī, where the eternal Lord resides;
there the god who wields the Pināka bow is present together with all the deities."
The boon-granting Lord is praised there incessantly by the gods, headed by Brahmā;
there also flow the rivers Asī, Varaṇā, and Nimnagā, frequented by the Siddhas.
O Goddess, that river where the Jāhnavī flows performs the cleansing of wicked embodied beings on earth who have accumulated sins over many births.
“By whose sight”—that is, by whose vision—[she is] in every way the best of rivers in heaven;
she who is the mother of all beings, that Gaṅgā is the river there.
“Dṛśā” means sight.
Avimukta is indeed the supreme field of Śaṅkara at all times;
therein lies the renowned abode of the Trident-bearer throughout the three worlds.
O Sage, that city is named Vārāṇasī after the two rivers flowing through it;
and it is there that the Lord, having performed his ablutions, resides at Oṃkāra.
[34] At that time, a boon was granted by Śambhu, the God of Gods.
The God of Gods said:
"Those men who shall always remember that place, Avimukta,"
Having shaken off all evils, they will become like a host.
Those people who come to see [the sacrifice] through the performance of the rite shall be liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin and will become my followers.
Having understood that the world is fragile, those who shall dwell in my city—
even at the time of their end— will find it to be the giver of liberation.
Since liberation is so difficult to attain and cyclic existence is so terrifying,
a man would rather live in Vārāṇasī even if he had to pierce his feet with a stone.
Whatever state of existence a mortal may attain by means of meritorious gifts, that state is not equal to what one who dwells constantly in Vārāṇasī attains, even in every condition.
O best of sages, that [state] is difficult for mortals to attain even through austerity;
therefore, O brahmin, go there quickly if you desire steadiness of mind.
Listen as I speak of how it is the cause of mental steadiness:
both the southern and the northern [currents] are always situated in that place.
Situated at the very center, even for the gods it is difficult to attain;
in the Kali age, however, it is the station that brings about liberation for mortals.
Through devotion alone— by means of bathing, worship, and libations—
the body of the fourfold social order is indeed the state of the Universal Lord.
The channel named Piṅgalā is proclaimed to be of the nature of fire;
it should be known as the dry river where Lolārka resides.
The channel named Iḍā is proclaimed to be lunar (saumyā);
it is to be known as Varaṇā, where Keśava is established.
[35] Between these two, however, is the channel known as Suṣumnā;
it should be understood as Matsyodarī, and that is proclaimed as the Viṣuva.
Likewise:
Having heard that the terrible Kali age is short-lived and unrighteous,
people do not resort to the field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), yet they are born and they die.
Those who bear the form of a *liṅga*, such as Dṛgacaṇḍeśvara and others at the sacred ford, all remain in Avimukta; even those who have committed sinful deeds are purified there.
Likewise: Avimukta is the supreme field; in Avimukta is the supreme goal;
in Avimukta is the supreme accomplishment; in Avimukta is the supreme state.
At the time of death, when the vital organs of men are being torn asunder and they are driven by the wind, memory does not arise at all.
Those Rudras who abide in liberation and bestow joy upon their devotees—
such as Dṛg, Caṇḍeśvara, and others— grant the whispered instruction into the ear.
Likewise: "Avimukta is a great sacred field frequented by those who perform meritorious deeds;
it brings about the destruction of all sins and is the manifest, great city of Śiva."
Know that the cremation ground is the supreme among sacred fields;
indeed, a man who enters there quickly casts off his evil.
[36] Likewise: "But whoever, even a slayer of a Brahmin, enters Vārāṇasī, he remains outside the sacred field; once he has departed, he is seized again."
“The [sin of] killing a Brahmin remains”—this is the ellipsis.
Likewise: “Assuming the form of lingas, embodied, there are seven crores everywhere.”
The Rudras abide in Avimukta, bestowing spiritual accomplishments upon their devotees.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Then the best of gods spoke to that goddess, the daughter of the mountain king:
"Having undertaken my vow, together with the most excellent of the twice-born who are full of devotion..."
By whatever yogas have been practiced here, for those [practitioners], it is accomplished in a single lifetime through the power of this sacred field and through my sincere devotion.
For in this way, I always bestow grace that grants liberation;
therefore, this great field of mine is frequented by Brahmā and the other gods.
And by the foremost of Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, by those perfected in knowledge, and by ascetics,
on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
During lunar and solar eclipses, especially on the full moon day of Kārttika,
on all meritorious festival days (parvan), at the equinoxes, and at the solstices.
All the sacred fords on earth are present in Vārāṇasī,
where the meritorious Jāhnavī flows northward, having issued from my crest.
Listen, O lady of beautiful countenance, how all [the gods] come from every direction to honor that auspicious daughter of your father Himavat, the king of mountains.
Having gathered at Kurukṣetra along with hundreds of other sacred fords (tīrthas),
as well as Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Prayāga, and Pṛthūdaka;
The twilight prayers, the Saptarṣi hymn, all rivers and lakes,
the seven oceans, and all the divine tirthas are present here in their entirety.
O Daughter of the Mountain, they shall all go to the Bhāgīrathī at Kāśī on every auspicious occasion,
as well as to me, Avimukteśvara, who resides in Kāśī.
On this auspicious day,
which is excellent in every respect, all the holy fords and sacred shrines on earth always come here, having arrived.
The Liṅga that is at Kedāra, the Liṅga that is at Mahālaya,
the one known as Madhyameśvara, and likewise Paśupatīśvara;
Śaṅkukarṇeśvara, both Gokarṇas,
Dṛgicaṇḍeśvara, and likewise Bhadreśvara.
[Situated] at Sthāneśvara, Ekāmra, Kāmeśvara, Ajeśvara,
Bhairaveśvara, Īśāna, and likewise at Kāyāvarohaṇa.
And whatever other meritorious places exist for me upon the earth,
all those many sites enter into me within the city of Kāśī.
This secret has been proclaimed for all meritorious festival days;
by means of it, even a dying creature attains the immortal state in this world.
O auspicious lady, by my merely seeing you after you have bathed in the Gaṅgā,
it is equal to the fruits of all sacrifices performed hundreds of thousands of times.
One attains this very instant; what could be more supreme than that?
[It surpasses] all the foremost sanctuaries, whether in heaven, on earth, or even upon the mountains.
O Goddess, understand that there is nothing superior to this in its entirety.
[38] By means of Brahmā, the Sun, Vaiśvānara, Cakra, the Moon, Varuṇa, Indra, Kubera, and Vāyu;
This supreme place is always frequented by hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, uragas, and siddhas.
O Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, this bath of mine is always secret; this field is most meritorious,
for its fruit is the attainment of liberation and the ultimate reality.
The perfected ones, the awakened sages, declare this.
Those virtuous men who dwell in this field,
who always behold the pair with reverence, being pure and ever devoted to me— they are mortals freed from fear, suffering, and sin, their ritual actions being perfectly purified.
Having pierced through the dense thicket of the web of bonds of existence, they attain supreme liberation.
Thus it is: this most beloved sacred field of mine is exceedingly vast, filled with various forest creepers, and adorned by the Ganges.
Having reached the Bhāgīrathī here in Vārāṇasī, my own abode,
one obtains the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices and attains the world of Brahmā.
O Goddess, there is nothing more meritorious than this, nor anything more secret anywhere;
there is nothing more auspicious than this, and nothing higher than this for me.
Having reached this field of mine, frequented by gods and siddhas, a mortal through the power of his meritorious deeds shall become renowned among all the gods and asuras.
And when dead, he shall go to the supreme state.
Likewise:

one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin, the slaughter of a cow, violated the bed of his guru, broken his livelihood, stolen a deposit, or engaged in deceit and other such forbidden modes of conduct.
With bodies liberated from the firm fetters of the elements of saṃsāra,
people enter Vārāṇasī, the city of existence.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The Varaṇā and the Asi are two rivers beloved by the gods;
the sacred field between them shall never be entered upon the earth by anyone."
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "That sacred field is recorded as extending two and a half yojanas to the west;
it is recorded as being half a yojana in width toward the south within."
From the Varaṇā river as far as it becomes a dry river—
this extent of the field has been proclaimed by the wise Lord.
Likewise:
that field is recorded as being two yojanas from east to west,
and half a yojana in width, situated within the south.
From the Varaṇā River as far as the dried-up river,
beginning from Bhīṣmacaṇḍīka and ending near Parvateśvara.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "I have granted you a sacred field measuring five *krośas*,
where the Gaṅgā flows toward the north or the Sarasvatī flows toward the east."
The river Jāhnavī flows two yojanas toward the north; this is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"This sacred field is proclaimed to extend four krośas in the four directions."
Know, O lady of beautiful limbs, that at the time of death, this *yojana* bestows immortality.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "Beginning from Kṛttivāsas, for one *krośa* in each of the four directions—
that sacred field (*kṣetra*) extends for a *yojana* there, surrounded by the Gaṇas and Rudras."
In its center, when a linga rose up, having pierced through the earth,
it became renowned among all the gods and asuras by the name Madhyameśvara.
Starting from this linga, know that for four krośas in each of the four directions—
that is, one yojana— it is a sacred field (kṣetra) that bestows immortality at the time of death.
Thus, O Goddess, the renunciation of the field (kṣetra-saṃnyāsa) has been proclaimed in the Purāṇa; beyond this, however, no further wandering (vihāra) exists.
Likewise, in the Liṅga Purāṇa: The Goddess said:
"O beloved, what secret place of yours is there in Vārāṇasī?"
What is the secret of the *liṅgas*, and who are those renowned as *krādas* therein?
What are the wells, what are the ponds, and who are the installers of the liṅgas?
In which place is the rite performed that results in steadfastness in knowledge?
[41] Tell me all of this, if I am worthy of your favor.
The God of Gods said:
Having reached my abode, the beautiful place called Avimukta, which is my home—
It has never been released by me; therefore, it is known as "unreleased" (avivukta).
In this very manner, it is called "Avimukta" (the Unreleased);
however, it is called "Aviśa" (the Unentered) by those who proclaim the Vedas, because sin does not enter there.
Because of that sin, O woman of excellent complexion, that sacred field was abandoned by the preeminent Siddhas and Pāśupatas, who were devoted to it and dedicated to it as their supreme goal.
And they always worship me, remaining constantly in that place,
in the north-eastern quarter of that sacred field, O beautiful one.
O illustrious lady, I was praised by the gods and asuras at that place;
for a thousand divine years, I was lauded with various hymns of praise.
O illustrious lady, my phallus has arisen, having pierced through the earth,
for the sake of bestowing grace upon those worlds out of their state of devotion.
O Great Goddess, I am indeed stationed at that place in Vārāṇasī;
by seeing it, O Goddess, a human being is liberated from the bonds of the Paśus.
Indeed, the well of Mahādeva is situated right there;
O Goddess, by performing ablutions there, one attains the state of Vāgīśvarī.
There, the goddess Vārāṇasī stands in embodied form;
for the welfare of human beings, she resides to the west of the well.
But he who, having beheld Vārāṇasī, bows down with devotion—
that goddess is pleased with him and grants him a dwelling.
To the east of Mahādeva is the place renowned as Goprekṣa;
by beholding it, O lady of beautiful hips, one obtains the fruit previously described.

“By the bonds of the bound” means by the fetters of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). “From contact” means from bathing. “The state of Vāgīśvarī” is the attainment of the world of Sarasvatī. “The previously mentioned fruit” is characterized by the severing of the bonds of the bound. [As stated] in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
“Having seen and worshipped Goprekṣeśvara, a human being...”
One does not fall into an evil rebirth and is liberated from defilements.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa,
Īśvara said:
"To the north of Goprekṣa, there is the Liṅga named Anasūyā."
O Goddess, having seen that, a person attains the supreme goal.
That linga is facing westward and was installed by Anasūyā;
it is known as Gaṇeśvara, situated in front of Anasūyeśvara.
By seeing that, one attains the same world as Gaṇeśa.
To the west of Gaṇeśvara, in ancient times, was Hiraṇyakaśipu.
He installed my Liṅga in the vicinity of the very well;
O Goddess, to the west of that very spot is the Liṅga known as Siddheśvara.
"O auspicious lady, my linga bestows all accomplishments merely by being seen;
now hear from me as I speak of another sacred site."
The Liṅga named Vṛṣabheśvara stands in that very place,
facing east, O Maheśānī, to the southwest of Goprekṣa.
O lady of beautiful hips, by seeing that [place], one obtains the desired fruit;
for that goal which is attained neither through gifts, nor through austerities, nor through sacrifices, nor even through knowledge,
is indeed obtained at Avimukta.
Likewise:
To the south of Goprekṣa is situated an excellent Liṅga named Dadhīceśvara,
which bestows the fruits of all desires.
O lady of excellent complexion, to the south in the vicinity of Dadhīceśvara,
there is a divine, auspicious Liṅga established by Atri that removes all distress.
To the south of Atrīśvara, at Sūryakhaṇḍamukha as well,
O fair-hipped lady, the installation of a linga was performed by Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
There, O Goddess, the Visamantha [mantra] is recited facing westward;
the linga of Kaiṭabha, renowned throughout the three worlds, faces eastward.
To the east of Goprekṣaka is the Liṅga known as Bālakeśvara;
in the vicinity of Bālakeśvara is the one designated as Vijvareśvara.
O lady of beautiful hips, by seeing that [liṅga], fever is destroyed at that very moment;
it is heard that the Lord of Devas is situated to the east of Vijvareśvara.
The liṅga faces Īśāna, and its faces are indeed located at its corners;
by beholding it, O lady of beautiful hips, a twice-born man becomes a knower of the four Vedas.
To the north of Vedeśvara, Keśava himself resides;
he is called the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the cause of this sacred field (kṣetra).
O lady of beautiful hips, by seeing that, everything moving and unmoving has been seen;
and near it, O lady of beautiful hips, is my Liṅga, Saṃgameśvara.
By seeing that, O lady of beautiful hips, one attains communion with the virtuous. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"And this river Vārāṇasī is meritorious and a liberator from sin."
Having adorned this field, she has united with the Jāhnavī.
At this confluence, the supreme Liṅga named Saṃgameśvara was installed by Brahmā; may it be seen as victorious in its renown.
For that pure person who, having bathed at the confluence of the celestial river,
worships Saṅgameśa, whence can there be any fear of rebirth?
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: "O auspicious lady, the four-faced Liṅga situated to the east of Saṃgameśa was established by Brahmā; it is celebrated as Prayāga."
By beholding that, one attains the supreme state of Brahmā;
there, the goddess Sāṅkarī resides within the Brahmā-tree.
He brings peace to all those who dwell at sacred fords;
beyond this, however, is the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the Varaṇā, which is to be experienced.
When the conjunction of Śravaṇa and the twelfth lunar day (Śravaṇadvādaśī) falls on a Wednesday,
a man who bathes on that occasion shall obtain the fruit of bathing at Sannihatī.
O illustrious lady, he who performs a śrāddha ceremony there at that time,
having delivered all his ancestors, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Having given food according to the prescribed rite at the world-renowned confluence of the Vārāṇasī and the Jāhnavī, one is not born again."
In the Liṅgapurāṇa: "On the eastern bank of the Varaṇā, it is remembered as Kumbhīśvara;
and to the east of Kumbhīśvara, it is remembered as Kāleśvara."
To the north of Kāleśvara, O fair-faced one, is a great sacred site known as Kapilāhrada, renowned among all the gods and asuras.
O Goddess, he who, devoted with supreme faith, performs a bath in that lake and beholds the one whose banner is the bull, shall obtain the fruit of a Rājasūya sacrifice;
consequently, his ancestors and grandfathers, even if they reside in hell, [shall be liberated].
[46] Indeed, when that śrāddha has been performed, they attain the world of the ancestors.
The great seers have declared that at Gayā the merit is eightfold;
O auspicious lady, when a śrāddha is performed there, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having bathed at this Kapilāhrada Tīrtha with a restrained mind and having beheld this Vṛṣadhvaja, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"O beautiful one, O Queen of the Gods, in the western quarter of Mahādeva, a liṅga was installed by Skanda out of devotion to me."
By beholding him, O beautiful one, they go to the very same world as Skanda,
along with Śākha, Viśākha, and the Naigameyas.
And many liṅgas were installed by all the Gaṇas;
these include the specific groups known as the Śākhās, Viśākhās, and Naigamīyas.
To the north of Skandeśvara is that established by Balabhadra.
O Goddess, by seeing that, one obtains infinite fruit.
To the south of Skandeśvara, a great liṅga has been established;
this liṅga, facing westward, was installed by Nandin in ancient times.
O Goddess, having seen that, a person shall attain the world of Nandin.
To the west of Nandīśvara stands a linga facing the west.
O blessed lady, it resembles Svarlīna; it was installed by Nandipitṛ and is worshipped by hosts of gods under the name Śilākṣeśvara.
[47] But another [deity] renowned there is the omnipresent Lord Hiraṇyākṣeśvara,
who was installed with devotion by the Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa for my sake.
In the vicinity of the one named Hiraṇya, thousands of other deities have installed lingas out of devotion and with the desire for their own rewards.
Indeed, another [form] of the God of gods is traditionally known as facing west;
it is located in that place, O lady of beautiful hips, to the south of Hiraṇyākṣa.
To the western quarter of them stands the auspicious Aṭṭahāsa;
O Goddess, its face and linga are situated facing westward.
O Goddess of serene countenance, upon seeing that which destroys all sins,
a human being, O Goddess, shall attain the world of Īśāna.
O illustrious one, near Aṭṭahāsa to the west,
those named Mitra and Varuṇa are stationed at the eastern gate.
By beholding those two, however, one attains the world of Mitra and Varuṇa;
another well-known site situated right there is known as Vasiṣṭheśa.
That four-faced *liṅga*, which destroys all sins, was indeed installed there by Yājñavalkya in ancient times; another auspicious one is fixed right there, installed by Maitreyī.
By seeing that, one obtains the supreme knowledge so difficult to attain;
it is the western face of Yājñavalkyeśvara, located in the west.
The one named Prahrādeśvara, who bestows the fruit of non-duality,
remains self-absorbed directly in front of Prahrādeśvara.
To the one named Svarlīneśvara, who bestows very great fruit upon those established in knowledge and realization who desire supreme bliss.
Whatever destination is ordained for them when one has died while merged in Svarlīna,
from that Svarlīna, the auspicious Linga remains situated facing the east.
O Goddess, a Liṅga named Vairocaneśvara was installed by the son of a Daitya; and to its north, another Liṅga is remembered as facing westward.
That [liṅga] established by Bali is devoted to the vision of Śiva;
furthermore, this other stable liṅga is known as Bāṇeśvara.
There is a most terrifying rākṣasī named Śālakaṭaṅkaṭā;
by her, O blessed lady, that auspicious [image] was established to its north.
O illustrious lady, there is another meritorious sacred site in that place;
the sight of the renowned Hiraṇyagarbha is also meritorious.
Mokṣeśvara is located right there, and Svargeśvara is beyond that;
having seen these two, O Goddess of the Gods, one attains both heaven and liberation.
To the north of those two is the auspicious Liṅga named Vāsukīśvara;
it has four faces and bestows the fruits of all desires.
In its eastern section, however, is the supreme holy site of Vāsuki;
one who bathes there, O lady of beautiful hips, is never overcome by diseases.
And in the very vicinity of that, to the east of Candreśvara, was established by Candra the auspicious and beautiful Liṅga known as Vidyeśvara.
"One shall attain the world of the Vidyādharas by beholding that Liṅga.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Liṅga Purāṇa.
[Likewise.]
The Goddess said: "O Lord, how did Vīreśvara come to be? I wish to know this;
please tell me out of your grace, O Maheśvara, God of gods."
Īśvara said:
In ancient times, there was a king here well-known by the name Niyukti.
His wife, O Great Goddess, was renowned by the name Arajā.
After a long time, she then gave birth to one son when the second foot of the constellation known as Mūla had arisen.
Then, O Goddess, the mistress of the Lord was addressed there by the ministers:
"O Goddess, this boy who has been born was produced under an inauspicious constellation."
Therefore, this boy must be abandoned by the king who desires his own welfare.
Having been addressed thus by the ministers out of a desire for her benefit, that queen—
Having meditated thus, the dejected woman, with her face cast downward, approached the Great Goddess and then said this to the nurse: "Take the child; do not delay."
On the northern side of Svarlīna, it was entrusted to the Mothers;
he said, "May they protect this child, for he is my son."
Then Dhātrikā carried out every word of the queen;
she indeed proceeded to entrust the child to the nurses.
Once, in the course of time, the mothers reflected:
"Without a doubt, this boy has attained the status of our son."
[50] We began to proceed toward the supreme circle of sky-farers (khecarī-cakra).
Then the goddess Brahmāṇī said, "O Goddess, let the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) be taken."
"By seeing the Yogapīṭha, a child shall become capable of ruling a kingdom.
Then all the Mothers rejoiced at those words.
He was led to the world of the Vidyādharas and shown the seat of yoga;
there, that boy was comforted by the hosts of Mothers and touched by them.
"Tell us your former history, my son, O young boy. Whose son are you, O one with the luster of the full moon, and how have you come to our house?"
Thus addressed, the boy then did not say anything at all. Pañcamudrā said:
"O boy, you ought to act in such a way that you become fit for sovereignty."
Having heard this, all the mothers turned toward him.
Having said, "It shall be so," the host of sky-faring goddesses was indeed pleased and said:
"Go, my son; rule your kingdom yourself as you please."
"O beautiful one, all these were requested by me in my youth out of a desire for progeny,
so that when I become the king of the earth and of all the worlds."
Then, with supreme devotion to me, an incarnation must be made;
thus indeed were all the Mothers, the mothers of the world, entreated.
They descended according to their respective positions on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
then, the five mudrās led that child back to the city once more.
Having arrived and stationed themselves as appropriate at midnight,
the five mothers of the mudrās then descended, filled with joy.
Having been worshipped by the boy and installed according to the prescribed rite, they all accepted his worship and returned once more to the sky.
Even today, the circle of the Mothers' host is seen in the sky;
one of meritorious deeds beholds it stationed facing the north.
That which is seen in the sky in the vicinity of the Mothers is called the Ākāśaliṅga; this is said to be Svarlīna.
Just as in space, so on the ground—it is seen thus everywhere. Having observed all that, one proceeds toward the circle of mothers.
By the power of the Mothers, however, a man becomes a possessor of siddhi;
from that time forth, O Goddess of the Gods, they have remained established in this sacred field.
Because she has come here out of fear of calamities, she is called Vikaṭā by the wise;
yet, O illustrious lady, this child has attained heroism through my grace.
"And by me, O Goddess, I too have dwelt happily in this region while still a child.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the glorious *Liṅgapurāṇa*. The Lord said:
O beautiful one, O Goddess, in the northwestern direction of that sacred seat (pīṭha),
it was formerly established in that region by Sagara.
That liṅga has four faces and is the destroyer of all sins;
to its northeast is the auspicious Bālīśvara by name.
O Goddess, having seen that linga established by the great-souled monkey Bālin, a human being does not go to a birth among the animal species.
And to the north of that, O auspicious lady, is the beautiful linga of the high-souled Sugrīva, which destroys all sins.
Likewise, an excellent liṅga was installed right here by Hanumān;
that liṅga was established there to the very west of Sagara.
And by my grace, O lady of beautiful hips, O supreme goddess,
it is remembered that on the northern side of that very place is the one known as Bhadradoha.
That which is produced from the milk of cows destroys all sins;
it yields the same fruit as that obtained by properly giving away a thousand tawny cows (kapilā).
A mortal who bathes there obtains that fruit; of this there is no doubt, when the full moon coincides with the constellation Pūrvabhādrapadā.
At that time, it is indeed the most meritorious period, bestowing the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
On the western bank of the lake stands the shrine known as Bhadreśvara.
O auspicious one, having seen that [liṅga] in the south-western direction (nirṛti) of Bhadreśvara, O illustrious lady, a man certainly attains Goloka.
To the north of the god Upaśānta, O lady of excellent complexion, is the place renowned by all the gods and asuras as Upaśāntaśiva.
Known as Cakreśvara, it is honored by all the gods;
O Goddess, there is a lake facing west directly in front of it.
Having bathed in that lake and having worshipped Maheśvara with a purified inner self, a person attains the world of Śiva.
To its western direction stands Śūleśvara;
O lady of excellent complexion, a trident-yantra was formerly placed there for the purpose of bathing.
A lake arose there in front of the God of gods;
having bathed in that lake and beheld the Lord Śūleśvara, [one attains liberation].
Having cast off the ocean of worldly existence, one attains the world of Rudra;
to the east of Śūleśvara is another auspicious sanctuary.
There, intense austerity was performed by Nārada, the celestial sage.
[53] My auspicious *liṅga* has been established in front of the pool;
having bathed in that pool and indeed beheld Nāradeśvara, a man [attains the fruit].
One shall cross over that terrible illusion of saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt.
To the east of Nārada’s place is the auspicious Dharmeśvara.
O auspicious one, my *liṅga* has been installed in front of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*),
in the northwestern direction of that deity, O beautiful lady.
There is a pool known as Vināyaka, containing excellent water;
having bathed in that pool and beheld Vināyaka, a man [attains his desire].
Completely liberated from all obstacles, one shall dwell for a long time in this field,
O illustrious lady, situated to the north of Vināyaka.
There is a well-known lake there named Amaraka;
to the south of the Kuṇḍa stands the Mukhaliṅga.
Having bathed in that pool and beheld Amarakeśvara,
whatever has been done here in this sacred field— even if out of ignorance— is [purified].
Having seen that supreme liṅga,
O illustrious lady, all of that dissolves away at a spot not far from its northern direction.
On the pure bank of the Varaṇā, a Liṅga is established in that very place;
it is renowned as Varaṇeśvara and stands facing the west.
O illustrious lady, in that place lived a Pāśupata adept named Aśvapāda,
who attained eternal perfection in this very body.
[54] I too am present there when that illustrious one performs the rite; by seeing me, O lady of beautiful hips, he attains the state of a Gandharva.
To its west is the auspicious mountain named Śaileśvara;
by beholding it, O Goddess, a human being obtains the fruit previously described.
And to the south of that very place stands Koṭīśvara,
where, O Goddess, the renowned Bhīṣmacaṇḍikā is seen.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in ten million sacred fords (tīrthas) and then worshipping Koṭīśvara,
that same fruit he gains by the gift of ten million cows.
O beautiful one, all that fruit is obtained by him through a single bath at the site established by hosts of sages to the east of Koṭīśvara.
"By seeing that *liṅga*, the entire world, including the moving and the unmoving, shall be seen.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the glorious *Liṅgapurāṇa*. The Lord said:
Situated in the south-eastern direction of the deity Koṭīśvara is the well-established [pillar] renowned as the Śmaśānastambha (Cemetery Pillar).
O Goddess, O beautiful lady, those men who have committed evil deeds here are cast down there, where I always abide upon that pillar, O passionate one.
O Goddess, whoever goes there and performs worship to me shall be liberated from all sins and go to the supreme goal.
[55] Furthermore, O illustrious lady, I shall tell you of another great sacred site (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds, named Kapālamocana.
O beautiful one, a skull fell there while I was bathing;
O lady of excellent hips, one who bathes in that place dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
O beautiful one, by beholding the deity named Kapāleśvara established at that sacred ford (tīrtha), one obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
And on its northern side is a sacred ford renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, a man shall be liberated from his debts.
O beautiful one, it is renowned on earth by the name Ṛṇamocanaka;
O beautiful one, three Liṅgas of mine are situated right there.
O lady of beautiful hips, upon seeing them, the threefold debt is destroyed;
O beautiful one, that is located in the southern direction of that sacred ford.
O Goddess, the Mukhaliṅga named Aṅgāreśvara is established facing west, situated in front of the sacrificial pit.
When there is a conjunction with Mars on the fourth or the eighth lunar day,
a man who bathes at that sacred ford and beholds Maṅgaleśvara [attains his goal].
And liberated from diseases, O illustrious lady, he is born wherever he may be, remaining in the vicinity of that very place to the north.
Having beheld the exceedingly great and meritorious Liṅga installed by Viśvakarman,
facing westward, may I attain omniscience.
Having beheld Budheśvara right there with devotion,
one of firm vows attains all desires upon seeing the god Budheśvara.
[56] To the south of Budheśvara is the four-faced Liṅga named Mahāmuṇḍeśvara, which bestows all supernatural attainments (siddhis).
In front of that god stands a truly auspicious well;
that auspicious goddess is situated above that well.
O Goddess, that garland made of skulls was thrown there by me for the purpose of bathing;
therefore, it is called Mahāmuṇḍā by human beings.
O lady of excellent complexion, O virtuous one, the Khaṭvāṅga indeed remains right there for the purpose of bathing,
established under the name Khaṭvāṅgeśvara.
O Goddess, there is a Liṅga named Bhuvaneśvara that bestows fruits;
it faces north and is situated on the southern bank of the Kuṇḍa.
Having bathed in that pool and beheld Bhuvaneśvara,
a person does not meet with misfortune and is liberated from all taints.
To the south of Bhuvaneśa, another pool remains;
and to its east is the linga named Vimala-īśa.
Indeed, by the sight of that linga, men attain purity;
having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, one rejoices in heaven with the gods.
