In that place, there was indeed a perfected Pāśupata sage named Tryambaka,
who attained the world of Rudra in this very body.
To the west of that pit of embers, O illustrious lady,
there is a great and meritorious sanctuary established of old by Bhṛgu.
[57] Those who, having seen that sanctuary, honor it with words of praise,
never fall from the meritorious worlds of Śiva.
To the south of that very place, however, is another auspicious sanctuary named Nandīśeśvara, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Merely by seeing him, one obtains the Pāśupata vow;
there indeed dwells the great-souled, highly ascetic sage Kapila, who has attained perfection.
Sleeping in a cave and with his self restrained, he worshipped the God three times a day;
thus, at the end of a thousand years, O beloved, I became pleased with him.
O Goddess, by my grace, he shall be a highly renowned knower of Sāṅkhya;
there, beneath Kapileśvara, a cave is situated right there.
Whoever indeed gazes upon that cave is not stained by sin.
The Goddess said: How is the Lord of Monkeys the deity known as Oṃkāreśvara?
Out of your grace, tell me about Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Īśvara said:
"O my beloved, there are three secret liṅgas in Vārāṇasī,
O Goddess of the gods, in whose very presence I myself am present."
And in this manner, O beautiful one, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
as well as Nandīśa, are designated by their measures (mātrās) in successive order.
Viṣṇu, established in the five abodes, resides in the syllable *A*;
O Dear One, the form of Brahmā is the syllable *U*, situated to his right.
I am named Nandīśvara, established to the north;
and that Oṃkāra, O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, is my very form.
[58] Indeed, for the sake of the welfare of human beings, I am stationed in that place,
on the northern bank of the Matsyodarī, O beloved.
I am established in the north under the name Nandīśeśvara;
Nandīśa is the supreme Brahman, and Nadīśa is the ultimate goal.
Nandīśa is the supreme abode, the liberator from the suffering of saṃsāra;
this which is not to be disclosed, O beloved, has been revealed to you out of affection.
Otherwise, O Goddess, it must be kept secret from those devoid of devotion to me; and in the seventeenth age, having made [this] single earth [my own], [it shall remain hidden].
Having performed the austerity of withdrawal, I have come to this place;
indeed, having assumed the form of Oṃkāra, I abide here in threefold division.
That place is proclaimed as the abode of all the Siddhas;
therein Śiva himself is personally and directly established as a Liṅga.
That god, facing the east, worshipped by hosts of Siddhas,
named Oṃkāreśvara, is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Vāmadeva, Sāvarṇi, Aghora, and Kapila likewise attained supreme perfection there, remaining established in the Pāśupata yoga.
And other sages, gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, and guhyakas will go there in age after age; he remains forever established in that place.
For that supreme, divine form known as Kapileśvara is indeed the beloved Jāhnavī herself, appearing at times for the vision of this deity.
One arrives at Matsyodarī, where bathing indeed bestows liberation;
by worshipping Kapileśa there, one becomes capable of protecting the three worlds.
O Goddess, those men who always recite "Om" are eternally dear to me; for that syllable Om is the Supreme Brahman, existing both with parts and without parts.
That secret gateway to the world of Rudra has been proclaimed,
O lady of excellent complexion, located to the south, beneath Kapileśvara.
[59] Sixty thousand crores and sixty hundred crores of holy places, together with the oceans, will enter Matsyodarī.
Every fortnight, on the fourteenth and eighth days,
the Gaṅgā shall meet Matsyodarī at Kapileśvara in the west.
O Great Goddess, that Yoga arrives, which is very difficult to attain;
O highly fortunate one, bathing during that time bestows the merit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
The majesty of that Liṅga, Kapileśa, has been proclaimed;
it must not be given to anyone and should be guarded with great effort.
"In that very place, the imperishable Brahman is proclaimed as that which is not to be acquired.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of Oṃkāra," in the Kapileśvara-māhātmya of the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa. The Lord said:
Furthermore, I shall declare those who have attained perfection in that place:
the excellent Mahāpāśupatas, my sons of great splendor.
In the past, I was always served by those who were pure and single-minded;
[the place] was free from cold and heat and adorned with palaces.
O Goddess, having constructed the temple of the God with a form even more magnificent than that beautiful residence of the God on the summit of Kailāsa, [he established it].
It is served by those equal to the perfected ones, who are compassionate toward all perfected beings;
then, having attained perfection, one goes first to the state of Nirvana.
In front of Kapileśvara, there is a linga known to face westward;
it was there that the sage Uddālaka attained supreme perfection.
Another linga facing west is situated there, and likewise one facing north;
it was at that linga that the great sage Pārāśarya attained perfection.
[60] Another auspicious [linga] is situated facing west, attached right there.
In that very sanctuary, the great sage Bāṣkali attained perfection.
But situated nearby that very place, facing the east, O beloved,
is where the Pāśupata Siddha, the sage Bhāvavṛtta, resides.
To the west of that very place, O Goddess, there stands a Mukhaliṅga;
there, one named Āruṇi attained spiritual perfection.
To the west of Aruṇīśa, another Liṅga stands;
here resides the great sage, a teacher of the Pāśupata system who has attained perfection through Yoga.
Attached to that very same place, on the right, is an excellent liṅga;
there, O Goddess, the sage named Kaustubha attained perfection.
On its southern side stands a linga facing the east;
there indeed resides the perfected sage Sāvarṇi, the Mahāpāśupata.
In front of it stands a great, auspicious linga facing the east;
in this linga, Śiva himself is personally present.
O lady of excellent vows, I remained there established in the form of the syllable Oṃ;
O illustrious one, four sages attained perfection at that liṅga.
Vāmadeva, Sāvarṇi, Aghora,
and Kapila likewise attained perfection at that liṅga through the power of Nandiśa.
Beneath that deity is a cave venerated by the Siddhas;
it is known as Śrīmukhī and is frequented by those perfected in yoga.
Among them, the Pāśupatas are the most excellent, being devoted to the worship of my liṅga;
for their residence, that cave was created by me.
At its gate, O lady of beautiful hips, dwells the great sage Aghora, a perfected one;
by this very body, that sage attained the state of Rudra.
Having gone there, whether a man or a woman, one should spend three nights with a single-minded focus; such a person shall not enter saṃsāra again.
To the north of the god Aghoreśvara is an excellent well;
by touching its waters, O Goddess, one obtains the merit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa.
The Lord said: O Goddess of the Suras, I shall describe another abode in Vārāṇasī.
Wherein, O blessed lady, he himself always sports visibly.
On the delightful bank of the Matsyodarī, which is honored by gods and siddhas,
I always take pleasure in dwelling in that auspicious sanctuary.
Among all places, O Goddess, those where the Pāśupatas are devoted to the worship of my liṅga are exceedingly delightful and dear to me.
All those sons of mine, endowed with celibacy, peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered anger, have attained perfection there; of this there is no doubt.
One who is attached to the objects of greed and other passions may turn away from hell,
provided they always worship my meritorious emblems here.
In their midst, right there, is indeed a linga facing westward,
renowned by the name Śrīkaṇṭha, located to the south of Kapileśvara.
In that place dwells a perfected Pāśupata known as Kratudhvaja;
by my very grace, he shall attain the sovereign power of yoga.
O auspicious lady, right in front of him stands a linga facing the east;
it was at that linga that Jābāla attained supreme perfection.
Furthermore, there is another linga situated to its south,
named Oṃkāreśvara, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
[62] There, the sage Kālikavṛkṣīya attained supreme accomplishment;
he stands as the most excellent among all accomplished ones.
To the south of that very auspicious place, a linga stands facing west;
it was at that linga that Gārgya, a man of great asceticism, attained perfection.
This, O auspicious one, is the "sixfold abode" (ṣaḍāyatana) which has been explained by me to you;
this most wonderful secret has not been told by me to anyone else.
This is renowned even today as the "Five Brahmas," O beautiful one;
for this reason, O Goddess, it is called the Pañcāyatana.
Whatever meritorious fruit is proclaimed for those belonging to the four stages of life,
that fruit is said to be fully realized simply by beholding the five shrines.
This is the supreme Pāśupata [system] for those practitioners of my vows,
for yogins seeking liberation, which destroys the fear of saṃsāra.
For men of little intelligence whose minds are afflicted by evil,
the supreme medicine is said to be the fivefold supreme refuge.
Therefore, one should always make an effort to behold the five sacred abodes;
O beautiful one, when in the vicinity of the five sacred abodes, a well stands [even] there.
Having sipped water at that well, one shall obtain the fruit of initiation (dīkṣā).
To the south of that place, the abode of Rudra is proclaimed.
To the north of Rudra and to the south of the Pañcāyatana,
there is said to be a great sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that destroys even the most heinous sins.
Having bathed in that pool, a person shall obtain their desired fruit,
when the fourteenth lunar day coincides with the conjunction of the Ārdrā asterism.
Then that time is most meritorious, and the fruit of bathing there is great;
having bathed in that sacred ford and beheld Rudra, O beautiful lady, a man [attains the highest goal].
O Goddess, wherever one dies there, one goes to the world of Rudra;
and I, O Maheśvarī, am present facing eastward within that liṅga.
O auspicious lady, the fruit that one obtains by reciting the Rudra-mantras ten million times is attained simply by the sight of that linga.
Moreover, O fair-hipped one, there are my lingas installed by the sages in the vicinity of Rudra, which grant the fruits of all desires.
To the southwest of Rudra is what is known as Mahālaya;
O beautiful one, from the new moon day, that step of his possesses great fortune.
In that auspicious and beautiful place, Pārvatī herself resides;
and right in front of her, O Goddess, stands a pure well.
The ancestors, both divine and human, reside there;
O beautiful lady, having touched the water in that well and taken it up, [one should offer it].
O Goddess, one who desires my station should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) there;
one should perform the śrāddha rite there with food and water.
O fair-faced one, the funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be cast right there into the well;
having done so at that sacred ford (tīrtha), the Rudramahālaya.
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Rudra;
there is a long pond named Vaitaraṇī, facing the west.
Having bathed in that auspicious place, O lady of beautiful hips, one does not see hell;
and whoever performs repairs there upon what is broken or cracked [is likewise rewarded].
O illustrious lady, his world of Rudra is imperishable for all time;
and to the north of Mahālaya are very great liṅgas.
O beautiful lady, they were established in the western quarter of the Rudrakuṇḍa by all the highly fortunate gods who seek auspiciousness.
There stands a brilliant linga, established for the worship of the deity,
named Bṛhaspatīśvara, which destroys all suffering.
[64] A *liṅga* established by the ancestors stands on the bank to the south of the well;
by its mere worship, the ancestors shall attain satisfaction.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the glorious *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
The Lord said: "O Goddess of the Suras, there is another supreme abode in Kālipurī."
O beautiful one, the god stands to the south of Rudravāsa.
It is renowned as Kāmeśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
indeed, in ancient times, intense austerity was performed there by Kāmadeva.
O Goddess of excellent complexion, both those ponds, filled with lotuses and water-lilies,
are situated on the delightful and supreme bank of that very pool.
O beloved, a divine *liṅga* is situated there, facing west;
it is to be worshipped in every way with perfumes, incense, prostrations, and musical instruments played by the mouth.
Whoever worships me there, I am always pleased with him;
when I am pleased, O Goddess of gods, he shall obtain all his desires.
From that time forward, O one of great asceticism, other preeminent gods as well have been worshipping me at that sacred ford (tīrtha).
Whenever anyone has whatever desire, I grant that very thing to them;
I grant all desires, as well as dharma and liberation.
Therefore, whatever other people are also stationed at that sacred ford,
they always propitiate the Lord of Gods and Kāmeśa.
Thus, whatever desire one has in one's mind, that one certainly attains;
and to the right, O fair-complexioned lady, is the presence of Kāmeśvara.
Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, a person becomes an attendant of Rudra on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra.
Those men who perform ablutions here are like the god Kāma himself;
so too is that man who always worships the Kāmeśvara Liṅga in this world.
In this very way, one will undoubtedly attain the world of the Vidyādharas;
to the east of Kāmeśvara is Pañcālakeśvara by name.
O Goddess of the Suras, I was honored by the son of Dhanada;
knowing that this field was dear to me, he established himself in that region.
He constantly propitiates me and is always devoted to my worship;
I am established in that region under the name Pañcāleśvara.
"O illustrious lady, I shall indeed bestow wealth upon men;
there, O Goddess, stands the Mukhaliṅga facing the east."
O Goddess, I am established there under the name Pañcakeśvara;
and right in front of it is a well that purifies all embodied beings.
O Goddess, stationed in that place under the name Aghoreśī,
you yourself reside there for the benefit of human beings.
Nine secret lingas were indeed established by the Kinnaras;
Divākara and Niśākara are situated to the east of Pañcakeśvara.
Those lingas are meritorious and destroyers of all sins;
they are located to the south of that very place, known by the name Andhakeśa.
There is a great and meritorious linga established by Andhaka;
through my very grace, he has gone to the supreme goal.
O beautiful one, in the western quarter of that deity,
to the south of Kāmakuṇḍa, there is a Liṅga named Deveśvara.
[66] "O auspicious lady, I myself am always established in that very place; Bhīṣmeśvara is right there, and Siddheśvara is beyond that."
Gaṅgeśvara is located right there, as is Yamuneśvara;
Maṇḍaleśvara is also right there, and to the north is the Ūrvaśī-liṅga.
Other lingas have been established there by great-souled beings;
by seeing them, a person shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
In the vicinity of Maṇḍaleśvara stands the Mukhaliṅga;
this auspicious Liṅga, established by Śānta, removes all sins.
In the northwestern direction, near Droṇeśvara,
is the one named Vālakhilyeśvara, who bestows happiness upon all embodied beings.
And that Linga faces west, located to the west of Kāmakuṇḍa;
having beheld Vālakhilyeśvara, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
And right in front of him, O blessed lady, stands a face-liṅga named Vālmīkeśvara; having seen it, one does not grieve.
On the bank of that very Kāmakuṇḍa, a highly meritorious Liṅga was established in ancient times; it was installed there by Cyavana.
O woman of excellent complexion, by the mere sight of Vālakhilyeśvara, located to its south, a man becomes possessed of knowledge.
O Goddess, by seeing that god named Vāteśvara, who destroys all sins, a human being goes to the world of Vāyu.
One should likewise visit Agnīśvara at that very place, as well as Bharateśa,
and Varuṇeśa, who bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
Having seen these, O Great Goddess, one shall attain the desired goal. There is another meritorious sanctuary established by Sanaka.
[67] O Goddess of gods, by beholding the one named Sanakeśvara, who is worshipped by all the Siddhas and immortals, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O lady of excellent complexion, right there to the south is the god named Dharmeśvara,
the lord of Dharma, who bestows the fruits of all desires.
In that very place, there is another linga established by the sages in ancient times,
to the north of Sanakeśvara, known by the name Gurudakeśvara.
O lady of beautiful hips, it was established by Garuḍa for the sake of attaining success;
it was established before the Lord of Garuḍas by the son of Brahmā.
O lady of beautiful countenance, I was established by Sanatkumāra through his devotion;
O Goddess of the gods, by seeing me, a man becomes possessed of knowledge.
And on its northern side is that which was established by Sananda;
by the mere sight of it, the highest siddhi is attained.
To the right side of that very place is established Āsurīśvara,
likewise installed by the high-souled Pañcaśikha.
Not far from its southern side,
situated right there, a face-liṅga was installed by Śanaiścara.
O Goddess, having seen that one named Śanaiśvareśvara, who is honored by all the worlds, a human being is never overcome by diseases.
Moreover, O noble-minded one, there is another great merit in the city of Kāśī;
it is renowned as Mārkaṇḍeya, and it is always dear to me.
To the west of that Liṅga, O illustrious lady,
is the lake named Mārkaṇḍeyahrada, renowned throughout the three worlds.
[68] Having bathed in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, why should one grieve further?
[For there,] bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, ancestral rites, and libations for the ancestors [bear fruit].
All that becomes inexhaustible there; of this there is no doubt.
Having bathed in that pool and having beheld the Four-faced One, a man [attains this].
O illustrious lady, the world of Rudra is forever his, and it is difficult for him to return [to this world] again,
situated to the north in the vicinity of Mārkaṇḍeśvara.
O sinless one, there stands a well, the best of all holy fords;
and to the north of that well, O illustrious lady, is the very center of the pool.
It is renowned as Kuṇḍeśvara, worshipped by all the Siddhas;
having crossed over the Pāśupata initiation, one obtains the fruit which is gained through the twelve-syllable mantra.
O Goddess, one obtains that fruit from Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
On the western bank of the pool stands a west-facing Liṅga.
O Goddess, it was established by Skanda and bestows rebirth in the world of Brahmā;
it is situated not far to the east of Mārkaṇḍeya.
O beautiful one, O auspicious lady, the one named Śāṇḍilyeśvara is situated right there;
that Mukhaliṅga stands facing the west.
O Goddess, having seen that, a person is liberated from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa).
On the right side of this very place, there is one known by the name Bhadreśvara.
There, a linga facing westward was installed by the Brahmanical sages;
by seeing it, O lady of beautiful hips, a man attains the status of a Brahmin.
Moreover, O Great Goddess, I shall explain in due order that which was previously set forth by me for you as Kapālīśa.
[69] I shall describe the lingas located in its southern direction;
there, the Goddess Śrī herself always resides.
It is renowned as Śrīkuṇḍa; in that pool, O fair-faced one, dwells the goddess Kuṇḍeśvarī, the bestower of boons upon all embodied beings.
Having bathed in that pool and beheld the goddess Mahāśrī, a man is never deprived of prosperity; wherever he is born, he remains endowed with it.
To the north of Śrī and to the south of Kapālīśa,
O highly fortunate lady, is the Liṅga installed by Mahālakṣmī.
Facing east,
O Goddess, having bathed in that very pool on its southern side, he shall indeed worship that linga.
Whether it be a man or a woman, hear now the fruit of their merit:
they shall always be surrounded by women with chowries held in their hands.
He remains situated in a magnificent celestial mansion until the dissolution of all beings;
then, when he returns to this world, he becomes endowed with fortune and possessed of beauty.
Endowed with wealth and grain, he is born into a great family;
that is the gateway to the heavenly world, a secret ordained by the gods.
When the gods depart from the world of the gods for Matsyodarī,
he then proceeds with ease by that very same path, surrounded by women.
Therefore, O goddess of great glory, O lady of excellent complexion, she is so addressed.
This secret has been proclaimed to you by me, O goddess.
To the west of that very Viṣṇudhruva stands my own Liṅga, which was installed by the great seer Dadhīca.
O Goddess, having seen that one known by the name Dadhīceśvara, renowned among all the gods and asuras, a person shall attain the world of Īśvara.
To the south of that, it was established there in ancient times by Gāyatrī;
and further to the south of Gāyatrī, it was established by Sāvitrī.
O Goddess, these two lingas facing westward are always dear to me;
and to the east of this one stands a linga facing the east.
O lady of beautiful hips, by beholding Satpatīśvara situated on the delightful bank of the Matsyodarī, one attains supreme perfection.
Behind the Liṅga of Lakṣmī, there stands the west-facing Liṅga of the Lord;
at Ugreśvara, it is greatly meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
O lady of beautiful hips, by seeing that, a man shall become a rememberer of his past births;
O Goddess, to the south of that very place, a great pool is situated.
O illustrious lady, just as merit is said to be gained by bathing at Kanakhala,
a man who bathes in that pool obtains a fruit equal to that.
To the west of Dadhīceśa is the shrine named Dhanadeśvara,
where, O Goddess, penance was performed by the high-souled Dhanada.
There, O Great Goddess, is the pool of the wise Dhanadeśa;
having bathed there, O Goddess, a man beholds Dhanadeśa.
Kubera, being pleased with him, bestowed upon him the status of a deity;
furthermore, other lingas were installed there by gods and asuras.
Having seen those exceedingly meritorious sites, a man shall go to the heavenly world;
to the west of Dhanada is the place named Karavīraka.
By beholding that, O Goddess of gods, a human being attains perfection;
for there, O Supreme Sovereign, reside meritorious lingas.
In its northwestern corner stands a linga facing west,
named Mārīceśvara, which destroys all sins.
And right in front of it, O Goddess, an excellent sacrificial pit has been established;
having bathed there with devotion, a man shines like the sun.
To the west of Mārīceśa is the great Liṅga Indreśvara,
O Goddess, situated on the bank of the pool and facing westward.
To the south of Indreśvara is the pond of Karkoṭaka;
having bathed there in the heroic waters and beheld Karkoṭakeśvara, [one attains merit].
One will undoubtedly attain lordship over the nāgas;
it is situated not far to the south of Karkoṭaka.
There is a place named Dṛmicaṇḍeśvara, which removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
there, a Pāśupata adept known by the name Kauthumi resides.
Having attained the Pāśupata knowledge, he departed from here for the world of Rudra;
there stands the west-facing Liṅga situated to the north of the Kuṇḍa.
A man who stands there in that pool of Dṛmicaṇḍeśvara attains the world of Rudra, having abandoned the ocean of worldly existence.
To its east, O Goddess, on the auspicious bank of the pond,
is the one named Agnīśvara, who causes the destruction of all sins.
O Goddess, having seen that, a man goes to the world of Agni;
indeed, in the eastern quarter of that very place is the shrine named Āmnātakeśvara.
O auspicious one, O woman of excellent complexion, having seen that, a man shall become an attendant of Rudra; know that it is indeed the Single Liṅga (ekaliṅga) and subtle.
Not far to the south of that very Āmnātakeśa is a divine pool originating from him, which bestows the world of the gods.
O Goddess, seeing that one named Urvaśīśvara situated on the ground facing west, a person certainly attains the status of a Gaṇa.
In the south-western quarter of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), not too far away and near Urvaśīśama,
Tālakarṇeśvara is remembered [to be located].
O Goddess, having seen that, a man attains the same world as Caṇḍa;
moreover, Liṅgas have been installed in its very vicinity.
By my hosts who know the Dharma, these excellent and very great [offerings] were made;
O beloved, to its east stands a very large well.
By touching the water in that well, a person becomes purified;
to the east of Caṇḍeśvara stands the auspicious Citreśvara.
O Goddess of the Gods, by seeing that [Liṅga], one attains equality with Citra;
and near Citreśvara stands the great Kāleśvara.
O Goddess of the Gods, by seeing that [Liṅga], one attains equality with Citra;
and near Citreśvara stands the great Kāleśvara.
"By seeing that, O Goddess of gods, a human being cheats death.
The Goddess said:
"How is it that the god Kāleśvara [cheats death], or by what means is the Lord deceived?"
In which place, however, is which Siddha established? Tell me that, O Lord of the Gods.
[73] Īśvara said:
O auspicious lady, in that place in former times there was indeed a sage named Piṅgākṣa,
a proponent of knowledge who stood in this world as a Pāśupata in the fivefold sense.
And by him alone, O blessed lady, was he formerly propitiated at this very liṅga;
then, through the power of the liṅga, the sage eluded death.
No end to time is seen for one whose mind is attached to Īśvara;
having remained there for a very long time, he shall govern all creatures.
Time is indeed unable to overcome him, for he is of terrible form;
and from that time forth, whoever else has remained in that sanctuary [is likewise protected].
Time does not overcome them, even in tens of millions of years.
Moreover, O lady of excellent complexion, I shall tell you another secret.
In front of that deity, O Goddess, there is indeed a well renowned;
there, O Goddess, stands water named Kālodaka.
O Goddess, by consuming that very [water], a human being becomes purified;
as do those men and women who have drunk the water there through their ritual acts.
Marked by the Lord Śarva himself with the sign of the trident,
there shall indeed be no transmigration for them even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Goddess, that which men drink and thereby release from the fear arising from the bonds of existence— this is declared to be the secret known as Kālodaka.
[74] Even those who are great sinners, by the sight of that deity, enjoy all pleasures; for them, worldly existence no longer prevails.
That *liṅga* is proclaimed as the most excellent of all *liṅgas*;
by the sight of that *liṅga*, a human being attains the state of Rudra.
For whatever gift is given there at that lake by those whose souls are devoted to Rudra,
that indeed yields great fruit for those of purified selves who bestow it.
Those men who carry out the repair of what is broken or cracked there reach the world of Rudra and rejoice happily forever.
Having seen the hermitage of Siddhiliṅga destroyed, one should report it to the king,
whether [the destruction] was done by oneself or by others, and however it may have occurred.
Those men are worthy recipients of enjoyments and, in the end, vessels for liberation;
they bestow liberation by means of the *liṅga* through their desire for the fulfillment of their purpose.
Those who, being addicted to accepting gifts from kings, honor artificial [deities],
are utterly consumed by the curse of Rudra and fall into hell with certainty.
Furthermore, those who perform worship and honor the temples of the Siddhas according to their own ability are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the man who causes a city to be built for Kāleśvara shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Whatever worship, recitation, or fire-offering is performed there at the Lord of Time (Kāleśa),
by the offering of a lamp therein, a person shall obtain the eye of knowledge.
Those who perform a vigil (jāgara) before Kāleśa himself attain that station frequented by Rudra through the offering of incense. [75]
Having died, O blessed lady, they became like Rudra— mounted upon bulls, with tridents in their hands and three eyes— and they went to the world of Rudra.
O Goddess, what need is there for much speaking here? Whatever is performed at this time, O Goddess, all that becomes inexhaustible in birth after birth.
All this has been recounted to you by me once again in detail;
it has not been told to anyone here and must be guarded with great effort.
The auspicious sanctuary of the god Śiva Kāleśvara is located near Kāleśvara,
to the south, O lady of excellent complexion.
The Liṅga established by Mṛtyu, which destroys all diseases, is located on the northern side of the well; there are great Liṅgas there, O lady of excellent vows.
One is named Dakṣeśvara and the second is Kaśyapeśvara;
that linga which faces west is known by the name Dakṣeśvara.
To the east of Dakṣeśvara stands Mahākāla;
having performed his ablution in the pool, the man who worships Mahākāla [attains the fruit].
O lady of beautiful hips, by him this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has been worshipped;
likewise, on the southern side, on the bank of that very pool.
A divine *liṅga* was established by the great-souled Antaka;
one obtains great fruit from the sight of that *liṅga*.
In the vicinity of Antakeśvara, a linga stands to the south;
it is named Śakreśvara and was installed by the elephant of Indra.
[76] To the south of that very place is the supreme Mātalīśvara,
established by Mātali, which bestows all happiness.
O lady of beautiful countenance, there is a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) in the pool in front of the God;
O beautiful woman, it is situated in the pool before Hastipāleśvara.
O blessed lady, there where Antaka, the bringer of death, formerly performed penance,
stands the east-facing Liṅga of Hastīśvara, situated to the east [of that place].
O lady of excellent complexion, to the north of Mahākāla is the pool named Vijayeśvara, which is worshipped by gods and siddhas.
O Pārvatī, I was propitiated by Vālin at that place;
it is known as Balikuṇḍa in Vārāṇasī, which is dear to me.
To the east of that pool, Bali installed a linga.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa. Likewise:
"The Rudras who are proclaimed as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyāvighneśvaras) and those who are called Śivas."
Where Kṛttivāseśvara is, there all are established.
In that place, the great Daitya, having become an elephant,
quickly tore open its hide— his own elephant-form which possessed the splendor of his father.
O great sage, because I formerly dwelt there clothed in animal skins, I am therefore called Kṛttivāsas; and I remain stationed in that place, Avimukta.
In the Dāruvana forest, there is a secret linga worshipped by hosts of sages;
I am stationed in that sanctuary, facing westward.
The auspicious Antakeśvara Liṅga is situated before me;
to my north, however, a Liṅga was installed by Śakra’s elephant.
The Mātalīśvara Liṅga is situated to my south,
while to my east is a well endowed with various supernatural powers.
Furthermore, the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* are established therein; likewise,
those Pāśupatas who are situated there in the presence of Madhyameśvara.
And for the sake of favoring them, the one clad in animal skins (Kṛttivāsas) stood there in ancient times.
The body of the Rudras is indeed Madhyameśvara, the Lord;
Kṛttivāsas is Śiva—this they say is my most profound secret.
And many other perfected ones and sages are established there;
with their minds fixed on my nature, they worship me constantly.
Those people who dwell there in Vārāṇasī are liberated;
even worms and insects, as well as those who have committed great sins, are liberated.
O Brahmin, by the mere remembrance of the Liṅga, sin is indeed reduced to ashes.
Likewise, those endowed with auspiciousness who worship the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga...
Having entered the body of Rudra, they shall not be born again.
With this very body, supreme nirvāṇa has been attained;
there are many sacred sites there, such that it is impossible to count them.
O Sage, ten thousand crores of sacred fords are indeed located right here;
wherever Kṛttivāseśvara is situated, there they all abide.
In that liṅga, however, there is a presence at the three times of day; of this there is no doubt.
It has been made by me unmanifest even to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods.
There, many sacred fords (tīrthas) were established by numerous twice-born ones—
by highly fortunate sages such as Pulastya and others, and by great-souled ones such as Lomaśa and others.
"The gods and demons do not know the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga.
Bhṛgu said:
"In the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, [they do not know] the Supreme Lord."
It is the great secret, the secret beyond secrets, which enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
O Lord of Gods, for what reason has this Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga, which is situated in Avimukta, not been revealed by you?
Īśvara said: Ten thousand crores [of beings] arrive day after day,
devoid of righteous deeds and bereft of truth and purity.
Constantly reviling the gods, the twice-born, and their gurus, devoid of devotion,
they are possessed by illusion and delusion, and filled with hypocrisy and infatuation.
[79] The Brahmins who were devoted to the food of Śūdras, agitated and longing for sensual pleasure—
all of them, having reached Kṛttivāseśvara, became free from their feverish distress.
Freed from the fear of saṃsāra and devoid of all evil,
they attain liberation with ease, just like those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Mounted upon divine celestial chariots resounding with the tinkling of small bells,
they go to the world of the gods, attaining the supreme state.
Liberation may or may not be obtained after a thousand previous births;
however, it is attained there at Kṛttivāsa in a single lifetime.
By the sight of that linga, the sin committed in a previous birth is destroyed;
there, a face-linga named Siddheśvara is situated.
And situated to the north of the god Antakeśvara is the abode of all the Siddhas; that place is supreme and great.
The imperishable, eternal, divine, stainless abode of Brahman;
established in the form of Śakti, peaceful, auspicious, and the supreme cause.
The unmanifest, eternal, subtle, subtler than the subtle, and great. Likewise,
the Lord said:
In the Kali age, this site of the Dāruvana forest is proclaimed as the place of the Lord;
it is that mutual knowledge which bestows the path to liberation.
O tiger among the twice-born, it is attained at Kṛttivāsa; of this there is no doubt.
Tryambaka is said to be for the Kṛta age, while Kṛttivāsas is for the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, the name of the god is celebrated as Māheśvara;
in the Kali age, it is celebrated by the Siddhas as Hastipāleśvara.
In ancient times, Śambhu, the God of gods, assuming the very form of a staff-bearer (Daṇḍin),
bestowed his grace upon the twice-born at that sacred place.
In age after age, however, the Brahmins who know reality and possess tranquil minds constantly worship me and recite the Śatarudriya.
O Brahmins, those devotees who recite the Rudrādhyāya in that sacred field until the fall of their bodies become Śiva himself, clad in animal skins.
The Lord is always pleased with them and bestows divine worlds upon those Rudras whom I previously recited at Śaṅkukarṇālaya.
They remain in Kṛttivāsa, which is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
That which is the gateway for the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is known as their dwelling place.
Likewise:
"The dark men, the fierce ones, those like lightning, and those yellowish-brown;
those who are bodiless and those who possess bodies—they too were created by me in the past."
They have blue throats, white faces, lips like the bimba fruit, and matted hair;
they have green hair, possess horns, have hanging lips, and wield sharp weapons.
Incalculable numbers have been enumerated, as well as thousands of others;
they all reside in Avimukta in the vicinity of Kṛttivāsa.
Among the Rudras, Śiva is to be known as the supreme Kṛttivāseśvara;
impelled by him, they go [there], which is difficult to reach for those of unrefined self.
[81] Having understood that this human condition is impermanent and fraught with much evil,
one should dwell in Avimukta and recite the Śatarudriya.
The god Kṛttivāseśvara should be beheld again and again,
if one desires the eternal, death-bestowing knowledge that grants immortality.
All this must be performed if one desires my state.
Likewise: "The self-existent Vināyaka, who has the face of an elephant, dwells here."
And Kūṣmāṇḍarāja, Śambhu, Jayanta, and Madotkaṭa.
Some had the faces of lions and tigers, while others were hideous, hunchbacked, or dwarfed;
there Nandin, Mahākāla, Citraghaṇṭa, and Maheśvara resided.
Dṛmicaṇḍeśvara, Ghaṇṭākarṇa of great strength,
and these and many other hosts indeed belong to Rudreśvara.
All of them constantly guard my house, which is indeed never forsaken;
my northern path, however, is to be known as Dṛmicaṇḍeśvara.
My southern Śaṅkukarṇa is my Oṃkāra Viṣuva;
ten crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) enter it during the festival.
The secret of the Brahmin mantras must be guarded with great effort;
and that which is called the Pāśupata state, when properly cultivated.
By worshipping it, one attains that very state within six months;
for there is always incomparable joy for me in that sanctuary.
And there, O lady of good vows, are many other perfected lingas;
yet among all those places, that place of mine is the most preeminent.
Having recognized the terrible Kali age, I have made this [teaching] non-public;
that goal is not attained through sacrifices, gifts, ablutions at sacred fords, or even through fierce austerities.
And by various other auspicious qualities,
those who have conquered their senses [attain] Kṛttivāsa.
Likewise: By the sight of the God of gods, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated;
by touching and worshipping him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
Those who, with supreme faith and concentrated minds, worship the eternal God on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna;
With flowers, fruits, and various other kinds of food, both high and low;
with milk, honey, water, and likewise with clarified butter.
They satisfy the supreme Liṅga and worship the auspicious God with shouts of "Huḍuṅkāra," prostrations, as well as with dance and song.
Having fasted for one night with supreme devotion toward Hara, [one should worship] with many musical instruments as well as hymns and mantras.
Indeed, those beings who go to the supreme abode, the ever-auspicious and stainless state,
should worship the Supreme Lord during the month of Caitra.
Having reached the city of the Lord of Wealth, he shall sport like the king of the Yakṣas—
he who, being self-restrained, worships Śiva on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
Having reached the world of Vaiśākha, he shall become an attendant of that very deity;
so too for one who worships Hara with faith on the fourteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
He who worships the Lord of the Gods on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Śuci attains the world of Agni as long as the moon and stars endure.
He who worships the Kāmaliṅga on the fourteenth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa shall sport most happily in the world of the Sun for as long as he desires.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara during the month of Bhādrapada, he goes to the world of Varuṇa and sports together with the Apsarases.
By worshipping Maheśvara on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors with various flowers and fruits, one attains the same world as Rudra.
Having reached the world of the ancestors, he sports there, honored by them;
for having worshipped Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, during the month of Prabhava.
Having worshipped the wielder of the Pināka bow during the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, he attains the world of the Moon and sports there for as long as he desires.
Having worshipped Sthāṇu with a contented mind under the Puṣya asterism, one attains the world of Viṣṇu and sports there for an imperishable time.
He attains the abode of Nairṛta and indeed rejoices there with him,
having worshipped [the deity] in the month of Māgha with auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits.
Having abandoned the ocean of saṃsāra, he indeed attains the world of Śiva;
one should worship the god Kṛttivāseśvara with great effort.
And one must dwell in Avimukta if one desires my state;
indeed, the Siddhas sing these songs:
"Blessed are those men who dwell in Avimukta!"
Those who have sought refuge in Kṛttivāsas, the sign of the state of heaven and liberation.
Likewise,
the Lord said: "O fair-faced one, there is another meritorious sanctuary in the city of Kāśī."
In ancient times, Dhanvantari was born in the auspicious palace of the King of Kāśī.
Therefore, O auspicious and virtuous lady, at that time I was propitiated by you;
there stands my own liṅga named Bhṛṅgīśeśvara.
I stood facing westward, and a well was before me;
there all the medicinal herbs, born of nectar, were situated.
O beautiful one, O Maheśvarī, in former times that place was cast [there] by the King of Physicians; therefore, it is called Vaidyanātha.
O Goddess, those men who drink the water in that well are completely liberated from diseases through the power of Vaidyanātha.
And on the northern side of the well is the one named Harikeśvara;
by the sight of Harikeśvara, people are also liberated from diseases.
[85] O lady of excellent complexion, near Tuṅgeśa, to the south,
there is the auspicious Śaiva lake said to be presided over by Śiva.
O lady of excellent vows, I am situated there on the delightful western shore;
O auspicious one, I remain established in that place facing the west.
Known as Śiveśvara, he is the bestower of boons upon his devotees;
it is situated not very far to the south of Śiveśvara.
A linga facing west was installed by Jamadagni;
it is situated not very far to the west of the Jamadagni-linga.
Renowned as Bhairaveśvara and saluted by gods and demons,
Durgā resides there, O auspicious lady, who is indeed terrifying even to me.
As that goddess danced in the vicinity of the Liṅga,
she beheld Bhairaveśa and would not fall into saṃsāra again.
To the north of that very Bhairaveśa stands a well;
by performing ablutions there, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
O beautiful lady, in the western part of the well stands a Linga known as Śukeśvara, which was installed by the son of Vyāsa.
O Goddess, seeing that, even a human being attains dispassion;
and on its northern side stands a pond.
Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, a man shall have fulfilled his purpose;
and in the southwestern quarter, O beautiful one, is the shrine of Śukeśa.
A face-linga was also installed by the great seer Vyāsa;
it is renowned as Vyāseśvara and is worshipped by hosts of sages.
Having bathed in Vyāsakuṇḍa and having worshipped the gods and the ancestors,
a man obtains inexhaustible worlds wherever he desires them.
To the west, O illustrious lady, near Vyāsatīrtha,
is the pool named Ghaṇṭākarṇahrada, which bestows all happiness.
Having bathed in that lake and beheld Vyāsa himself,
one becomes as if dead in Vārāṇasī, whether one dies anywhere else or there.
There, O Goddess, having cast off the body, one shall attain the state of a Gaṇeśvara;
specifically to the north, near Ghaṇṭākarṇa, O illustrious lady.
The merit of the Apsarases is renowned as being fashioned by Pañcacūḍā;
having bathed in the lake of Pañcacūḍā and beheld that Lord, one gains that merit.
A man who is always devoted to Pañcacūḍā goes to the heavenly world;
and to the north of that place is situated the Aśoka grove.
There, situated in the midst of an Ashoka grove, is a pool of auspicious water;
having bathed in that pool, a man becomes truly visible.
And to the north of Viloka is the auspicious river named Mandākinī;
she is meritorious in the heavenly world, how much more so in the auspicious world of men!
O Goddess, O beautiful one, wherever the presence of the God of gods is always found, there,
in the midst of that sacred field, is a self-manifested linga.
Likewise,
the Lord said: "Having bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī and having beheld Madhyameśvara..."
Endowed with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall dwell for a long time in the world of Rudra.
[87] This, indeed, is what the ancestors and grandfathers have always declared:
even he who is born in this family and has emerged from the waters of the Mandākinī.
The wise man should feed the Brahmins, the ascetics, and the Pāśupatas;
for bathing, giving gifts, austerity, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors [bear fruit only when done for them].
The offering of funeral cakes and all other rites likewise become inexhaustible;
I have thus clearly explained to you this field in brief.
On the southern portion of the ground belonging to Madhyameśa,
there is a linga facing east, installed by the Viśvedevas.
The Lord of Gods is indeed facing westward, installed by Vīrabhadra;
by beholding him facing westward, one attains the same world as Vīrabhadra.
To the south of those two, O Goddess, is known the lake of Bhadrakālī;
it was established by Śaunaka on the western bank of the pool.
The linga named Mataṅgeśvara stands right there;
that linga faces the east and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O illustrious lady, in the north-western corner of Mataṅgeśvara,
there are lingas installed by high-souled men.
On its very southern side, it was established by Jayanta,
the son of the King of the Gods, desiring victory for himself.
[88] And Brahmatāreśvara is indeed in that place, O Sovereign of the Gods;
there, a *liṅga* was installed by the Pitṛs and by Yājñavalkya.
To the southern quarter of that [place], Siddhikūṭa is proclaimed.
There, the Siddhas and Pāśupatas are devoted to the worship of my liṅga.
For them, this peak there is indeed the Peak of Siddhas; it is perfected for them.
There, some are devoted to meditation, while others perform recitation.
Some perform the private recitation of sacred texts, others perform austerities;
some sleep in the open air, while others have taken refuge in pure being.
Likewise, others remain with their faces turned downward; others still subsist on smoke;
some perform circumambulations, while others observe silence like a piece of wood.
Others likewise perform the fetching of flowers for the *gaḍūkas*;
by all of them, intent upon worship and adoration, the *liṅga* was installed.
Having perceived their devotion there at that time toward the God of virtuous vows,
I established my presence here out of a desire to bestow grace upon them.
The auspicious Siddheśvara, renowned as the remover of all sins,
is that linga facing eastward, situated on Siddhakūṭa.
Indeed, I am stationed in that place for the welfare of human beings;
O beautiful one, there is a pond situated to the west of the deity.
Having bathed there in the water of the step-well and beheld Siddheśvara,
whatever impurity from the remains of offerings (nirmālya) has entered this sacred field is thereby removed.
[89] All that goes to dissolution by the sight of Siddheśvara.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the Vārāṇasī-māhātmya of the Śrī-liṅga Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
To the east of Siddhakūṭa stands the deity facing west,
renowned as Vyāghreśvara, who is praised by all the gods, O auspicious one.
By beholding him, one attains the supreme, imperishable state;
and to the south of Vyāghreśvara, the Self-Existent One (Svayaṃbhū) resides there.
The divine Liṅga situated there is difficult even for the gods to attain;
it is the secret of all the deities, having arisen by piercing through the earth.
By seeing, worshipping, and praising that sign,
O Goddess, one becomes one who has accomplished his purpose and shall not enter into saṃsāra again.
That auspicious Jyeṣṭhasthāna is indeed a linga facing east;
for the benefit of human beings, I am established in that very place.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the Mukhaliṅga stands before it;
O Goddess of auspicious gaze, Pañcacūḍā stands facing west behind it.
On its right side is the one named Prahasiteśvara;
by seeing him, O Goddess, one attains the bliss of the state of Brahman.
To the north of that, O Goddess of gods, is the meritorious Liṅga established by you,
renowned among all yogins as Nivāsa.
O Goddess, by seeing that, one attains the Yoga of Śaṅkara;
O beautiful one, there stands a well renowned as the Four Oceans.
O auspicious one, whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing in the four oceans,
all that fruit belongs to him simply from touching the water.
There itself, O Great Goddess, you shall take delight with me;
and those men who, endowed with devotion, shall worship you.
For them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, to the north of the well and to the south of Vyāghreśa...
O beautiful one, a linga indeed stands there, facing the east.
Known as Daṇḍīśvara, the bestower of boons upon all embodied beings—
by beholding him, the imperishable state of lordship is attained.
To the north of that, O Goddess, is a lake renowned everywhere;
it was there, O Sovereign of the Gods, when [the Ganges] became enraged by the salutation at twilight.
Having manifested his many forms, Hara himself, the God of gods,
then cast that radiant Daṇḍaka before the gods.
By him, a divine lake was created there, world-renowned;
yet the Goddess, out of anger, set out toward the Snowy Mountain.
Right there before him was a great and wonderful lake;
having seen it, O Goddess, she then turned back once again.
Having entered the palace, O Goddess of gods, O beautiful lady, she remained right there;
by the staff of the God of gods standing there, a very great lake was formed.
Those people who are knowers of the ancient lore call it Daṇḍakhāta;
therefore, one desiring the highest good should perform a ritual bath right there.
O Goddess, having bathed there, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose;
having bathed in Daṇḍakhāta and offered libations to his own ancestors, a man [attains the same].
But those who dwell in hell, O Goddess, and those who reside in the world of the ancestors,
as well as those men who have attained the state of a piśāca due to their sinful deeds;
It is taught that by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) to them, one effects the salvation of their bodies;
having bathed at Daṇḍakhāta, why should a man grieve further?
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of it, or by the sight of Daṇḍakhāta, the cage of the multitude of sins is shattered into a hundred pieces.
O highly illustrious one, hear the majesty and merit of that Daṇḍa;
O Goddess of gods, O lady of excellent vows, men come there during a solar eclipse.
Kurukṣetra is greatly meritorious and is saluted by all the gods;
O Goddess, when an eclipse has ended, there is no place superior to Kurukṣetra.
They come to the Daṇḍakhāta for the purpose of purifying themselves;
by the mere sight of that pool, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
O Goddess Maheśvarī, there is another sacred site for me there,
established by that great-souled one under the name Jaigīṣavyeśvara.
In that cave of Jaigīṣavya, in the presence of the God of gods,
he worshipped the Liṅga with devotion at the three times of day, his soul purified by that [devotion].
Thus propitiated by the wise Jaigīṣavya, O Goddess,
I was questioned by him and granted all his desires.
Therefore, O Goddess, for those men who worship the well-fashioned *liṅga*,
knowledge will certainly arise for them on this earth before long.
Indeed, that man who performs a three-night rite there and offers worship shall enter the secret [state], and that man shall become endowed with knowledge.
To its west is indeed Siddhakūpa,
and to the south is that Liṅga facing eastward, which was installed by Devala.
O Goddess of the gods, by beholding that, a man becomes possessed of knowledge;
and situated near it is [the shrine] established for a hundred kalpas.
O auspicious and virtuous lady, not far from that place in the southern direction is a face-liṅga, facing westward.
And the great seer established the shrine named Śātātapeśvara;
by beholding it, one attains the desired and eternal goal.
In its western quarter stands a great liṅga named Hetukeśvara, which bestows the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments.
On its very southern side stands the Mukhaliṅga,
known by the name Kaṇādeśvara, situated facing the west.
In ancient times, the perfected sage Kaṇāda resided nearby;
there is a well situated close by that bestows merit upon all embodied beings.
To the south of Kaṇādeśa is another beautiful sanctuary;
there is Bhūtīśa, facing west, who destroys all sins.
On its very western side stands a linga facing west;
that linga has four faces and is renowned by the name Āṣāḍha.
Other great liṅgas were also installed there;
however, to the east of them is the liṅga that was established long ago by the Daitya.
O Goddess of the Gods, by seeing that deity Bhārabhūteśvara situated there to the south, a man becomes possessed of sons.
O beloved, that Bhārabhūteśvara Liṅga faces west;
situated to the east of Vyāseśvara, the Liṅga stands facing west.
That which was established by the sage Parāśara out of devotion to me stands facing west;
indeed, it remains as a Mukhaliṅga surrounded by the gods.
O blessed lady, that Liṅga, which bestows all the scriptures, was installed by Atri, who was devoted to me, and it faces the west.
To the east of Vyāseśvara, O lady of excellent vows, two lingas were installed there by Śaṅkha and Likhita, O Goddess of the lords of gods.
O auspicious lady, having seen these two, a man shall attain the world of the ṛṣis;
and there is another secret place of the God of gods, O illustrious one.
The Liṅga named Viśveśvara is worshipped by all the gods;
by beholding it, one obtains the fruit of the Pāśupata vow.
O beautiful one, in the north-eastern direction of that deity,
there is a great sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Avadhūta, which removes all sins.
Attached to its east is the shrine named Paśupatīśvara;
by the mere sight of it, one does not go to a birth as an animal.
That four-faced liṅga stands facing the west;
on its southern side stands a five-faced liṅga.
It was established, O blessed lady, by the high-souled seer Gobhila;
having seen it, O Goddess, a human being goes to the world of the seers.
To the west of that very place, O Goddess, there stands a linga facing westward,
which was established by Jīmūtavāhana, the lord of the Vidyādharas.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa.
The Lord said: "O Goddess, my beloved, there is another abode of mine in Vārāṇasī."
The linga named Gabhastīśvara is situated facing west.
O auspicious one, it was indeed established by Sūrya, who is devoted to me;
O illustrious lady, my presence is always truly present within it.
O Goddess, having assumed the Īśāna form, wherever I am stationed, a human being who beholds that place shall attain the world of Īśāna.
To its right side stands the Dadhikarṇa lake, and to its north is a well, O beautiful one; such are the names of these places belonging to him.
The god Dadhikarṇeśvara and Mukhaliṅga are situated there;
O Goddess of gods, they face the east, to the north of Gabhastīśa.
O lady of virtuous vows, to the south of Gabhastīśa, in the direction of Varuṇa,
you are established there for the benefit of human beings.
O Goddess, those who propitiate you while standing facing north,
and those who worship you in that place— there indeed do I abide.
To those who keep a vigil before you while holding lamps, you shall grant various worlds, and they shall rejoice.
O beautiful lady, O woman of excellent complexion, you shall bestow inexhaustible worlds upon those who establish a dwelling for your sake.
To those who make a dwelling place and sweep the ground, you undoubtedly grant inexhaustible worlds.
O Goddess, he who, with you in mind, [honors] both Brahmins and Brahmin women, shall obtain the fruit of eight thousand pieces of gold.
O Goddess, hear the fruit of merit for him who shall feed [you]:
he shall dwell in your world for an eon and then return here once again.
Whether a man or a woman, endowed with all enjoyments and possessed of wealth and grain, they are born into a great family.
O Goddess, may they both be fortunate and handsome, proud of their beauty and youth, and become such that they are partakers of every happiness.
Having obtained a human birth, which is difficult to attain and as fleeting as a flash of lightning—
he who has beheld you, O lady of beautiful hips, from where could he have any fear of rebirth?
O Goddess of gods, whatever fruit one obtains by beholding Lalitā in the city of Māyāpurī,
that same fruit belongs to him who gazes upon you there.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by circumambulating the entire earth, that same fruit is obtained at Lalitā and in Vārāṇasī; of this there is no doubt.
By that, your name shall become renowned; likewise, one who gazes upon the face—having seen such a face-gazer—shall obtain supreme good fortune.
O Goddess, he who, having fasted at that time on the fourth day of the month of Māgha, worships and performs a vigil there;
O Goddess, his family becomes possessed of supernatural power and becomes difficult to find even in the three worlds;
furthermore, there are two famous lingas there known as Sukhaprekṣa and Uttara.
O Goddess, both Vṛtreśvara and Tvaṣṭreśvara face westward;
the merit that a man obtains by giving the golden earth is attained there.
O woman of excellent complexion, whatever merit is gained from beholding two golden lingas, that same merit is obtained by one who stays right there for three nights.
His world shall be Gaurī’s eternal realm, from which return is difficult to obtain;
therefore, one should always exert effort with the desire to behold all things.
To the north of Lalitā is the auspicious one presided over by Carcikā;
for the benefit of human beings, she grants boons to all embodied beings.
Likewise, O Goddess, the supreme linga stands before Carcikā;
it faces the east and was installed by Revanta.
O lady of excellent hips, in front of that is the Liṅga Pañcanadīśvara;
it faces west, O Goddess, and bestows the fruit of all ritual ablutions.
To the east of Lalitā, there stands a well;
by touching the water in that well, one obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Then, O Goddess, to the south is the sacred ford known as Pañcanada;
having bathed at Pañcanada and beheld the Liṅga of Gabhasti, a man [attains merit].
[97] One obtains infinite fruit wherever one is born;
likewise, O fair-hipped lady, Upamanyu established a *liṅga*.
O illustrious goddess, his faces are situated upon that linga;
and it faces westward, O goddess, to the south of Lilita.
O Goddess of gods, by beholding that, one shall not be subject to rebirth;
and right there, O lady of excellent complexion, in its western vicinity—
Moreover, O lady of beautiful hips, there is another linga established by Vyāghrapāda;
by the sight of it, O goddess, one is liberated from all sins.
O Goddess, in front of Gabhastīśa is the [liṅga] established by Viśvakarman;
other liṅgas have also been installed there by great-souled ones.
O lady of excellent complexion, to the southwest of the Gabhastīśa Liṅga stands the Liṅga named Śaśāṅkeśvara, facing the east.
O Goddess of the gods, by going to Gandharvanagara and beholding it with King Citraratha, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
To the west of Citreśvara stands a linga facing west;
it was formerly established by Jaimini and is the destroyer of great sins.
At the head, however, was the Liṅga established by Sumantu for the Lord Jaimini,
and there were also very many other Liṅgas erected there by other sages.
To the south of them stands the Budheśvara Liṅga, facing west; likewise, located in the corner, it bestows all forms of happiness.
[98] To the northwest, at a short distance from Budheśvara,
there is the one named Rāvaṇeśvara, established by the Rākṣasa.
To the east of Rāvaṇeśvara, O Goddess, is the four-faced Liṅga;
by beholding it, O Queen of the Gods, one is not slain by the Yātudhānas.
To the south of Rāvaṇeśa stands a linga facing the east,
named Varāheśvara, which destroys all sins.
To the south of Varāheśa stands a linga facing the east;
by worshipping it alone, O Goddess, one shall attain yoga within six months.
To the south of that place is a Linga facing the south,
named Gālaveśvara, which bestows devotion to the Guru.
The Liṅga of the deity Gālaveśvara is situated facing west;
it is named Ayogasiddhi and bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
O Goddess, to the south of that very place is the auspicious Vāteśvara by name;
and right in front of it, O Goddess, stands the Mukhaliṅga.
There stands the Linga renowned as Someśvara, facing the west;
by beholding that Lord of the gods of gods, all diseases shall be destroyed.
To the southwest of that very place stands a linga facing the east,
named Aṅgāreśvara, which is saluted by all the Siddhas.
To the east of that deity stands another linga named Kukkuṭeśvara, which bestows happiness upon one's state of existence.
And further north of that very place, O Goddess, are five meritorious lingas facing westward, established by the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.
O Goddess of the gods, for them this linga named Saṃvarteśvara, which was installed by the great seer, stands facing the west.
O Goddess of the Suras, my very presence is constant within that linga;
indeed, for whoever worships that linga, spiritual perfection rests in the palm of their hand.
To the west of Saṃvarteśa stands the Liṅga known as Śveteśvara, facing eastward; it was established in ancient times by Śveta.
By seeing that sign, one will certainly attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
In its western direction is the one known as Kalaśeśvara.
The Liṅga, which arose from the pitcher and was terrifying to Time (Kāla), [was seen].
Sūrya said:
"How does it cause fear to Kāla? How did it arise from the pitcher?"
O Lord, please explain this to me, since you are so gracious toward me.
Viṣṇu said:
O Bhāskara, hear of the power of that very God of gods.
There was a most righteous sage of great splendor named Śveta.
He constantly worshipped the linga of the destroyer of Tripura;
while he was thus intent on worship, after some time had passed, [an event occurred].
Then arrived that most dreadful time—
a great and terrible figure with blood-red eyes, holding a staff of snakes in his hand.
[100] Terrifying with his fangs, deformed, with a luster like crushed collyrium,
clad in red garments, massive-bodied, and adorned with all ornaments.
Then, approaching Śveta with noose in hand, he cast the noose around him;
with the noose placed upon his neck, Śveta then spoke to Kāla.
Wait but a moment, O Destroyer of the Three Worlds,
while I complete my worship of the Enemy of Manmatha.
Then Kāla, smiling, said to the Lord of the Gods:
"I think you have not heard that which has been told by the elders who know the origin of things."
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not.
Whether in the womb, or in childhood, in old age, or likewise in youth—
when the life-span and its activities are exhausted, this world dissolves into me.
Neither the hymns of the Nishadhas, nor sacred mantras, nor burnt offerings,
nor even victory can protect human beings when they are overtaken by death or old age.
Many thousands of Indras and hundreds of Pitāmahas have passed away because of me; therefore, O sinless one, you should not feel resentment in this matter.
Perform the worship of this Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident;
O Śveta, I have indeed performed many kinds of the ritual placement of the deities within the body.
I am not my own master, nor is my course dependent on my own will;
for no being that has come into existence can escape destruction through the power of karma.
"O Three-eyed One, I have been impelled by the Creator according to the course of karma; being led along, I tread upon and carry away everything."
Thus addressed by Kāla, while being led away, he went with his whole being for refuge to Trilocana, who is compassionate toward his devotees.
When Śveta had sought refuge, the Lord of the Gods contemplated a means for the destruction of Kāla and the Liṅga that brought about the end of the three cities.
Having broken that jar which stood there, filled with water,
he rose up with eyes wide open in rage.
Then Kāla was seen by him merely with a glance; the three worlds were illuminated by the flame from his third eye, and [Kāla] was consumed by the splendor of that gaze.
Suddenly reduced to ashes, that destroyer of all beings approached Śveta and likewise attained the status of a Gaṇeśa.
Having brought about the restraint of Kāla, he vanished right there;
from that time forward, O Goddess of the Gods, Kāla began to reckon the lifespan of all creatures.
Because of his bodiless state, no one in the three worlds beholds him;
therefore, there the self-born God of gods, the slayer of the enemies of the Suras, resides.
Having pierced the jar of Śveta, it is called Kalaśeśvara;
therefore, whatever man gazes upon the deity situated there, [attains his desire].
O beautiful lady, birth, death, old age,
and disease are destroyed for that man who worships with devotion the Linga fashioned by Śveta.
"Having pierced through the fear of birth and death, one shall not enter saṃsāra again.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the *Vārāṇasī-māhātmya* of the glorious *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
[102] Īśvara said:
To the north of that deity stands Citragupteśvara.
O Goddess of the gods, the Lord faces westward in Vārāṇasī.
The man who sees Citragupta here shall not behold him again;
O auspicious one, another linga of Citragupta stands at the western side.
Having seen that Liṅga established by Chāyā, one shall not experience the heat of the sun;
and Vināyaka is right there to the west, O illustrious lady.
Merely by the sight of it, one is never overcome by obstacles.
To its east is the sacrificial pit, and the Linga is situated facing west.
O Goddess, O beloved, that very Virūpākṣa is a self-manifested face-liṅga;
to its south, O beautiful lady, there stands a well.
By beholding that well, one does not see the gateway of Yama;
and the well situated there bestows the merit of ritual ablution.
There are other lingas established there by the gods as well;
to the south of Kalaśeśa stands a linga facing west.
Known by the name Guheśvara, it bestows the fruit of all merit;
on its very southern side, these two are situated there.
Beyond that is Vāmadeva, named Uttameśvara;
O Goddess, to the west of that very place stands a linga facing the west.
The Kambalāśvatarākṣa [Liṅga], which bestows the status of a Gandharva,
is another Liṅga of that deity situated facing west.
The one named Nalakūbareśvara bestows all spiritual accomplishments;
O Goddess, to the south of that very place is the renowned Maṇikarṇī.
And before it is a great sacred site that destroys all sins;
there stands the deity Maṇikarṇīśvara in the middle of the pool.
Indeed, by the mere sight of it, one attains perfection even with this very body;
and to the north of that place stands a linga facing westward.
By worshipping the one named Parameśvara, one becomes free from old age;
and near him stands a linga situated facing west.
O lady of beautiful hips, the destroyer of sins was established there by Dharmarāja;
O Goddess, to the west of that very place is another four-faced Liṅga.
There is a supreme destroyer of diseases named Nirjareśvara;
in its southwest corner stands a linga facing the east.
And the grandfathers of immense bodies, who had performed auspicious deeds and bathed,
offered the funeral cakes and likewise spoke after beholding the Lord, the Master of the River.
Those meritorious ones never fall from the world of Brahmā;
moreover, another linga of that deity stands to its south.
Indeed, the one named Vāruṇeśvara was established by Varuṇa;
on its southern side stands a linga facing the west.
O Goddess, to the south of that very place where it was installed with devotion by Bāṇa, the king of the Daityas,
there stands a west-facing Liṅga.
O Goddess, to the east of that very place is the one named Kūṣmāṇḍeśvara, who bestows the fruits of all dharmas, and was installed by a Rākṣasa.
On its right side,
however, was established by Gaṅgā the one known by the name Gaṅgeśvara, which bestows the world of the gods.
To the north of that, O Goddess of gods, O auspicious and illustrious one, Liṅgas were then established here on the bank of the Gaṅgā by the rivers.
Having seen the one named Vaivasvateśvara, which removes the fear of death,
there stands to the west of Vaisvata a linga facing the west.
O auspicious lady, it was established by the Ādityas seeking their own spiritual welfare;
and right in front of it, O auspicious lady, stands a linga facing westward.
The one known by the name Vajreśvara destroys all sins;
O blessed lady, his linga stands directly in front of him, facing westward.
O illustrious Goddess, when that eternal, secret [liṅga] named Kanakeśvara was being installed, it appeared like a shadow within the liṅga.
He who indeed beholds the shadow is not defiled by sin;
O Goddess, right in front of him stands a Linga facing the east.
The auspicious one named Tārakeśvara removes all sins;
by worshipping this liṅga, men shall attain knowledge.
Furthermore, O Goddess of gods, there is a place there known as Kanakeśvara;
by worshipping it, one is granted gold here of its own accord.
To the north of Kanakeśvara is the one named Manujeśvara,
and to the west is the Mukhaliṅga, which destroys all sins.
And right in front of him, O Goddess, stands a linga facing the east;
it was established by Indra, O Goddess, and installed out of devotion to me.
O Goddess, by the mere sight of it, knowledge arises;
O Goddess, it was established by Rambhā to the right of that very place.
And that Mukhaliṅga, O Goddess, stands facing the south;
to the north of Indreśvara is a liṅga situated facing the west.
And it was established, O blessed lady, by Śacī, the wife of the king of the gods;
on its northern side, it was installed by the world-protectors.
There are other signs there [left] by the hosts of gods, asuras, and maruts,
as well as by the yakṣas, nāgas, and the throngs of kinnaras and apsarases.
Indeed, lingas were installed by the world-protectors and the gods;
to the south of that very [liṅga] is a linga that destroys great sins.
O auspicious lady, that [liṅga] was installed by Phālguna facing the east;
to its southern side is Mahāpāśupateśvara.
O Goddess, by seeing that [place], one becomes a vessel for all-knowledge;
O Goddess, it is situated to the west of that very place, established by the ocean.
On its very right side, O Goddess, one should uplift Īśāna, world-renowned; the Liṅga stands facing west.
To the east of that as well, O Goddess, in Vārāṇasī, is the auspicious Liṅga of Lāṅgalin;
it bestows liberation and is filled with all sovereign powers.
Having recognized that the Kali age was terrible, filled with cries of "Alas! Alas!", and devoid of consciousness, I indeed remained in that region for the sake of the welfare of the Brahmins.
For that supreme form is divine, and that is remembered as divine knowledge;
for the sake of favoring the brahmins, I shall indeed unite it with the vow.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—
these indeed have their distinctions, and they are divided separately and individually.
All those devoid of knowledge are said to return again;
therefore, for the benefit of the Brahmins, knowledge itself has been revealed.
Having taken up all the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs and the Pada and Krama recensions,
as well as all the Yoga-shastras, together with curds and clarified butter;
Likewise, O beloved, in the Veda it is said that for one of great fortune,
the Pāśupata vow brings about the sovereignty of yoga within six months, O highly blessed lady.
Whatever power belongs to yoga and to the vow, one should abide among those who know yoga; for indeed, the Dharma and happiness reside within them.
O illustrious lady, the dharma of Brahmins is the same as that of others: self-restraint, or indeed discipline, non-violence, truthfulness, and the pursuit of knowledge.
A Brahmin who is ever-compassionate attains the highest state;
likewise, he should remain lying on ashes and perform his ritual duties between the three daily libations.
Wearing the sacred marks and the remains of offerings, the ascetic should dwell in his own temple,
constantly devoted to the practices of recitation, song, the *huḍiṅkāra* sound, and praise.
Having taken recourse to the southern form of the God of gods through meditative cultivation,
one should not suddenly discharge urine or feces there.
One should not converse with women or Śūdras, and one should always avoid the food of Śūdras;
for one who is nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food, what kind of atonement can there be?
The food of a Brāhmaṇa is nectar; the food of a Kṣatriya is remembered as milk;
the food of a Vaiśya they call mere food; and the food of a Śūdra is remembered as blood.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should avoid that [conduct] if one desires my state;
one who dwells in the cremation ground is righteous-souled and subsists on whatever is obtained.
By constantly recollecting Rudra, one shall attain union with Rudra;
in this sacred field especially, one obtains knowledge within six months.
Those who constantly worship the Lord, being liberated from passion and hatred, will certainly attain liberation; of this there is no doubt. They are the worshippers of the abode of the Siddhas.
I have declared their liberation for those humans who performed [these rites] during the twenty-second cycle at Vārāṇasī under the Great Vow.
I shall indeed abide in that place by the name Nakulīśa;
in that Kali age, the gods will behold me there, fallen from my station.
In this place as well, O Goddess of gods, are my sons who dwell in heaven:
Vakrāṅgi, Madhupiṅga, and another, Śvetaketu.
In this place, having attained the supreme state of Yoga through the Māheśvara Yoga,
stands the east-facing Liṅga of the deity known as Nakulīśa.
That linga is endowed with four persons and is established there;
having seen it, O Goddess, a human being attains the very same world as Rudra.
The god Nakulīśeśvara and Kapileśvara—
this indeed is the pentad of shrines (pañcāyatana) which was previously described.
[108] This supreme secret Veda, which is my practice of vows,
must not be told to those who are devoid of devotion to me.
O Goddess, Śakra has declared that the state taught in the Pāśupata is perfectly cultivated;
one attains that state by means of these very [visions], of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, by seeing these, one constantly becomes filled with joy;
[this is] Avimukta, the great field, frequented by hosts of Siddhas.
O Goddess, one who worships here certainly attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, those best of the twice-born who desire spiritual accomplishments shall attain them.
"Whatever is given here shall always be imperishable for the high-souled twice-born ones who are constant in dharma and devoted to my vow."
O illustrious lady, he who observes a fast for a single day while being devoted to me obtains here the fruit of a hundred years.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the *Vārāṇasī-māhātmya* of the glorious *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of the gods, I shall describe another sacred site in Vārāṇasī,
where there is indeed a beautiful and desired place for the God of gods.
O Goddess, in former times, that linga of the moon-crested Lord was being carried away with great speed by Rākṣasas stationed in the sky as it proceeded toward Vraja.
When they arrived in this place, the Lord thought:
"In Avimukta, how will my liberation not be possible?"
[109] While the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign, was contemplating this matter,
the sound of a cock suddenly arose in that place.
O Goddess, having heard that sound, the Rākṣasas, their hearts terrified,
abandoned the linga and fled in fear at the time of dawn.
O Goddess, when the Rākṣasas had departed,
the Lord of gods himself remained right there in that very place, a beautiful and auspicious spot, as the sovereign master.

Because it is not liberated from that [bond] in its midst, it is therefore called Avimukta. Indeed, in that Avimukta, the gods remember the name of Hara, which is rich with most meritorious syllables.
It bestows liberation upon all beings, both stationary and moving,
those living creatures who have gone there to their death.
O Goddess of gods, cocks also always remain in that place;
even today they are seen there, being worshipped by those seeking auspicious results.
The person who shall behold the eternal Liṅga here at Avimukta will not undergo rebirth even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
To the south of the god stands a beautiful pond;
by drinking its water, one is not subject to rebirth again.
O illustrious lady, by merely drinking that very water,
three signs appear in the heart of a man.
This is a secret, O Great Goddess; it must not be given to just anyone.
Daṇḍapāṇi, stationed there, always protects that water.
Having reached the western shore by the command of the God of gods,
the god Tāraka always protects the water on the eastern side.
[110] And Nadiśa protects that water constantly from the north, while Mahākāla protects it from the south; it is a deluder even for those devoted to me.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Goddess, that auspicious body of mine consisting of water is also supreme;
it is unattainable and difficult to reach, O Goddess, for men who have not disciplined their souls."
But those men who did not drink that water have achieved their purpose;
the liberating knowledge will arise within them, without a doubt.
Having bathed in the waters of the pond and beheld the one named Daṇḍa,
and then having seen Avimukta, a person attains liberation (kaivalya) in an instant.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: That cremation ground named Avimukteśvara leads to liberation,
where Rudra was propitiated by the sage Jaigīṣavya.
Where a Brāhmaṇa, having performed the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) even once,
has effectively performed it for six years from that point on.
Having seen that city of Vārāṇasī, the cremation ground of Avimuktaka,
and that Lord Avimukteśvara, one becomes a Gaṇapati.
