In the *Matsyapurāṇa*, regarding the granting of boons by Daṇḍapāṇi,
the God of gods said:
"Free from old age and death, and devoid of all sorrow..."
He shall become a leader of the assembly, a bestower of boons, and honored by all.
Invincible against all, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga,
he shall become the protector of the field (kṣetrapāla) and a provider of food for the worlds.
The one of great strength and great being is dear to both Brahmā and me;
likewise are Akṣa, Daṇḍapāṇi, and the Great Yogi.
Udbhrama and Saṃbhrama are your two attendants;
by your command, they shall cause confusion and agitation among the world.
Likewise:
those who hate the gods and Brahmins, those who obstruct devotion to the gods, slayers of Brahmins, ungrateful persons, and those who are deceitful; |||
Those hated by the world, those who hate their gurus, those who defile sacred fords and shrines, those devoted to every kind of sin, and whatever others on earth are contemptible;
They have no dwelling place; indeed, the leader of the rod stands ready—the supreme leader of the rod appointed for the sake of protection.
Having worshipped according to one's ability with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth,
the knower of mantras should then perform a prostration to that Leader.
In this field covered by all castes and filled with various kinds of crawling creatures,
those indeed who are graced by Īśvara have attained the state of Gaṇeśvara.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*: "In front of Avimukta, there stands a west-facing Liṅga named Prītikeśvara; it bestows eternal joy."
To the north of Avimukta, the Linga stands facing west;
and that, O Goddess, is indeed known by the name Mokṣakeśvara.
O Goddess of the gods, by seeing that, a man becomes possessed of knowledge;
and to the north of that, O Goddess, is the four-faced Liṅga.
The one named Varuṇeśvara, who grants liberation from the fear of sins,
stands with its face-linga attached to its front.
The deity named Suvarṇākṣeśvara bestows the fruits of sacrifices;
and to its north, Gaurī herself dwells, bestowing merit.
From the sight of that goddess, supreme good fortune arises;
to the right of that god is indeed the Gaṇa named Nikumbha.
O Goddess, having seen that, a human being attains residence in the sacred field;
and there, O illustrious one, is Vināyaka to the west.
Merely by seeing it, one is never overcome by obstacles.
To the east of Nikumbha stands a linga facing westward.
O Goddess, O beloved, that which is the face-linga there is itself known as Vijaya;
and to the south of that very place, it is remembered as Śukreśvara.
O auspicious lady, that Mukhaliṅga was established in ancient times by Śukra;
it faces the east, O auspicious lady, and bestows sorrow upon Śiva.
And to the north of that very place, O Goddess, there stands a face-linga (mukhaliṅga);
it faces west, O Goddess, and was installed by Devayānī.
And right in front of him, O blessed lady, stands a linga facing westward,
installed by Kaca, the son of the preceptor of the gods.
[113] And right near that very place, O lady of virtuous vows, there stands a well;
by touching its waters, O Goddess, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
On its western side dwell the God and the Goddess;
they bestow devotion upon all people, even those men who have committed evil deeds.
To the east of Śukreśvara stands a west-facing Liṅga named Anarkeśvara,
which bestows liberation upon all embodied beings.
To the east of that very place, surrounded by the Gaṇas,
is the one renowned as Gaṇeśvara, the bestower of all joy.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the Vārāṇasī-māhātmya of the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe another sacred site in Vārāṇasī:
the Liṅga established by Rāma after he had returned from Laṅkā.
On its right side stands a Linga facing the east,
named Tripurāntakara, which destroys all sins.
To the south of that very place is the Liṅga installed by Dattātreya;
O Goddess, knowledge arises from the sight of that Liṅga.
To its west is the auspicious Harikeśeśvara;
there, O Goddess of excellent vows, it was propitiated by Harikeśa.
To the west of that deity Harikeśeśvara, who destroys all sins,
there is the famous place named Gokarṇa.
Having bathed there, O lady of beautiful hips, one shines like the moon, O Goddess;
for in the city of Kāśī, O observer of good vows, there is a Liṅga facing westward.
To the north of all the perfected ones (siddhas), bestowing infinite fruit,
is the lake renowned among the gods, situated in front of the God of Gods.
Having bathed there, O lady of excellent hips, one shines like the moon, O Goddess;
on its western bank stands a linga facing the east.
"O blessed lady, it was indeed established by the King who was devoted to me;
O beautiful goddess, a sacrificial pit stands right in front of that very place."
O lady of beautiful hips, one who bathes there shall attain the world of the gods;
it was established of old by the Piśācas to the north of Deveśvara.
O Goddess, in front of Dhruveśa stands the Mukhaliṅga, known by the name Piśāceśvara, which bestows liberation upon all embodied beings.
O beautiful lady, that Liṅga is facing westward on the bank of the Kuṇḍa;
one should know it as Vaidyanātha, the bestower of all happiness.
In the south-western quarter of that very place, established by Manu in ancient times,
is that linga facing east, situated to the south of that pool.
O lady of beautiful hips, by seeing that [Liṅga], there shall be the destruction of all sins.
To the east of Vaidyanātha stands a Liṅga facing the east.
O Goddess, that place named Mucukundeśvara bestows boons upon the gods;
it belongs to Priyavrata and grants the fruit of all sacrifices.
[115] O Goddess, to the south of that very place stands a linga facing the east,
known by the name Gautameśa, which pacifies all sins.
O Goddess of the gods, by beholding that [Liṅga], one obtains the fruit of the Sāmaveda.
To the south of that very place, O Goddess, is the one known as Vibhāṇḍeśvara.
To the south of that is the one named Ṛṣyaśṛṅgeśvara;
to the east of that very place, O Goddess, is the one remembered as Brahmeśvara.
O Goddess, from the northeast corner of Brahmeśvara is the one known as Piśāceśvara;
and from Parjanyeśvara is the one named Paścimābhimukha.
To the east of Parjanyeśvara is Nahuṣeśvara, known by that name, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
To the east of Nahuṣeśvara dwells the Goddess of gods,
renowned as Viśālākṣī, who bestows the fruits of her grace upon her devotees.
On the southern side of that very place stands Jarāsaṃdheśvara;
O Goddess, having seen that four-faced Liṅga, one obtains the fruit.
To the right of that very [place], O Goddess, is Bhogadā, who bestows enjoyments upon all embodied beings;
and Lalitakā, O Goddess, who grants all supernatural attainments (*siddhi*).
In front of Jarāsaṃdheśvara stands a Linga facing the east,
named Hiraṇyākṣeśvara, which bestows golden rewards.
To the south of that very place is the Liṅga known by the name Yayātīśvara;
that Liṅga faces the east and bestows the fruits of all desires.
On its very western side, near Brahmeśa,
one who beholds that linga facing westward shall obtain the fruit of the Vedas.
Near Agastya, however, there stands a face-liṅga;
formerly, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu installed that liṅga.
To the east of Agastyeśvara is the one known by the name Muṇḍeśa;
that Liṅga faces westward and bestows heroic accomplishments upon men.
O Goddess Pārvatī, to the right of that very place stands Vidhi;
the Liṅga installed by Vidhi is situated facing the west.
To the south of Vidhīśvara is a tīrtha renowned everywhere;
there, the liṅga named Daśāśvamedhika stands of its own accord.
O Goddess, having seen that, a person obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
and to the north of the Ten Ashvamedhas, the Mothers are stationed there.
O woman of excellent complexion, that pool stands at their mouth;
there, a man or even a woman or a male may establish a sacred site.
One obtains the desired fruit through the grace of the Mothers.
To the south of Agastyeśa stands a linga facing the east.
To the south of that [Liṅga] stands another Liṅga named Pulastyeśvara, which increases all forms of health.
[117] There is the one named Puṣpadanteśvara, the bestower of all accomplishments;
and right in front of it, in the corner, there are very great liṅgas.
Nourished by hosts of celestial sages and bestowing all accomplishments,
it lies in the eastern direction of that very place, granting great wonders.
Through the five-fold ritual worship (pañcopacāra-pūjā), he will achieve the accomplishment of dreams;
there is a linga named Siddheśvara situated facing the east.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the *Vārāṇasī-māhātmya* of the glorious *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
Īśvara said:
Moreover, I shall describe another auspicious [site], Hariścandreśvara,
where the great-souled and mighty Hariścandra indeed attained perfection.
O Goddess, having seen that, a person shall attain the state of Rudra;
that Liṅga faces the east and bestows the world of heaven.
O Goddess, to the west of Hariścandreśvara there is another liṅga;
O Goddess, it faces east and is indeed named Nairṛteśvara.
O Goddess, by beholding it, one shall attain the knowledge of liberation (kaivalya).
To the south of that very place stands a linga facing the east.
Indeed, by name it is Āṅgiraseśa, which bestows the happiness of dispassion;
to its very south, O Goddess, is the unsurpassed Kṣemeśvara.
[118] To its southern quarter is the famous place named Kedāra;
having seen it, O Goddess, a human being shall become an attendant of Rudra.
To the south of Kedāra, there stands a Liṅga facing the east,
known by the name Nīlakaṇṭha, which bestows the world of the gods.
In the very same south-western corner [of that place] is the auspicious Ambarīśeśvara;
to the south of that is a linga facing the south.
There is the deity named Kālañjara, the destroyer of all sins;
indeed, on his very southern side is the sun named Lokārka.
By the mere sight of it, one shall attain the world of the Sun;
and to the west of Lolārka, the goddess Durgā resides.
O Goddess, for the benefit of human beings, there stands a linga facing east on the peak to the south of the field and to the west of Durgā.
And that [liṅga], O Goddess, was indeed installed with devotion by Asita;
it is remembered as Śuṣkeśvara, named after the dried-up river.
[119] To the west of Śuṣkeśvara is the one named Janakeśvara;
it was installed with devotion by the illustrious Janaka.
That linga faces west; by beholding it, O auspicious one, one becomes free from suffering. Not far from it, on its northern side, O illustrious lady, [is another].
The Liṅga named Śaṅkukarṇeśvara stands in that very place;
by the mere sight of it, the perfection of vows shall be attained by men.
To the north of Śuṣkeśvara stands a west-facing Liṅga named Siddheśvara,
situated right on the bank of the Kuṇḍa.
Having bathed in that pool and beheld Siddheśvara,
a man indeed reaches the further shore of all supernatural powers.
In the northwestern quarter, however, is the shrine of Śaṅkukarṇeśvara,
known as Māṇḍavyeśa, which is worshipped by gods and siddhas.
And right near him, O Goddess, the Great Lord himself stands,
surrounded by his attendants together with the Goddess.
O Goddess, you stand at your own gate and personally protect the sacred field;
it is situated not far from the northern side of the deity.
The Mukhaliṅga is located right there, facing the east, O auspicious one;
and on its northern side is the one known as Chāgaleśvara.
That linga faces westward and bestows all accomplishments;
there is another shrine to the west, O illustrious goddess.
To the east of that, O lady of beautiful hips, stands the supreme bestower of all things named Kapardīśvara, a linga facing the east.
To the south of that stands the one named Kātyāyaneśvara, known as Hariteśvara, which causes the destruction of all sins.
By beholding that, a person obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
furthermore, right beside it is the one known as Aṅgāreśvara.
And there is also a lake situated there, known by the name Aṅgāreśvara,
located not far from it toward the southern direction.
The Linga named Mukureśvara, which bestows the fruits of all pilgrimages,
stands facing west in front of the Kuṇḍa.
Beside that pool is the one known as Chāgaleśvara;
by the mere sight of it, mastery over yoga is attained.
There are other signs by the hundreds and thousands;
they have not been mentioned by me because of their great number and their names.
Indeed, seventy million lingas are situated on the earth in this place.
Merely by seeing them, knowledge arises in an instant;
I have given you this brief indication, O fair-faced one.
It is not possible to describe these in detail, even in hundreds of millions of years—
these signs of the Siddhas, as well as the sacred wells and lakes.
I have thus described to you the ponds, rivers, and pools;
whoever performs a ritual bath in these with a concentrated mind, [shall obtain great merit].
And having touched the lingas, one shall not enter into saṃsāra again;
[so too] those holy places on earth and those that move through the atmosphere.
[121] Among those, O auspicious one, I have described to you those which are the most excellent;
O lady of beautiful hips, this pilgrimage to sacred sites has been told as the destroyer of sins.
"O Goddess, he by whom this was created shall certainly partake in liberation.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the *Śrīliṅgapurāṇa*, within the "Glorification of Vārāṇasī."
Īśvara said:
Furthermore, O fair-faced one, I shall declare another matter of great fortune:
having established fourteen shrines, or indeed eight shrines.
The Pañcāyatana, as well as Lalitā and Vināyaka,
and likewise the nine Durgās— these, O fair-faced one, are said to be the ritual duties.
This secret has been told; it must not be given to just anyone.
Having first beheld Śaileśa and bathed in the Varaṇā river, one should proceed.
Having performed his bath at the confluence and indeed having beheld Saṅgameśvara,
and having performed his bath at Svarlīna and beheld the Lord Svarlīna;
Having bathed in the Mandākinī and beheld Madhyameśvara,
and having bathed at Hiraṇyagarbha and likewise beheld Īśvara;
Having bathed at Maṇikarṇikā and beheld the Lord Īśāna,
and having sipped water from that well and beheld the Lord Goprekṣa;
Having bathed in the lake of Kapilā and beheld the Vṛṣabhadhvaja [liṅga],
one reaches the excellent well to the south of the tranquil deity.
Having performed ablutions in that well and beheld the tranquil Lord,
one should bathe in the Pañcacūḍā lake and then worship the Jyeṣṭhasthāna.
Having bathed at the well of the four oceans, one should then worship the deity;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (upasparśana) there at the well in front of the deity.
Thereafter, one should worship Śuddheśvara, the Lord of Gods;
then, having bathed in Daṇḍakhāta, a man should worship Vyādeśa.
O illustrious lady, having performed a bath in the Śaunakeśvara-kuṇḍa, one should then worship the deity named Jambukeśvara after beholding him.
O Goddess of gods, having seen [this], a mortal is not born again in this ocean of suffering in saṃsāra,
from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
In this sequence, O auspicious one, this great sanctuary should be constructed.
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme eightfold sanctuary.
Having seen him, O Goddess, a person should then go to Lāṅgalīśa;
having seen him, O Goddess, one should then worship Āṣāḍhīśa.
O Goddess, having seen Āṣāḍhin, one should then proceed;
and having seen that deity, one should indeed go to Tripurāntaka.
Having seen that, O Goddess, one should then proceed to Nakulīśa;
to the south of Nakulīśa is Tryambaka, which one should then visit.
[123] Thus have I proclaimed to you this very eightfold base (aṣṭāyatana). Indeed, those men who shall practice this eightfold base—
Even when dead, they become recipients of the world of Rudra in an external field.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, previously by me this supreme Pañcāyatana was established.
I always find delight in dwelling in this supreme five-shrine temple.
O Goddess, O beloved, this direction is always to the north of Vārāṇasī;
it is eternally to my north, especially in this place.
The Brahmins who dwell in solitude, devoted to the sacred ash and firm in their vows—
for them, some indeed declare that there is a supreme abode.
For that supreme, divine form is always situated within the syllable Oṃ;
at the time of creation and maintenance, I am stationed in that very abode.
And he who understands it thus is not defiled by evil.
Truth, truth, and again truth—truth thrice, and nothing else, O auspicious one!
And let him go there quickly if he desires my state;
thus, O Goddess, have I explained this to you again in detail.
Īśvara said: Avimukta, Svarlīna, and likewise the auspicious Madhyamaka—
this is known as Trikaṇṭaka, which bestows immortality at the time of death.
O auspicious one, I have told you the reason for that field:
this Vārāṇasī is meritorious, supreme, and the sacred ground of Pāśupati.
[124] And for all living beings, O beautiful one, it is the cause of liberation. Likewise, there is Avimukta, Svarlīna, Oṃkāra, Caṇḍa, and Īśvara.
The middle one is Kṛttivāsas; thus Īśvara is said to have six limbs.
In the great field of Avimukta lies this supreme secret of mine;
it should be understood through the oral instruction if one desires the highest state.
This secret majesty must not be given to just anyone.
Hereafter, I shall always explain the proper time for the pilgrimage.
In the month of Caitra, this auspicious procession was indeed performed by the gods,
who were intent upon bathing and worshipping at that very Kāmakuṇḍa.
In ancient times, this pilgrimage was performed by the kings of the Daityas during the month of Vaiśākha,
as they were intent upon bathing and worshipping at the Vimaleśvara Kuṇḍa.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, this pilgrimage was also performed in ancient times by the Siddhas,
who were devoted to bathing and worship at the Kuṇḍa of Rudravāsa.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, this procession was also performed for me by the Gandharvas;
moreover, the gods, intent upon bathing and worship, [attained] welfare while remaining in the sacred pools.
Furthermore, this procession was undertaken by the Vidyādharas, who were devoted to it, staying at Lakṣmīkuṇḍa during the month of Śrāvaṇa and intent upon bathing and worship.
And by the Pitṛs as well, who were intent upon that [rite] in the month of Āśvina,
staying at the Kapilāhrada lake and devoted to bathing and worship, this [river] was reached.
[125] And by the sages as well, who were intent upon it, staying at the Mārkaṇḍeya lake during the month of Kārttika, and devoted to bathing and worship;
And this pilgrimage was performed every month of Mārgaśīrṣa by the Vidyādharas residing at Kapālamocana,
who were intent upon bathing and worship.
This procession should be carried out by the Guhyakas with devotion in the month of Puṣya;
and it should be carried out by the Piśācas with devotion in the month of Māgha.
This pilgrimage is also attended by the lords of the Yakṣas, who reside at the Dhanadeśvara Kuṇḍa, intent on bathing and worship, and devoted to this rite during the month of Māgha.
At Koṭitīrtha, this pilgrimage should be undertaken by Piśācas who are intent on bathing and worship, remaining there in the month of Phālguna with devoted minds.
When, on the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna, Piśācas dwelling at Gokarṇakuṇḍa are intent upon bathing and worship;
Therefore, O Goddess, she is proclaimed by the name Piśācī, which is well-known.
Hereafter, I shall declare the supreme expiation for the pilgrimage.
Water-pots filled with sweet food should be given;
by that, O Goddess, he then obtained the very fruit previously described.
Henceforth, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the pilgrimage;
on the third day of the bright fortnight, your pilgrimage yields great fruit.
Listen, O fair-faced one, to where Gaurī is to be seen;
having performed your ablutions, O illustrious lady, you should go to Goprekṣa.
On the day [of the lunar month], the goddess Kālikā should be worshipped with diligence;
thereafter, in the place of Jyeṣṭhā, Gaurī should be worshipped with diligence.
From that place, however, one who has not yet attained liberation must proceed further;
there, the goddess Gaurī should always be worshipped with devotion.
Or another supreme one is proclaimed, the auspicious Saṃvartalalitā;
that goddess also should be beheld, for she bestows the fruit of all desires.
If a man should meditate [upon this], he attains all his desires;
thereafter, he should feed Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva and pure in their vows.
O Goddess, he who, being composed and devoted, performs the Pañcagaurī rite with garments and sacrificial fees that are most abundant and appropriate to his means;
The ellipsis is that one should give all flavors and fragrances to a Brahmin dedicated to Gaurī;
he attains the highest welfare, endowed with good fortune.
I shall describe the Vināyakas who cause obstacles in that field.
Having first seen Ḍhuṇḍhi, as well as Koṇavināyaka,
the Vināyaka of the Goddess, and Goprekṣa, who is remembered as Hastin;
Likewise, another Vināyaka, renowned by the name Sindūra, is the fourth; O Goddess, he too must be seen—thus there are five Vināyakas.
And sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) should be given to a Brahmin dedicated to these [deities];
by this very dharma, a man becomes successful.
Hereafter, I shall describe the Caṇḍikās who protect the sacred field:
Durgā protects in the south, and Uttareśvarī in the southwest (nairṛta).
Aṅgāreśī is in the west, Bhadrakālikā in the northwest;
Bhīṣmacaṇḍī is in the north, and Mahāmuṇḍā follows after her.
Ūrdhvakeśī is joined with Śāṅkarī and is remembered as being present everywhere;
Ūrdhvakeśī is in the southeast, while Citraghaṇṭā is in the center.
And whatever man shall behold these Caṇḍikā goddesses here, they,
being pleased, will all protect that sacred field with devoted intent.
O Goddess, they constantly create obstacles for the wicked at all times;
therefore, Caṇḍikā and Vināyaka should always be worshipped.
O Goddess, if one desires to dwell constantly in the auspicious Vārāṇasī,
I shall tell you something else regarding that sacred field, O Mistress of the Gods.
Three rivers with auspicious waters flow there,
by the mere sight of which the sin of killing a Brahmin is removed.
One is Pitāmahasrotas, another is Mandākinī, and the third is Matsyodarī; these three indeed bestow merit.
Likewise, the meritorious Mandākinī is situated at Madhyameśvara,
and the Pitāmhasrotikā bestows merit upon Avimukta.
And Matsyodarī at Oṃkāra bestows merit upon all the deities;
O beautiful lady, if the Gaṅgā should come to that place, [it will be even more auspicious].
Then it is the most meritorious time, difficult even for the gods to attain,
when the waters of the Varaṇā have been poured together with the waters of the Jāhnavī.
Having bathed there at the meritorious Nādeśvara, one does not grieve;
and at that very time, O Goddess, I performed my ablutions right there.
O Goddess, by that [act], the skull fell from the palm of his hand in an instant;
right there is the very great lake named Kapālamocana.
[128] It is the purifier of all beings and the bestower of merit upon all embodied souls;
there, I performed my ablutions at the place named Oṃkāreśvara.
Therefore, that god is called by the name Oṃkāreśvara;
the Gaṅgā, my sister, flows in the water in the vicinity of Oṃkāreśvara.
Then, having bathed in that water and beheld the Lord in the form of Oṃkāra, one casts off the sin of killing a Brahmin by bathing in the waters of Matsyodarī.
Neither grief, delusion, old age, nor death shall touch him again.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abode," in the *Vārāṇasī-māhātmya* of the glorious *Liṅga Purāṇa*.
Viṣṇu said:
Having heard these words, the Goddess, her eyes wide with wonder,
approached Kapileśa for the purpose of beholding the syllable Oṃkāra.
Therefore, you too should worship Sadāśiva, the Lord of Gods;
thus you shall attain this supreme bliss, the highest state.
Having heard this supreme secret from the presence of Cakraprāṇin,
one whose mind is ever fixed upon it should worship the god Oṃkāra.
Sūrya said:
Therefore, you too should propitiate the invincible Lord of the Gods;
through him, you shall attain that station which is difficult even for others to obtain.
Having heard the words of Sūrya, he arrived at Vārāṇasī;
there, O Goddess, having seen that Oṃkāra and having bowed down to it, he remained.
Having become intent on propitiation and having installed the four-faced Liṅga,
one shall indeed become pure and have fulfilled one's purpose in the presence of the God of gods.
[129] He who, having attained the Great Principle (mahattattva), has reached a firm resolve regarding the Lord—
therefore, O Gāṅgeya, you too should strive if you desire the highest good.
Propitiate the Lord of Gods with steadiness of mind and self;
for in that place resides Śiva himself, known by the name Oṃkāreśvara.
O great sage, out of affection for you, this majesty of the secret has been proclaimed;
it is celebrated as the syllable A, the syllable U, and the syllable M.
In this *liṅga*, however, the sage Kālikavṛkṣaya attained perfection;
there, the letter "A" is to be known as that which bestows the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu.
On its southern side, however, is the place celebrated as Oṃkāra;
there Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods, attained supreme perfection.
There, the syllable *ukāra* should be known as the imperishable station of Brahmā;
and in its northern direction is the syllable *makāra*, which is named Viṣṇu.
And upon that linga, the great sage Kapila Ṛṣi attained perfection;
therefore, O Gārgya, if you also desire steadiness of mind, [worship it].
Exert yourself in the worship of the Liṅga with firm vows;
having obtained the Pāśupata knowledge, take refuge in that one worthy of praise.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, you shall attain the eternal state.
Having heard these words and having praised Yājñavalkya, they were shown [the way].
Having arrived at Vārāṇasī, the supreme Pañcāyatana,
the Lord of Gods remains forever established in that place, being worshipped there.
Therefore, for others as well who are devoted to the propitiation of the Liṅga,
knowledge will always arise in them during the final age.
Knowing this, whatever mortal is constantly devoted to the worship of the Liṅga shall not undergo rebirth even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Therefore, having attained this human state— which is difficult to find and as fleeting as a flash of lightning— one should worship with great effort according to the authentic tradition.
The Brahmin who fashions a *liṅga* shall uplift himself;
he who does not worship the *liṅga* constantly destroys himself.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Secret Abodes," in the *Vārāṇasīmāhātmya* of the *Śrīliṅgapurāṇa*.
[In the] *Skandapurāṇa*:
Having reached that garden, the Lord of the World said to the goddess:
"O beautiful goddess, in former times, while I was staying in this place..."
Above, in the abode of Goloka, as the cows were being milked with speed by their self-born calves,
the froth fell upon my head.
Then he did not see those cows and calves staying by the side of Soma;
thereafter, those cows were beheld there by me at that time.
But being consumed by that splendor, their actions were not accomplished;
O Goddess, these cows were formerly of a tawny-brown color.
Then, appearing in many colors, they were constantly beheld by me;
they went for refuge to Brahmā, the supreme among the gods.
Then, having approached me from the front with palms joined in reverence,
Brahmā spoke to me as he was being tormented by those cows.
O Lord of the Vedas, show favor to these Surabhis of radiant splendor;
O you who are worshipped by the gods, act in such a way that they do not perish.
[131] Then, O Goddess, I myself established myself in this very place,
renowned as Goprekṣaka and praised by all the deities.
Having come to Gauprekṣeśvara, seen it, and worshipped it,
a person does not fall into an evil state and is liberated from all impurities.
Then, being scorched by my fragrant offspring, they approached this lake and fell into it; exhausted, they likewise drank the water.
From that time forth, it has been called Kapilāhrada;
here too, I myself remain present as the Bull-bannered One.
"O Goddess, he has established his presence here; behold him standing always visible.
Having bathed in this Kapilāhrada-tīrtha with a restrained mind,"
Having seen this bull-bannered [liṅga], one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
and by worshipping me here, even after death, one attains the heavenly world.
Upon the dissolution of the body, he attains the state of a Gaṇa, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
for even in this very region, those cows were created by Brahmā himself.
For the sake of the peace of all worlds, all those cows yielded milk that was nectar;
from their milk, this enchanting lake was produced.
O Goddess, in this region I was propitiated by all the gods at the auspicious and meritorious Devahrada, which is renowned as Bhadradoha.
"Go, O Lord; attain tranquility. Thereupon he became tranquil and auspicious (*śiva*). Having become auspicious, I remained here; even the sight of him is meritorious.
Upon seeing this, a mortal who is self-restrained shall attain the heavenly realm.
Here I was brought and established by Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
[132] Having seized it from Brahmā as well, it was established again by Viṣṇu.
Then Viṣṇu was addressed by Brahmā, whose mind was agitated:
"Why have you installed this linga brought by me?
Viṣṇu spoke again to Brahmā, whose face was contorted with anger.
My devotion to the god Rudra is exceedingly great;
though established here by me alone, he shall be known by your name.
"O Goddess of gods, having seen even this [mantra] 'Hiraṇyagarbha' as established therein, one is glorified in my world."
Furthermore, O auspicious one, Brahmā then again installed this *liṅga* of mine according to the prescribed rites and with supreme devotion.
Thus, I am established there as Svarlīneśvara,
once that Pradhāna, my own cause, has merged into that which is beyond it.
Therefore, it is established that the secret field (guhyakṣetra) is thus called "absorbed in its own nature" (svarlīna);
having abandoned the vital breaths here, a person is never born again anywhere.
Infinite is that destination which is prescribed for yogins alone;
yet even in this great region, there was a Daitya who was a thorn in the side of the God.
Having assumed the form of a tiger, that proud and powerful one was slain;
he is reckoned as Vyāghreśvara, and I am eternally established here.
Furthermore, having seen that Great Lord, he does not go to an evil rebirth—
just as Utpala and Vidala, those two sons of Brahmā in ancient times.
O auspicious lady, seeing those two arrogant men who were destined to be slain by a woman, you yourself killed them here with a ball; this mark remains as evidence of that act.
In the beginning, I came here and remained together with the Gaṇapas;
therefore, this is the station of the Eldest, and thus it is a meritorious sight for me.
[133] Having thus seen my linga situated at the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna,
a mortal no longer grieves, being perfected in birth after birth.
Furthermore, lingas have been established by the gods all around me;
indeed, a mortal who beholds them with self-restraint shall become a member of the Gaṇas upon the dissolution of the body.
Now I have come and established myself here personally;
because it has not been abandoned by me, it is therefore called "Avimukta" (the Unreleased).
The sacred field of Vārāṇasī will become a bestower of liberation for that man who beholds me here as Avimukteśvara.
Indeed, for one who has cast off their life-breaths and dies anywhere, the goal is the state of the Lord of Ganas; there, the highest liberation is attained.
Your father, the king of mountains, Himavat himself,
knowing that place to be dear to me, personally installed a linga there.
Behold here, situated before you, that which is renowned as Śaileśvara;
having seen it, O Goddess, a person shall not fall into an evil state.
And this river Vārāṇasī is meritorious and the destroyer of sins;
having adorned this sacred field, it has joined with the Jāhnavī.
An excellent Liṅga was established by Brahmā at this confluence;
it is seen in the world as renowned by the name Saṃgameśvara.
For that pure person who, having bathed at the confluence of the two divine rivers,
worships Saṅgameśāna— whence can there be any fear of rebirth for him?
And this Liṅga was established by your son Śukra;
the Liṅga is named Śukreśvara, worshipped by all the Siddhas and immortals.
Upon merely seeing it, a person would instantly be liberated from all sins;
moreover, that man would not undergo rebirth in saṃsāra after death.
Formerly, the Asura Jambuka, a thorn to the gods,
having obtained a boon from Brahmā, feared death at the hands of a jackal.
O daughter of Himavat, I am indeed Jambukeśa;
therefore, I am known as Anavadyagati, honored by gods and asuras alike.
By beholding even this Lord of Gods, one shall obtain all desires;
for these were indeed established by the gods, with Śakra at their head.
These five lingas are meritorious and indeed bestow all desires;
thus, O Pārvatī, these meritorious ones are situated together.
These have been told to you in this sacred field; now hear this secret word:
I am situated on Mount Mahālaya and established in Kedāra.
One attains the state of being a Gaṇa upon seeing this field; liberation is said [to occur there], and for that reason, the station of the Lord of Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya) is the supreme liberation.
O auspicious one, this field of Avimukta is remembered as the most meritorious of all, even compared to that Mahālaya and the Middle Kedāra.
Kedāra is a middle station, and Mahālaya is also a station;
these are my meritorious places on the earth, but this one is the most excellent of them all.
"These worlds were created by me; therefore, O auspicious one, this is my field.
Because it is endowed with wealth in the world, it became known as Avimukta."
Having beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga here,
a human being is instantly liberated from sin and released from the bonds of Paśu.
Śaileśa, Saṅgameśa, Svarlīna, Madhyameśvara,
Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, Goprekṣa, and Vṛṣabhadvaja.
And also Upaśāntaśiva, who dwells in the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna;
and the renowned Śukreśvara, Vyāghreśa, and Jambukeśvara.
"Having seen [this], a mortal is not born again in the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.

[154] 4. Now, the majesty of the Gaṅgā.
In that regard, in the Mahābhārata, Śilavṛtti said:

From Viśveśvara to Ekarātri, and from there to Sarasvatī,
the lake known as Saṃnihita should be understood to extend for half a yojana in every direction.
Relying upon this, the gods and sages have gathered together;
and the Gandharvas and Apsarases remain here, desiring liberation.
When a solar eclipse occurs at some time in the future,
having gathered together and bathed then, you shall go to heaven purified.
But those great-souled ones who have attained perfection, by the mere touch of the *liṅga*,
attain the supreme perfection from which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to find.
Having understood this, Gaṅgā, desiring the welfare of the gods,
then established seven Liṅgas there, one above the other.
Then those who desired liberation, the perfected ones devoted to sacrifice,
having served him with great effort, departed for the supreme state.
Even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, when raised by the wind,
lead one who has committed most heinous deeds to the supreme goal.
Then, seeing those creatures obscured by that radiance, I was seized by great anger; tearing out my linga, I cast it away.
Contracted in the middle of the lake, he then stood upright once more;
from that time forth, he became renowned throughout the worlds as Sthāṇu.
By the mere sight of it once, one is liberated from all sins and attains supreme liberation, from which one does not return again.
Whoever dwells here at this sacred ford on the eighth day of the dark fortnight with a concentrated mind is liberated from all sins arising from approaching women who should not be approached.
In the Mahābhārata:
"From there, O king of kings, one should go to the highly praised Kurukṣetra;
all living beings who have gone there are liberated from their sins."
"I shall go to Kurukṣetra; I dwell in Kurukṣetra"—whoever should constantly speak thus is also liberated from sin.
A wise man, O Yudhiṣṭhira, should indeed dwell there on the Sarasvatī,
where the gods headed by Brahmā, as well as the ṛṣis, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas reside.
O lord of the earth, O descendant of Bharata, the Gandharvas, Apsaras, Yakṣas, and Pannagas resort to that most meritorious field of Brahmā.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even for one who merely desires Kurukṣetra in their mind,
sins are destroyed and they go to the heavenly world.
O best of the Kurus, even by merely going to Kurukṣetra endowed with faith,
one then obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
[178] Likewise; from there, O knower of dharma, one should go to the sacred ford called Saṃnihitī,
where Brahmā and the other gods, as well as sages whose wealth is asceticism, reside.
Endowed with great merit, they shall assemble month after month at Saṃnihatyā,
having performed their ablutions when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu.
A hundred horse-sacrifices performed there shall become eternal;
so too shall all the sacred fords on earth and those that move through the atmosphere.
Rivers, streams, ponds, and all springs,
as well as wells and the meritorious efforts of the brahmins.
As soon as one has bathed, all that perishes; of this there is no doubt.
By means of a lotus-colored vehicle, one attains the world of Brahmā.
Having reached that liberation, one should touch the gatekeeper Anantaka and the well Koṭīkūpa; thus one shall obtain much gold.
And right there, O best of the Bharatas, is the Gaṅgāhrada tīrtha;
there the knower of dharma, practicing celibacy and composed in mind, should bathe.
A person obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices by visiting Naimiṣa on earth and Puṣkara in the intermediate space.
Kurukṣetra is superior even to the three worlds;
even the dust particles of Kurukṣetra, when raised by the wind, [purify].
They lead even one who has committed most grievous deeds to the supreme destination—
[the region] north of the Dṛṣadvatī and south of the Sarasvatī.
Those who dwell in Kurukṣetra dwell in Triviṣṭapa;
I shall go to Kurukṣetra, I shall dwell in Kurukṣetra.
Then, having uttered but a single word, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
Kurukṣetra is the sacrificial altar of Brahmā, a holy place frequented by Brahman-sages.
O King, those who dwell there are not to be grieved for in any way—
those who live in the region between Raṇtuka and Araṇtuka,
and between the lakes of Rāma and Macakruka.
This Kurukṣetra, known as Samantapañcaka,
is called the northern altar of the Grandfather.

Thus ends the "Glorification of Kurukṣetra" in the Section on Sacred Fords (*tīrthakāṇḍa*) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*), son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[180] 7. Now, the majesty of Pṛthūdaka.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states:
"Then, O king of kings, one should go to the pilgrimage site renowned throughout the three worlds,
known as Pṛthūdaka, belonging to the wise Kārttikeya."
There, one devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods should perform the consecration,
whether by a woman or by a man, through ignorance or even through knowledge.
Whatever unwholesome deed has been committed by means of human intellect,
all that is destroyed, O King, Kaurava, merely upon bathing.
He obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world;
they say Kurukshetra is meritorious, but the Sarasvati is more meritorious than Kurukshetra.
I have heard that among the sacred fords of the Sarasvatī, Pṛthūdaka is superior to all other fords; he who casts off his body there [attains the highest goal].
One devoted to recitation at Pṛthūdaka will not be tormented by the thought of death tomorrow;
the meaning is that even the prospect of dying on the morrow shall not cause him distress.
This was sung by Sanatkumāra and by the high-souled Vyāsa.
And it is declared in the Vedas, O King, that one should certainly go to Pṛthūdaka.
[181] O lord of men, there is no other sacred ford more meritorious than Pṛthūdaka;
it is pure, holy, and purifying—of this there is no doubt.
"O best of men, the wise have declared that even those people who are doers of evil go to heaven after bathing there at Pṛthūdaka."

Thus ends the "Glorification of Pṛthūdaka" in the Section on Holy Places (Tīrthakāṇḍa) of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war and son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now follows the majesty of Puṣkara.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states:
"In the three worlds, there is a sacred ford belonging to the world of the gods, renowned throughout the triple universe;
it is celebrated by the name Puṣkara, and a person of great fortune should enter it."
O lord of the earth, O descendant of Kuru, ten thousand crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) are present at Puṣkara during the three junctions of the day.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and Śādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts,
as well as the Gandharvas and Apsarases, are always present here, O Lord.
O great king, it is there that the gods, Daityas, and likewise the Brahman-sages, having performed austerities,
possess divine enjoyments through their accumulated merit.
Even for a wise man who merely desires the Puṣkara lakes in his mind,
all his sins are purified, and he is honored in the vault of heaven.
At that sacred ford, O great king, the Grandfather always dwelt with supreme delight, honored by both gods and dānavas.
O highly fortunate one, in ancient times, the gods together with the hosts of sages attained perfection at Puṣkara, being endowed with great merit.
[183] Regarding this, the wise declare that he who performs the consecration ceremony while devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods obtains ten times the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Even if one residing in the Puṣkara forest feeds but a single Brahmin,
by that deed he rejoices constantly both here and after death.
Whatever one sustains oneself with— whether vegetables, roots, or fruits—
that indeed one should give to a Brāhmaṇa, being full of faith and free from malice.
By that alone, O best of kings, a wise man— whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra— shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Having bathed at the sacred ford of the Great-Souled One, one shall not go to a lower womb after death;
this is especially true for whoever goes to Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika.
That man who, with palms joined in reverence, remembers the Puṣkara lakes at dawn and at dusk, shall attain imperishable worlds in the abode of Brahmā.
By that [act], O Bhārata, one has effectively bathed in all sacred fords;
whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man since birth is thereby cleansed.
For one who has merely bathed at Puṣkara, everything perishes;
just as Madhusūdana is the primordial source of all the gods.
In the same way, O King, Puṣkara is said to be the foremost of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having dwelt at Puṣkara for ten years, self-restrained and pure, one attains the highest goal.
He obtains all sacrificial rites and goes to the world of Brahmā—
he who performs the Agnihotra for a full hundred years.

[184] Or one may dwell for a single Kārttikī festival at Puṣkara; that is indeed equal [to other merits]. Difficult to perform is the ritual bath at Puṣkara; difficult to perform is ascetic penance at Puṣkara.
It is difficult to travel to Puṣkara, and it is indeed difficult to dwell there.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
ten million sages residing in the southern region arrived [there].
O King, for the sake of bathing at Puṣkara, that Puṣkara which has gone to the earth—
Then all those sages, devoted to the practice of breath control,
remained for twelve years meditating upon the Supreme Brahman.
There, Brahmā, the great seers, and the gods led by Indra restrained those sages from that most difficult vow.
O twice-born ones, summon the aerial chariot by means of the mantra;
through the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," it will come into your presence.
Through the recitation of the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, it becomes fruit-bestowing;
then, at the conclusion of their speech, all those Brahmins did exactly so.
O twice-born ones, those Brahmins of the south and north who are censured in the treatises on Dharma attain merit only through their actions, provided they are free from the defects of birth.
And those others who are mountaineers do not deserve an invitation to a śrāddha;
for this reason, the vehicle remained suspended in the sky for a long time.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, O King, he himself goes to Puṣkara to bathe, accompanied by Brahmā; it bestows merit upon all.
Whatever castes come there, O King, they are all vessels of merit;
they are equal to the twice-born, of this there is no doubt, even without the sacred mantras.
The auspicious Tīrtha of the Grandfather has descended from the intermediate space;
those who perform their ablutions here shall attain worlds of great prosperity.
O Great King, they will be indifferent to the merit of others, whether it has been performed or not; this which has been uttered is the truth.
It is recited here that among all sacred fords on earth, this is the supreme ford;
no sacred ford superior to this is proclaimed in this world.
Yama: One who bathes at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika is liberated from all sins. Viṣṇu: [Thus it is said.]
For at Puṣkara, a śrāddha, as well as recitations, oblations, and austerities, become inexhaustible;
indeed, by merely bathing at Puṣkara, one is liberated from all sins.

Thus ends the *Puṣkara-māhātmya* in the *Tīrtha-kāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[186] 9. Now, the majesty of Mathurā.
In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states:
Varāha said:
"Mathurā is renowned as my supreme field of liberation."
It shall come to pass, O fair-limbed one, when the Dvāpara age has been established.
This most delightful and praiseworthy birthplace is dear to me;
O fair-faced one, taking up four forms, I shall be born here.

“The forms”— namely the essential natures of Kṛṣṇa, Balabhadra, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna— “O auspicious lady, shall indeed become my secrets, which are dear, meritorious, and praised for men seeking liberation from saṃsāra.”
"The 'secret' places are those which will be described;
there I shall slay the Dānavas, O fair-faced one.
There, O lady of excellent hips, is a river with auspicious and most meritorious waters."
The beautiful Yamunā shall indeed be the daughter of Vivasvat;
O lady of lovely hips, she shall be auspicious at Prayāga, the sacred field of Brahman.

There is no doubt that immediately after that, at Prayāga on the Gaṅgā—[as it is said]: "But at Prayāga"—"immediately after that" means immediately after Mathurā—at Prayāga, the field of Brahmā, through its connection with the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā will become auspicious; likewise, here in Mathurā itself, it will be auspicious from the very beginning.
Men who are devoted to their own duties shall attain perfection.
By the power of my field, the earth is the liberation from saṃsāra.
O slender-waisted one, on the southern bank of the Yamunā at Mathurā, there is a supreme and fragrant pool of blood named Asikuṇḍa.
There, having fasted for six meals, a man should perform his ablutions;
having resorted to the Nandana grove, he rejoices, his purpose accomplished.
Then, if one gives up their life here on that auspicious bank or shore,
they leave behind the Nandana grove and attain my world.
In that sacred field, there is a supreme place of mine named Vṛndāvana;
there I shall sport together with the cows and the cowherd boys.
There, O illustrious lady, is a pool surrounded by hundreds of creepers and shrubs;
a man who has stayed there for four periods of the day should perform his ablutions therein.
One who, having made a firm resolve, constantly gives up their life there among the vast and divine families of the Gandharvas, rejoices.
Leaving behind the city of the Gandharvas, he goes to my world;
there is my supreme, secret field named Bhāṇḍīraka.
Even the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and great asuras do not know it;
there a man, eating but one meal and fasting, should perform his ablutions.
He rejoices in the worlds of the nāgas; of this there is no doubt. Moreover, having performed extremely difficult deeds, he may even cast off his life-breaths here.
Having abandoned the world of the Nāgas, he attains my own realm;
there, O illustrious lady, is a pool surrounded by trees, shrubs, and creepers.
There, on its eastern side, is that most righteous *tīrtha*.
"Righteous" (*dhārmika*) means having the purpose of dharma or being productive of dharma.
It is adorned with *campaka* and *pāṭala* trees, as well as various other flowers.
There, a man who has fasted for a day and a night should perform his ablutions.
Having gone to the world of the Vidyādharas, he rejoices with firm resolve;
then, if he gives up his life here, he attains my own world.
The sacred field called Yamalārjunakuṇḍa is my supreme pool;
and that pool, O highly fortunate one, is overgrown with trees, shrubs, and creepers.
Having fasted for a day and a night, a person should perform a bath there;
having gone to the abode of the Apsarases, he rejoices, freed from all sin.
Then, having performed his deeds with firm resolve, he gives up his life-breaths here;
having gone to the abode of the Apsarases, he attains my world.
In that very same way, there is my supreme sacred site named Arkasthala within that field;
and there the Sun-god is seen established as the twelve-fold self.
There, O illustrious lady, is a well with clear water;
it is difficult for those who perform evil deeds to obtain, but easy for those who perform meritorious acts.
[189] Then, having fasted for one night, a man should perform his bath here;
he rejoices in the worlds of the Sun—of this there is no doubt.
Then, having restrained his senses, he who gives up his life here abandons the world of the sun and goes to my own realm.
Therein lies my supreme, ancient, and secret place named Vīrasthala;
it is overgrown with shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants, and abounds in flowers, fruits, and water.
A man who has fasted for five nights should perform his ablutions right there;
by my very grace, he rejoices in the worlds of heroes.
Then, if one who is single-minded and firm in his vows gives up his life here,
he leaves behind the world of heroes and attains my own world.
Furthermore, O highly fortunate one, there is another supreme secret field of mine named Kanaka;
on the ridge of the Vindhya mountains, a well is established there.
There, having fasted for one meal and performed his ablutions, a man rejoices upon the vault of heaven; he has accomplished his purpose, of this there is no doubt.
Then, one who gives up their life there attains the supreme, divine goal;
the proclamation of my name is my own supreme secret field.
And there was a single stone slab resembling red sandalwood,
charming, delightful, and bringing happiness to my devotees.
The man who stays there on that ground for even one night,
having made a firm resolve, goes to the abode of Vāyu and rejoices.
[190] Now, if one releases the vital breaths here, one goes to my imperishable world;
it is renowned as Somakuṇḍa, my supreme field within that sacred site.
One should perform a ritual bath there; one rejoices in the world of Soma.
Furthermore, if one gives up one's life here, free from greed and delusion, [one attains that same state].
Having abandoned the world of the moon, he rejoices and beholds me;
in that sacred field is my supreme place, renowned as Rādhākuṇḍa.
There, a man should perform his ablutions after fasting for one night;
thereafter is my supreme secret sacred field named Piṇḍāraka.
At the southern bank, in the pure waters of the Yamunā,
a man who has fasted for one night should perform his ablutions there.
The doer of merit goes to the world of the meritorious, which rests upon the peak of Mount Meru;
in that field is my supreme [abode] named Jambīra Campaka.
There, O large-eyed one, is a pond with clear and pure water;
having stayed there for one night, a man should perform his ablutions.
A human being obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice at that supreme field of mine, which is named Karmāvarohaṇa.
There, at the auspicious head of the Vindhya range, one should perform the consecration;
that field is named Vitānaka, and there lies my supreme secret.
To the west of Mathurā, within a distance of half a yojana,
lies the field named Ballabhaka, which is my supreme secret.
[191] Now, if one gives up one's life here at my holy site of Ballabhaka,
having abandoned the world of heaven, one is glorified in my own world.
In that place is my supreme secret known as Ūṣabhañjanaka,
where a single stream, having issued forth from the peak of the Vindhya mountains, falls down.
There, a person who has fasted for one night should perform the consecration;
if he then gives up his life-breaths there, he quickly attains the supreme goal.
Therein lies my supreme secret, named Binduprabha;
a single drop falls there from a mountain that is difficult to traverse.
There, a man who has fasted for one night should perform the consecration;
if he then gives up his life-breaths there, he quickly attains the supreme goal.
There exists a supreme secret of mine called Astamāna;
there, a single stream flows forth from the Vindhya mountains.
There, having sipped water according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the consecration.
To the south of that field, there is a place named Tāmraprabha.
Then, at a distance of five krośas, there is a supreme, great pool;
one should perform ablutions there, engaged in the four periods of the day.
In that place, there is my supreme secret known as Vatsaprakrīḍana;
it is on the western side of Mathurā, not far away, at a distance of half a yojana.
There, O illustrious lady, is a pool with clear and pure water;
having fasted for a day and night, a man should perform his ablutions there.
Having gone to the abode of Agni, he rejoices, freed from all distress;
and if he releases his life-breaths there, he attains perfection and the supreme goal.
There is a supreme secret field of mine named Govardhana,
located not far from Mathurā, eight krośas to the west.
O highly fortunate lady, there is a lake there, covered with trees, shrubs, and creepers;
it belongs to Indra on its eastern side and is indeed the ninth on the southern side.
There is a sacred ford (tīrtha) of Varuṇa in the west and one of Kubera in the north;
O auspicious lady, he stays there in the middle, sporting according to his own will.
I was praised with hymns by the world-protectors and by those who recite mantras;
even there, my four [disciples] witnessed a great marvel.
On that Govardhana mountain, which is dear to all devotees of the Lord,
on the twenty-fourth twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), at the very summit of its peak—
Indeed, a thick lamp is seen illuminating the ten directions;
and whoever, devoted to my ritual service, beholds that lamp of yours, [attains the goal].
One attains supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt. There is a sacred and most secret pool of mine called Kāliya-hrada.
There, at the conclusion of the Dvāpara Yuga, I shall slay Kaṃsa;
a man who has fasted for five nights should perform his ablutions there.
Having gone to the abode of the Gandharvas, he rejoices, freed from all distress. There I dwell, O blessed lady, taking refuge in the eastern direction.
Having fashioned a golden image of Bṛhadrūpa with four arms,
there is a well of pure water on the right side as one proceeds.
A man who has stayed there for four periods of the day should perform an ablution at that place where the water known as Saptasāmudraka is situated.
He rejoices in the seven continents, having a dwelling where he may travel at will;
then, when he releases his vital breaths here, he rejoices in my world.
In my Maṇḍala at Mathurā, which extends twenty yojanas,
those who release their vital breaths there attain perfection and go to the supreme goal.
In that place there is a cave named Nandiguhā, which is my supreme secret;
here sleeps Mucukunda, the destroyer of Dānavas and Asuras.
There, O illustrious lady, is a pool with clear and pure water;
having fasted for six meal-times, a man should perform his ablution there.
Those people who, O highly fortunate lady, practice [this] in the forest of Mathurā, rejoice for ten thousand years, having reached firm resolve.
They too, by my grace, attain supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt.
This greatness concerning Mathurā has been told to you, O blessed lady.
This should be remembered even at the time of death with the mind,
if one desires the supreme accomplishment that liberates from all saṃsāra.
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "O best of sages, having bathed in the waters of the Yamunā during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha on the twelfth lunar day, a man who observes a fast..."
Having properly worshipped Acyuta in Mathurā with a concentrated mind,
one obtains the complete fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Then, observing the supernatural power that had arisen in others born of their own lineage,
the fathers and grandfathers of those others reportedly said this:
"Will someone born in our family, having fasted and bathed in the waters of the Kālindī, worship Govinda in Mathurā?"
Having worshipped Janārdana during the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha under the asterism Mūla,
we shall attain supreme perfection, having delivered those born of our own lineage.
At that time, one born into a virtuous family, having worshipped Kṛṣṇa there with a concentrated mind, shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) into the Yamunā.

Thus ends the *Mathurāmāhātmya* in the *Tīrthakāṇḍa* of the *Kalpataru*. Thus [ends] the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
The section on sacred fords (tīrthakāṇḍa), containing the majesty of Mathurā, is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of Ujjayinī, it is stated there in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"In the southern direction, there is a great sacred field known as Ujjayinī."
Therein lies the Mahākāla Liṅga, which, by the mere sight of it, conquers all sins.
Wherein the ascetic attains supreme, desired perfection;
thus [it is said]. Rudra said:
Formerly, in Avantī, when the auspicious ceremony of the first tonsure had been performed for the prince, Skanda was then gratified by me.
Having arrived, the Mothers requested unprecedented food;
the host of gods came from the world of the gods to eat with the Mothers.
Thus addressed by them at that time, Maheśvara, the God of gods,
spoke for the sake of dharma to those [goddesses] in the presence of the deities and Pārvatī.
Indeed, I have prepared food made in many varieties;
all of that has been consumed, and nothing else is seen here.
"Now that you have arrived, what indeed should be given by me?
Especially for you, who are unprecedented, something extraordinary must be given by me."
I shall give you those two which have not been tasted by others, which are to be eaten,
and which are round, situated below the navel, and near the organs of generation.
"Eat together, indeed, both my pendulous testicles;
by this non-eating as well, there will be supreme satisfaction."
Having shown great favor, O auspicious one, all those goddesses prostrated themselves and departed; then they all spoke these words.
Those of virtuous conduct who perform that [rite] without laughter— for them, indeed, their children, wives, homes, and so forth will surely become like beasts.
Whatever else is desired by the mind shall be granted by me;
even long-term illness and poverty, which are censured, shall be dispelled through laughter.
Therefore, a wise person should neither engage in censure nor in laughter;
for by this, the name "Mothers" will become renowned in the world.
Those men who shall cause votive offerings to be made during the month of Kārttika—
namely chickpeas, fried cakes (pūrikās), and fried cakes together with testicles— [shall attain their desires].
Their lineage is not broken by kinsmen or even by their own people;
one without a son obtains a son, and one seeking wealth obtains wealth.
Possessed of beauty, fortunate, and an enjoyer of pleasures, he becomes proficient in all scriptures;
by means of a vehicle drawn by swans, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[197] In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "O beloved, liberation may occur at Prayāga, or at Mahākāla, or likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka, as well as at Kāyāvarohaṇa."
Just as my two eyes are situated upon my face, so too are these two sacred sites (tīrthas) of the earth located at Kālañjara and Mahākāla, which are under my protection.
"Mahākāla and Avimukta, together with the Gaṅgā and the Siprā.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
The section on sacred fords (tīrthakāṇḍa), containing the glorification of Ujjayinī, is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Narmadā,
Mārkaṇḍeya spoke thus to Yudhiṣṭhira in the Matsya Purāṇa:
The Narmadā is the best of rivers, the destroyer of all sins;
she shall deliver all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Likewise: "The Gaṅgā is meritorious at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra;
but the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere, whether in a village or in a forest."
The water of the Sarasvatī purifies in three days, that of the Yamunā in seven days,
that of the Gaṅgā immediately, and that of the Narmadā by mere sight.
In the western half of the Kalinga country, on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
there is a sacred, venerable, and delightful [place] throughout the three worlds.
Having bathed there, O King, a man who is observant of his vows and has conquered his senses,
by fasting for a single night, shall deliver a hundred of his lineages.
Having bathed at Jaleśvara and offered funeral cakes according to the prescribed rule,
his ancestors remain satisfied until the dissolution of all beings.
Ten million Rudras are established all around the mountain;
whoever performs a ritual bath there with perfumes, garlands, and ointments [attains great merit].
The entire multitude of Rudras, numbering ten million, will undoubtedly be pleased with him;
on the other side of the mountain, the Lord Maheśvara himself resides.
Having bathed there and become pure, remaining celibate and with senses subdued,
one should perform the rites for the ancestors according to the procedure prescribed by the rules.
O Pāṇḍava, by satisfying the ancestral deities right there with water mixed with sesame seeds, his lineage rejoices in heaven for seven generations.
For sixty thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world;
then, having descended from heaven, he is born into a noble family.
He is born wealthy, charitable, and indeed righteous;
he remembers that sacred ford again and desires to go there once more.
Having delivered seven generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Rudra;
this most excellent river is heard to extend for more than a hundred yojanas.
But in detail, O Indra among kings, it is two yojanas in length,
and likewise possesses sixty thousand and sixty million sacred fords (tīrtha).
On that most beautiful mountain, Amarakaṇṭaka, he dwells,
having become pure and practicing celibacy, with his anger conquered and his senses subdued.
But he who has desisted from all violence, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
and whose conduct is thus pure— if such a person should give up his life;
O King, listen attentively to me regarding the fruit of his merit:
he rejoices in heaven for a hundred thousand years, O Pāṇḍava.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a righteous king;
he obtains the palace of Śauri, adorned with various jewels.
Having dwelt in that house, which is endowed with play and enjoyments,
one shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all diseases.
Thus indeed do those who have died at Amarakaṇṭaka enjoy such pleasures—
those who entered the fire, or likewise into water, or through fasting unto death.
O lord of men, his movement is unimpeded like that of the wind in the sky;
he who falls upon Amareśa shall not fall again.
Three thousand maidens, and yet another for each one,
dwell in his palace and wait upon him, seeking his command.
Endowed with excellent divine enjoyments, he sports for an inexhaustible time;
such a person as this is never born again upon the earth, as far as the oceans.
[201] As excellent as this deceased one was on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka,
so should that holy site (tīrtha) on the western side of the mountain be known.
There is a lake named Jaleśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there and by performing the rite of twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), [one gains great merit].
The ancestors remain satisfied for ten years;
on the southern bank of the Narmadā is the great river named Kapilā.
Abounding with Sarala and Arjuna trees, it is situated not far away;
it is indeed meritorious, highly blessed, and renowned throughout the three worlds.
In that regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, more than a hundred koṭis of sacred fords are mentioned in the Purāṇas, O King; the fruit thereof is said to be multiplied by a hundred koṭis.
Those trees that have fallen at those sacred fords due to the passage of time,
even they attain the supreme goal when touched by the waters of the Narmadā.
The second, however, is the highly fortunate and auspicious Viśalyakaraṇī.
Having bathed there on that shore, a person becomes free from their thorn-like afflictions in an instant;
there, all the hosts of gods, along with the Kinnaras and Mahoragas, [reside].
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and sages whose wealth is asceticism—
all of them assembled there on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
And all those sages, whose wealth is their asceticism, having gathered together,
resorted to the holy Narmadā, which is known by the name Viśalyā.
O King, having bathed there, a man who is celibate and has conquered his senses obtains that highly auspicious [tirtha] which destroys all sins.
Having observed the fast for a single night, one may deliver a hundred families;
O best of kings, it is heard that both Kapilā and Viśalyā are likewise effective.

In ancient times, O Yudhiṣṭhira, this was proclaimed by the Lord out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds: "By bathing there— whether at the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, or the Narmadā— a man, O King, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
O lord of men, he who practices fasting unto death at that sacred site goes to the world of Rudra, his soul purified of all sins.
O King of kings, as I have heard in the Purāṇa regarding the Narmadā:
by bathing anywhere along it, a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who dwell on the northern bank reside in the world of Rudra,
as do those on the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, and the Narmadā.
Bathing and giving gifts are equal, as Śaṅkara told me:
for whoever abandons their life-breaths on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka.
For more than a full hundred million years, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
the holy water of the Narmadā is adorned with waves of foam.
This sacred [text], when honored with the head, liberates one from all sins.
Likewise: "The Narmadā is the best of rivers; she is indeed meritorious and most meritorious."
But it has been divided by the highly fortunate sages who were desirous of dharma.
O Pāṇḍava, O lord of kings, the sacrifices and the purifying mantras are distributed there;
by bathing in them, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
Likewise:
"The Narmadā is meritorious in every respect and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by fasting for a day and night, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Thus, O son of Pāṇḍu, the Narmadā is meritorious and delightful;
indeed, that great river is sacred to all the three worlds.
At Vaṭeśvara, which is highly meritorious, at Gaṅgādvāra, and at those places rich in asceticism—
in all these locations, there are twice-born ones who are firm in their vows.
It is heard that the merit at the confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean is tenfold;
during lunar and solar eclipses, one should go to Amarakaṇṭaka.
The wise declare that it is ten times more meritorious than the horse sacrifice;
by beholding Maheśvara there, one attains the heavenly realm.
I shall go to Sannihati when the sun is seized by Rāhu;
that entire merit is found on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
Whoever mentally recollects the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka obtains more than a hundred Cāndrāyaṇa fasts; of this there is no doubt.
He is renowned throughout the three worlds as Amarakaṇṭaka; likewise,
whoever should perform a circumambulation on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
A person obtains the fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
There, on the mountain named Amarakaṇṭaka, is the peak called Jvāleśvara;
having bathed there, those who have attained immortality go to heaven and are not born again.
O Great King, listen also to the fruit that belongs to one who gives up their life at Jvāleśvara during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
The lord of the immortals himself resides on the mountain Amarakaṇṭaka;
one attains the world of Rudra there until the dissolution of all beings.
On both banks of the mountain of the god Amareśa,
those millions of sages, firm in their vows, are indeed performing austerities.
Within a league in every direction lies the field, as well as Mount Amarakaṇṭaka;
whether free from desire or possessed of desire, one [should bathe] in the auspicious waters of the Narmadā.
Having bathed, one is liberated from sins and goes to the world of Rudra. Likewise,
there is the confluence of the Kāverī, which destroys all sins.
Those men who do not understand this are undoubtedly deceived.
Therefore, a person should bathe there with every effort;
for both the Kāverī, which is highly meritorious, and the great river Narmadā are present there.
Having bathed there, O king of kings, one should worship the bull-bannered Lord;
having obtained the fruit of a horse sacrifice, he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
For one who enters the fire and for one who practices fasting unto death, there is no turning back from their destination; this is what Śaṅkara told me.
Served by women, that man sports in heaven like Rudra for sixty thousand years as well as another sixty crores of years.
Dwelling in the world of Rudra, he rejoices wherever he goes;
when his merit is exhausted and he falls away from there, he becomes a righteous king.
One who is wealthy and charitable shall be born into a great family;
having properly drunk water there, one obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Those mortals who drink the auspicious water at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā go to heaven; such is the fruit that a man would obtain there.
"Whoever bathes at the confluence of the Kāverī obtains that fruit.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
The section on sacred fords (*tīrthakāṇḍa*), containing the *Narmadāmāhātmya*, is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of Kubjāmraka, it is stated therein in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Varāha said:
Thus, O illustrious lady, is this sacred ford known as Kubjāmraka;
those who die there go to my world, free from all blemish.
The holy site of Kubjāmraka is meritorious and brings happiness in my world;
and the holy site of Kumudāraka is likewise situated within that Kubjāmraka.
O lady of beautiful hips, merely by bathing during the month of Kaumuda as well as Mārgaśīrṣa, that indeed bestows the path to heaven.
Having performed difficult deeds during the month of Vaiśākha,
whether it be a man, a woman, or a eunuch, whoever should renounce their life—
He attains partless perfection and goes to my world;
he who is thus designated there as "Mānasa-tīrtha" [attains this].
Having bathed there, the large-eyed woman goes to the Nandana grove;
he who gives up his life there on the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika [Kaumuda] attains that state.
One obtains abundant perfection and goes to my world;
it is known as Māyātīrtha, by which one understands illusion (māyā).
O Brahmin, by performing the water-libation ceremony at that Māyātīrtha, a man becomes my devotee for ten thousand years and attains great renown.
Or else, O illustrious one, he dies there on the bank of Māyā;
having then become a yogi of Māyā, he goes to my world.
There is a sacred ford named Sarvapika, endowed with the merits of all ritual acts;
whoever bathes there on the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha, indeed [attains the fruit].
One obtains the Niṣkala heaven for fifteen thousand years;
at that holy place named Pūrvāmukha, some are not even reborn.
The water of the Gaṅgā is always cool there;
however, wherever the water becomes warm, that should be known as Pūrṇamukha.
Having bathed, O fair-hipped one, he of great renown goes to my world.
Listen further, O Mādhavī, as I shall explain another matter according to the truth.
Having bathed right there at the place named Aśoka, one no longer sees sorrow;
liberated from all attachments, one goes to my world.
And there is a sacred ford named Karavīra, which brings happiness in my world;
I shall describe its sign by which it is recognized on earth.
O lady of beautiful hips, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, [you should worship] with men who possess knowledge and are firmly resolved in devotion to me.
One should cultivate the *karavīra* at midday; there is no doubt that one dies there on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the month of Māgha.
One may behold Brahmā, myself, and likewise the one whose banner is the bull;
there is a great and highly renowned sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Puṇḍarīka.
O lady of beautiful hips, by bathing there one obtains a highly meritorious fruit,
which is the very fruit obtained by one who performs the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Or else, if that person of great austerity dies there free from fear,
that man obtains the fruit of ten *puṇḍarīka* sacrifices.
Having attained auspicious success, he goes to my world;
indeed, having bathed at Agnitīrtha and staying there at Kubjāmraka.
O highly fortunate lady, whatever fruit a man obtains by entering the fire seven times, he attains that merely by bathing; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, if one dies there on the single twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
having fasted for twenty nights, one goes to my world.
This ground and the prosperity of Kubjāmraka have been described to you.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
In the section on sacred fords (tīrthakāṇḍa), the glorification of Kubjāmraka is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Boar, in that *Varāha Purāṇa*,
Varāha said:
The supreme place is Kokāmukha, the supreme place is Kubjāmraka,
and the supreme place is Saukara, which grants liberation from the entire cycle of worldly existence.
O Goddess, at the place where I raised you from the netherworld (Rasātala),
there the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā arrived for the sake of my purification.
Listen, O highly fortunate and beautiful lady, to the merit that one obtains, O noble one, by going to the Saúkara field within my domain.
He leads ten of his own preceding ancestors and fifteen descendants— seven on the mother's side and five on the father's side— to heaven.
O lady of beautiful hips, simply by going [to him] and likewise by beholding his face,
O blessed one, one is born after seven lifetimes into a noble family.
Thus, having become a human being free from transgressions,
one should effect his departure for that sacred field and cause him to die there.
O lady of beautiful hips, those who have died there in my field of Sūkarakalpa are delivered from the entire cycle of existence and go to Śvetadvīpa.
[210] O highly fortunate lady, at Cakratīrtha, where the Discus is established—
having gone there, O highly fortunate one, one who is pure and auspicious through that lineage [should perform rites].
One should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rule on the twelfth day of the month of Mādhava;
[one thus gains] ten thousand years and ten hundred years.
He is born into a vast family, prosperous with wealth and grain;
delivered from the entire cycle of existence, he goes to Śvetadvīpa.
Becoming four-armed, bearing a bow, quivers, arrows, and a sword,
and having become a man, O highly fortunate lady, he is liberated from all sins.
O illustrious and glorious lady, I shall describe the merit of one who goes toward Śaukara at the time of death, even if he has already bathed.
Even one who, having committed sins and become a fool, has become firm in his vows,
[should observe] the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight of the month of Kaumuda.
By him his fathers and likewise his grandfathers were delivered;
as many as are the drops of water upon his limbs, O beautiful one.
O large-eyed one, having died there at the highly powerful Rūpatīrtha, my devotee is likewise born for thousands of years.
They shall be born radiant and resplendent, possessing four arms.
Furthermore, I shall explain another matter concerning that Saugarakam of mine.
It is renowned as Yogitīrtha, difficult to comprehend even for a seer;
and those who, devoted to my rites, bathe in Yogitīrtha—
Freed from anger and passion, those who have made their resolve go there; O illustrious lady, so does he who stays there for a day and night and performs [the rite].
[211] Having bathed at the sacred ford and being liberated, yet remaining devoted to my ritual action, he,
established in the abode of yoga, seeks that very ford.
And he shall obtain that sacred ford by my grace, without a doubt;
having renounced his life there, being solely devoted to my service.
Equipped with all weapons, radiant, and four-armed,
having become the most excellent of yogis, he goes to Śvetadvīpa.
This has been told to you, O blessed lady, regarding the Yogitīrtha of great fruit;
O beautiful one, I shall now describe the sign of this Yogitīrtha.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
darkness suddenly arises at that sacred bathing place.
