O large-eyed one, the measurement is prescribed as three thousand cubits, three hundred cubits,
and three cubits.
O large-eyed one, whoever performs a bath here after seeing this confluence, which brings about death, attains the destination previously described.
O illustrious lady, while I am present at Yogitīrtha,
one who desires success and seeks the supreme goal should take refuge in this sign.
Furthermore, I shall describe the final sacred site of mine, Saugarakam,
where Soma subsequently performed his austerities.
The ground fashioned by Soma appears with the luster of the moon;
he who stands on the path of righteousness beholds his own reflection therein.
And yet the moon itself is not seen; this is indeed a supreme marvel.
This, O blessed lady, has been related to you as the definitive account of Soma-tīrtha.
By means of which human beings cross over the ocean of saṃsāra;
on its eastern side is known the sacred ford (tīrtha) called Gṛdhravaṭa.
O Mādhavī, he who performs a ritual bath at the Sākoṭaka tīrtha— where the vulture Kāma died and attained human birth—
remains [purified] for ten thousand and ten hundred years.
Resorting to the Nandana grove, he indeed rejoices there forever;
I shall speak of another [grove] as well, so listen to that, O Vasundharī.

O illustrious and renowned lady of great fortune, there is a sacred ford named Vaivasvata where the Sun-god performs austerities; it was for the sake of obtaining a son that he performed those penances there.
But he who bathes on the eighth meal-day, O beautiful one,
rejoices with the Sun for ten thousand years.
Or else, if one dies there at that auspicious sacred ford of Vaivasvata,
O lady of beautiful hips, he never goes to the abode of Yama.
And I shall describe death on that earth at Saukaraka:
having indeed undertaken fasting for fifteen days.
"Having abandoned all attachments, he goes to my world.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, the Great Minister for Peace and War.
The section on sacred fords (*tīrthakāṇḍa*), containing the majesty of Sūkara, is complete.
Now, regarding the majesty of Kokāmukha, therein in the Varāha Purāṇa,
Varāha said:
There is no sacred field superior to Kokāmukha; there is no auspiciousness greater than Kokāmukha;
there is no bathing more meritorious than at Kokāmukha; and there is no object more dear than Kokāmukha.
Being pure, one who goes to Kokāmukha shall attain the supreme yoga;
being impassioned, one may perform ritual actions, and these become ordained for oneself.
And whatever fields have been traversed by you on the beautiful earth,
there has never been, nor will there ever be, a sacred ford equal to Kokāmukha.
That is my supreme form; deluded beings do not know it as it stands at Kokāmukha on earth. This has been told to you by me.
Likewise: "In my sacred field of Kokāmukha, five yojanas in extent,
he who knows the holy fords (*tīrtha*) is not smeared by sin."
There, at the holy site of Kokāmukha, I stood facing south;
the Blessed One, in the form of a boar, remained there in the likeness of a man.
Having made my face upward-turned and endowed with five fangs,
I behold the entire world and those who are my devotees, dear to me.
If one should ever go to Kokāmukha by the turn of time,
he would not return from there, provided he desires the supreme goal.
One does not attain the great state through Sāṃkhya nor through Yoga;
rather, it is he who goes there by [visiting] Kokāmukha—this which has been told to you by me.

In that regard, the Mahābhārata states: "Having touched the waters at Kokāmukha, being a celibate student and restrained in his vows, one attains the memory of past births; this was ordained in ancient times."
"Diṣṭam" means "declared," and "purātane" means "in the Purāṇa.
Thus [ends the section] in the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War (Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika).
The section on sacred fords (tīrthakāṇḍa), containing the glorification of Kokāmukha, is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of Badarikāśrama, it is stated therein in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Varāha said:
On that ridge of the Himalayas is my supreme, secret abode;
there I was fully gratified by Agni through his austerity upon the earth.
Having become like fire and having performed most difficult deeds,
my devotees attain the supreme Badaryāśrama.
That field on the surface of the Himakūṭa rock is extremely difficult to attain;
indeed, the man who reaches that field has accomplished all that was to be done.
On that mountain peak there is a place renowned as Brahmakuṇḍa;
the man who fasts for three nights and performs his ablutions there—
A person who, having dwelt there while performing penances, should give up his life, obtains a fruit equal to that of a hundred Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Having transcended the world of Brahmā, he goes to my own world;
there, in that pool renowned as Agnikuṇḍa, is my supreme abode.
If one has offered his life there and performed the Cāndrāyaṇa vow,
he transcends the world of Agni and goes to my own world.

Thus ends the *Badarikāśrama-māhātmya* in the *Tīrtha-kāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Mandāra tree, it is stated therein in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Varāha said:
O beautiful one, listen again in private to another [matter]:
my supreme, secret abode, which brings happiness to those engaged in ritual action.
On the southern bank of the Jāhnavī, situated upon the slopes of the Vindhya mountains,
there is a place renowned as Mandāra, which is dear to all devotees of the Lord.
In that Tretā Yuga, there will undoubtedly be one of great splendor named Bhūmikāma; he shall establish my image.
While playing there, I saw the Mandāra tree in bloom;
O beautiful one, know that eleven ponds belonging to me exist there.
And by my very power, that great tree Mandāra,
the best of trees, blossoms on the twelfth and the fourteenth lunar days.
A man who, having fasted for one meal at the sacred site of Mandārakuṇḍa,
performs his bath with a purified soul, shall go to the supreme goal.
One should release one's life-breaths here in the pool known as Mandāra;
having performed austerities, that fortunate person goes to my world.
Likewise:
On that secret mountain peak, the supreme Mandara,
there stands the Discus in the southern half and the Mace indeed in the northern part.
The plow, the pestle, and the conch shell stand before me;
some, deluded by my illusory power, do not recognize this.
"The liberated Bhāgavatas [worship] all those known as Śvetavārāhas.
Thus ends [the section] in the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and the Great Minister for Peace and War (Mahāsāndhivigrahika).
The section on sacred fords (tīrthakāṇḍa), concerning the majesty of Mandara, is completed.
Now, regarding the majesty of the Śālagrāma, in that regard the Varāha Purāṇa states:
Varāha said:
There is a supreme, secret place on that secret mountain mass,
on the northern side of the Gaṇḍakī and to the south of the Lord of Mountains.
Known as Śālagrāma, it brings happiness to my devotees;
this place on the mountain peak, amidst the lofty rocks, is pleasing to me.
It is renowned as Śālagrāma, which grants liberation from the cycle of existence for devotees;
O illustrious one, there are fifteen secrets here in Śālagrāma.
Even today, those liberated ones known as the Vārāhas do not know that;
likewise, O illustrious lady, there is my sacred field there named Devahrada.
There, the stage was traversed by me during the destruction of Bali’s sacrifice.
That lake is the best of givers of boons, charming, auspicious, and cool;
it is unfathomable and always difficult to attain even for the gods upon earth.
In that illustrious lake where I always perform my ablutions,
fish marked with wheel-signs wander here and there on all sides.
In that Devahrada, on the twelfth day of the twenty-fourth lunar period,
golden lotuses are seen when the sun has risen.
These [lights] are visible as long as [the sun] remains at midday;
there, a man who has fasted for ten meals should perform his bath.
A person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices;
moreover, if one who is established in my mind gives up their life here, they attain that same result.
Having enjoyed the fruit of the horse sacrifice, O illustrious lady, he goes to my world;
for I am there in Śālagrāma, facing the east.
"I shall become a lover of the Bhāgavata soil, of this there is no doubt;
and I shall tell you something else, O beautiful Vasundharā—listen to that."
Where the deluded do not know that supreme secret field,
Śiva dwells free from all affliction in my right place.
O beautiful one, having paid homage to Govinda— the most excellent and supreme among the worlds, the sustainer of all worlds, and Hara— whoever offers salutations [to him]...
"It is a futile journey," they say; this is indeed so, without a doubt—[for] whoever, having paid homage to the god Śiva, pays homage to me, the Earth.
One obtains abundant success, as has been proclaimed by me;
and my entire field extends ten yojanas in width.
"Men who follow virtuous deeds go to me after they die here.
[221] In the *Mahābhārata*: "O Bhārata, wherever Hari dwells, he is always present there."
It is known as Śālagrāma, belonging to Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds.
Having approached Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, the giver of boons, the imperishable,
one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
O Knower of Dharma, the gift of sesame seeds brings liberation from all sins;
there, the four oceans are always present within that well.
Having sipped water there, O Indra among kings, one shall not fall into an evil state of existence,
after approaching Viṣṇu, the Lord of the three worlds, the giver of boons, and the imperishable.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, like the moon released from the clouds, he shone forth—
pure and with a restrained mind— having performed the ritual sipping of water and remembered his former births.
By bathing there, one attains the memory of past births; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the "Glorification of Śālagrāma" in the Section on Sacred Fords (Tīrthakāṇḍa) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika), son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now follows the majesty of the Lord Stutasvāmin.
In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states:
Varāha said,
"My sacred field shall become renowned as 'Stutasvāmī' (the Lord praised)."
Having reached the Dvāpara Yuga, O beautiful one, I shall remain there.
I am the son of Vasudeva, born from the womb of Devakī;
I am known as Vāsudeva, the destroyer of all demons.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
by merely bathing, one obtains the fruit of three Vājapeya sacrifices.
O lady of beautiful hips, a man who holds me within himself attains the fruit;
furthermore, if he gives up his life here, he proceeds according to my own karma.
Having enjoyed the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, he attains my world;
there, an iron image of mine exists, which is impenetrable—of this there is no doubt.
Some say it is wood; others said it is iron;
others might say it is stone, and still others that it is made of diamond.
Whether they are above or below, or at my side,
they touch them all in that same way, yet never once do they touch the middle of my head.
And those who see me, O beautiful one, dwelling on the Maṇipūra mountain during the three junctions of the day, shall do so by my grace.
All of them, liberated from their sins, go to that supreme goal. Likewise,
O beautiful one, there is Suguhya on the eastern side of my field.
The distance of three *krośas* is prescribed as the measurement for what is not far.
There, not far from my field to the west, extending for five *krośas*, lies my supreme secret known as Dhūtapāpa.
In that highly auspicious pool, a man who has fasted for five nights should perform a bath in whatever water pleases me.
Whatever misdeed has been committed in your lineage and whatever resides within yourself— having offered water for those, O auspicious one, O illustrious one whose sins have been shaken off!
He shall rejoice in the world of Indra along with Mahendra; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, O illustrious one, he who gives up his life here at Dhūpapāpa [attains the same].
Having abandoned the world of Indra, he goes to my own world;
O highly fortunate one, whose sins have been washed away, hear from me the marvel that occurs there.
And it continues, O large-eyed one: "The stream does not fall as long as the mountain Maṇipūra is not shaken."
O fair-hipped one, when the rain falls upon the earth at Dhūtapāpa,
that sacred field, O lady of excellent limbs, extends for five yojanas in every direction.
There, O Goddess, I abide, situated in the western direction;
and there, O auspicious lady, the Āmalaka trees are not far away, at a distance of half a yojana.
No one who is a doer of evil deeds or the lowest of men understands them;
yet, by fasting for three nights with faith and with senses subdued, [one may know them].
Having gone there, O lady of excellent hips, at sunrise,
or at the time of midday, or when the sun has set;
One should proceed with a single-pointed mind, maintaining firm and perfectly unshakable resolve.
O auspicious lady, whoever obtains the pure and beautiful fruit there shall behold me on that mountain of spirits within five nights.

Thus ends the "Greatness of Stutasvāmin" in the Tīrthakāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, the majesty of Dvārakā.
In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states:
Varāha said:
"There is a city named Dvāravatī, constructed by Viśvakarman."
And the assembly hall named Sudharmā has been brought by the wind for me.
O lady of excellent hips, I dwell here for fifty-five years in this place which is five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long.
"Having relieved the burden and performed a great service dear to the gods,
I shall return again, O lady of beautiful hips, after having slain the great asuras."
O Earth, listen as I describe to you my form within myself;
therein lies my supreme secret, known as Pañcaśara.
Having left the seashore, a man who has fasted for six meals should perform his bath at a place where food is brought to one's mouth.
He rejoices on the summit of heaven, crowded with throngs of Apsarases;
or else, when he gives up his life-breaths, he attains me alone.
O woman of beautiful hips, there is indeed a great tree there with a hundred branches;
on the twelfth day of the twenty-fourth [lunar period], that tree shall bear fruit.
No one obtains the fruit there except for the pure devotee of the Lord;
those who obtain the fruit there are [the ones devoted] to the secret of the five-arrowed god.
They obtain supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt.
It is renowned as Prabhāsa, and therein lies my supreme secret.
There, a man who has fasted for five nights should perform the consecration;
he rejoices in the seven continents and attains the secret [realms].
Alternatively, a man who has cast off his sins at Prabhāsa gives up his life-breaths and,
abandoning all worlds, attains my own realm.
It is known as Pañcakuṇḍa; therein lies my supreme secret.
A man who has fasted for five nights should receive initiation there.
On the twenty-fourth and twelfth [lunar days], at midday when the sun is shining, a lotus made of silver and gold is seen; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise:
"In my supreme field, there is a sacred pool known as Kādevaka;
having drunk here, O highly fortunate lady, the Vṛṣṇis attained imperishable [merit]."
There one should perform the consecration, endowed with the four times.
Likewise: "The city named Saṅgama is my supreme field therein."
And on my left side, not far away, at a distance of seven yojanas.
That lake, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, is by my side;
in that sacred field, there is also my supreme abode named Raivataka.
Renowned throughout all the worlds, the Moon sports there;
in its ten directions are caves filled with abundant water, rocks, and mud.
And there is a beautiful bathing pool, difficult even for the gods to attain;
a man who has observed the sixth-meal fast should perform his ablutions there.
A man who has fulfilled his duty goes to the world of Soma;
furthermore, if he gives up his life-breaths here, he attains my own world.
In that sacred field, there is my supreme site called Viṣṇucaṅkramaṇa;
there I was pierced by a hunter and regained my own original form.
O illustrious lady, there stands a sacred pool on Mount Maṇipūra;
one should perform ablutions there at all times without weariness.
Likewise:
"In that illustrious field, I am situated facing north,
having taken refuge on the shore of the ocean for the sake of pleasing all devotees of the Lord."
Together with Rāma and that auspicious sister Rākā,
we three remain right there in Dvārakā, O illustrious lady.

Thus ends the "Glorification of Dvārakā" in the Section on Holy Places (*Tīrthakāṇḍa*) of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*), son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, the majesty of Lohārgala.
In that regard, the Varāha Purāṇa states:
Varāha said:
"O auspicious one, I shall declare another secret cause that is eternally beneficial."
O auspicious lady, I indeed went thirty yojanas along the bank of the Sindhu river.
O lady of excellent limbs, having taken refuge in the Himavat among the Mlecchas,
my residence is established there at the place named Lohārgala.
And the supreme secret place extends for five yojanas in every direction;
it is difficult to access, hard to endure, and surrounded by running [waters].
There, O blessed lady, I abide, established in the northern direction;
some do not recognize my own form as being present there.
But those who go there, O lady of beautiful hips, being fully established in their own karma, see me here as well, and likewise all secret things.
O lady of beautiful hips, one should certainly perform a bath in that pool after fasting for three nights according to the ritual prescribed by rule.
There he rejoices in thousands of heavens; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, I shall tell you another thing that is most wonderful therein.
[229] On the twenty-fourth and twelfth days, no offering is made to me without meat;
for there, an offering that purifies all desires is presented.
There my horse was prepared, adorned with all kinds of jewels;
it was white, resembling a water-lily, and marked with the conch and the discus.
There, this Śārṅga bow, a rosary, and a water-pot are present;
a divine seat, ornaments, and excellent food are offered.
In this secret and highly blessed field of mine, Lohārgala, a mortal who desires spiritual accomplishment must go; of this there is no doubt.
Within twenty-five yojanas all around, O lady of beautiful countenance, no one’s karma can prevail; this is my supreme certainty.

Thus ends the *Lohārgala-māhātmya* in the *Tīrtha-kāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*) and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, the majesty of Kedāra.
In that regard, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"There is a place named Īśānaśikhara, resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon;
there the Supreme Lord himself dwells in person."
He is indeed known throughout the world as Īśāna, renowned across the three realms;
there, O Śakra, the seed-fluid was first created by the God.
And that which is hidden and concealed is not known even by the gods and asuras;
likewise, it is the means for crossing over saṃsāra and the severer of the net of other evils.
Having drunk the water of Kedāra, rebirth no longer exists;
one shall not be joined to wombs again, but shall go to the eternal state.
Likewise:
"That which was hidden from me has been made manifest in the sacrificial pit for the benefit of human beings who are sinking in the ocean of existence."
Knowledge has been shown: having drunk the water, there is no further birth;
neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor Purandara is able to drink it.
All human beings drink [the water] of him with whom Śiva is truly pleased;
there is no liberation superior to Kedāra—thus Śiva himself has declared.
One may travel across the earth to sacred fords, lakes, and oceans as far as the sea;
yet these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water that is the semen of knowledge.
Even if a lord of the earth were to perform a thousand horse-sacrifices,
it would not equal even a thousandth part of the water of the semen of one possessing knowledge.
Whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, he who, endowed with sacrificial offerings, should perform a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices as well as a hundred Pauṇḍarīka sacrifices;
All that would not equal even a thousandth part of Kedāra’s [merit];
O Kāmāpa, drink, eat, and rejoice with thousands of women!
Having drunk the water of Kedāra, one overcomes all evil deeds.
Likewise: "O Śakra, whether it be knowledge, initiation, or even the wearing of ashes,
all that is not worth a sixteenth part of the water of semen."
Likewise:
I shall describe the procedure for how they drink that water.
Having gone to the holy Mandākinī and bathed there, that man—
Having offered water to the gods, one should cause the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to be given to the ancestors,
having likewise paid homage to Īśāna with a mind endowed with devotion.
Having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, he stood there according to the prescribed rite on the Himalayas;
having bowed there to the god Śiva and also to Umā, the Great Goddess.
Having reflected, "I am Śiva," one should drink from the left hand all those— Nandin, Gaṇapati, and indeed all the lords of the Gaṇas.
Having drunk three times with the left hand, one should drink again with the right;
having drunk three times with that [right hand], one should drink once more with both hands joined as an añjali.
Having drunk three mouthfuls of water, he should then drink like a bull,
pressing his knees and both hands against the ground.
Extending his head, he should drink [the water] three times with his mouth;
then, rising up, he should roar three times and likewise snap his fingers three more times.
Having paid homage to the Lord in that manner, he stood with palms joined in reverence;
having accomplished his purpose and performed meritorious deeds, he attained union with Śiva.
Water drunk according to the prescribed rite shall deliver a hundred generations of one's lineage.

Thus ends the Kedāra-māhātmya in the Tīrtha-kāṇḍa of the Kṛtyakalpataru, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (mahāsāṃdhivigrahika) and son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[233] 22 Now follows the majesty of Naimiṣa.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states: "Thereafter, one should go to the holy Naimiṣa, frequented by the Siddhas;
there Brahmā dwells eternally, surrounded by hosts of gods."
For one who seeks Naimiṣa, half of their sin perishes;
as soon as a man has entered it, he is liberated from all sins.
There, the wise man, devoted to sacred fords, should dwell for a month at Naimiṣa;
for whatever sacred fords exist on earth, O Bhārata, they are all present at Naimiṣa.
There, a man who is self-restrained and restricted in his diet, having received the consecrations,
obtains the fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice.
O best of the Bharatas, he who, devoted to fasting, gives up his life at Naimiṣa purifies his lineage even unto the seventh generation.
"He rejoices in the heavenly world; thus say the wise. O best of kings, Naimiṣa is eternally pure and meritorious."
Having reached Gaṅgodbheda, a man who fasts for three nights obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice and becomes one with Brahman.

Thus ends the "Glorification of Naimiṣa" in the Section on Sacred Fords (Tīrthakāṇḍa) of the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war and son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
Now, the majesty of various sacred fords (tīrtha).
In the Vāmana Purāṇa:
Having bathed in that best of holy places, having beheld the three-eyed Lord,
and having worshipped the one named Suvarṇa, they then proceeded with self-restraint to Naimiṣa.
There, on the Gomatī, are thirty thousand holy sites that remove sin,
including those at Kāñcanasthāna and those situated in the midst of the Sunandā.
Having bathed in them and worshipped Acyuta, the Lord of Gods who is clothed in yellow garments,
and having likewise worshipped the God of gods, Īśāna, according to the prescribed rite;
That great asura went to Gayā to behold Gopati;
having bathed in the lake of Brahmā and performed its circumambulation.
He performed the meritorious offering of funeral cakes for his ancestors;
then, having bathed at Udapāna, he proceeded to the Sarayū river.
Having bathed there and worshipped the Lord who reclines upon the waters at Gopratāra— as stated in the Mahābhārata:
"One should then go to Gopratāra, the supreme sacred ford (*tīrtha*) on the Sarayū."
[235] Wherein Rāma went to heaven together with his servants, army, and mounts.
Having cast off his body, he went to heaven by the power of that sacred ford,
O Bhārata, through the grace of Rāma and his own resolute effort.
O lord of men, having bathed at that holy ford of Gopratāra, a man,
his soul purified of all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*,
after describing Gopratāra:
"Having fasted for one night, he went to that river Virajā."
Having bathed at the Virajas tirtha and likewise having offered a funeral cake (piṇḍa) to his father, he—
The illustrious one went to see the unconquerable Puruṣottama;
having seen that lotus-eyed, imperishable, and supremely pure one, he became purified.
Having observed a fast for six days, he went toward Mahendra as his sacrificial fee;
there he beheld Śambhu, the best of gods, Hara, who is half-woman and half-man.
Having seen and worshipped the ancestors, he went to the north of Mahendra;
there he beheld Śambhu, the best of gods, Gopāla, who is as cool as the moon.
Having seen [it] and bathed at Somatīrtha, he proceeded to the Sahyācala mountain;
having bathed there in the Madhudhī lake and having worshipped Vaikuṇṭha with devotion.
Having worshipped the ancestors with funeral cakes (piṇḍas), he went to the Pāriyātra mountain;
having bathed there in the Lāṅgulinī river, he worshipped Aparājita.
Having withdrawn his hands and feet, he beheld the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa),
wherein Śambhu, the best of gods, was being highly honored by the deities.
Then the knower of yoga revealed his universal form;
having bathed there in the waters of the Saṃkuṇikā and worshipped Maheśvara.
Then Prahlāda went to Mount Saugandha, the Malaya mountain;
having bathed there in the great lake, he worshipped Śaṅkara.
Then, with his soul absorbed in yoga, he went to the Vindhya mountains to behold Sadāśiva;
having fasted for three nights, he went to the lord at Avantīgarī.
Having bathed there in the waters of the Śiprā and worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion,
Hara, in the form of Mahākāla, then proceeded to the cremation ground.
In that [state], Śaṅkara, the self-controlled one, assumes a tamasic form and brings about the dissolution of all beings through that very form.
While staying there in fine attire, the king named Śvetaki protected [the people] by slaying Antaka, the one who carries away all living beings.
There he dwells forever, joyful together with Umā,
surrounded by the first ten million [gods], saluting him and honored by the thirty deities.
Then he beheld Mahākāla, the bringer of the end to Death himself,
the restrainer of the Daityas like Yama, the death of death, and the wondrous one.
Having worshipped Śambhu— the lord of beings, the master of the world, the wielder of the trident, whose abode is the cremation ground— he departed toward Niṣadha.
Having seen and worshipped the god Amareśvara there with devotion,
he approached Mahodaya and beheld Hayagrīva.
Having bathed at Aśvatīrtha and beheld the horse-faced one (Hayagrīva),
and having worshipped the omnipresent Lord Śrīdhara, he proceeded to the region of Pāñcāla.
Then the chariot-warrior, having seen Bhadreśvara protected by his attendants and the fivefold son of Arthapati at Prayāga, proceeded there with devotion.
Having bathed in the world-renowned Yamunā-tīrtha located nearby,
and having beheld Rudra as Vaṭeśvara and Mādhava reclining in Yoga, [one attains liberation].
Having worshipped Maheśvara with devotion according to the two [prescribed] methods,
and having fasted during the month of Māgha, he then went to Vārāṇasī.
At Daśāśvamedha on the Gaṅgā, at the sacred ford, in temples of the gods,
and in other such places that remove all sins, one should worship the ancestors and the deities.
Having circumambulated the city and worshipped Avimukta and Keśava,
and having beheld the flickering sun, he then proceeded to Madhuvana.
There, having seen the self-existent god who had come to the Puṣkara forest, that best of asuras, possessed of great splendor, paid him homage.
Having bathed in all three of those sacred fords and having worshipped the ancestors and the gods,
he also paid homage to Brahmā, who has lotus-like eyes and is free from the odor of worldly attachment.
Then, once more at the world-renowned sacred ford of the Sarasvatī,
Koṭitīrtha, he beheld Rudra, whose banner is the bull, together with ten million Rudras.
Those best of the twice-born from Naimiṣa, from Māgadha, and from Saindhava;
likewise those from Dharmāraṇya, Pauṣkara, and Daṇḍakāraṇya.
[238] Those twice-born men from Cāmpeya, from Bhṛgukaccha, and those dwelling on the banks of the Devikā, all arrived there to behold Śaṅkara.
O Sage, ten million women, perfected and longing for the sight of Hara, were saying, "I first! I first! in this manner.
Seeing those great seers whose sins had been burnt away by his glance, Hara,
the Sustainer, assumed ten million forms out of compassion for them alone.
Then all those sages, being delighted, worshipped Maheśvara with devotion, having each established his own sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Thus, the auspicious name "Rudrakoti" arose;
the highly resplendent and devoted Prahlada beheld them.
Having bathed at Koṭitīrtha and offered libations to the Vasus and the ancestors,
and having worshipped Rudrakoṭi, the man went to Kurujāṅgala.
There he beheld Sthāṇu, the best of gods, Śaṅkara, the beloved of Pārvatī,
who was immersed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and honored by the deities.
Having bathed in the waters of the Sarasvatī and having worshipped Sthāṇu with devotion,
she approached Kṣīrikā and beheld Nīlakaṇṭha.
Having bathed in the waters of Nīlatīrtha and worshipped Śiva there,
he went to Prabhāsa on the shore of the ocean to behold the Lord.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Sarasvatī and the ocean,
he beheld Someśvara, the Lord of the World, who bears matted locks.
The moon, the lord of the stars, who was consumed by the curse of Dakṣa and was wasting away,
was nourished by Śaṅkara and by Viṣṇu, the wearer of matted locks.
Having worshipped those excellent gods, he returned to Mahālaya;
having worshipped Rudra there, he went to the Northern Kurus.
Having worshipped Padmanābha, he went to Saptagodāvara;
having bathed there and worshipped the Lord of Gods, Bhīma, the knower of the three worlds.
Having gone to the Dāruvana forest, the illustrious one beheld the Śrī-liṅga;
having worshipped that, he then went to Brahmāṇī and worshipped the goddess of the lords of the thirty gods.
Having gone to Plakṣa-taraṇa, he worshipped Śrīnivāsa;
and then, having gone to Kuṇḍina, he worshipped [the deity] who grants satisfaction to all living beings.
Having worshipped the four-armed one on the solar disc according to the prescribed rite,
the lord of the earth reached the Māgadha forest and beheld it.
Having worshipped that Lord of the Universe, he proceeded toward the face of the people;
then, having bathed in the great holy ford and bowed down to Vāsudeva, he departed.
Then, having reached the Śoṇa river and worshipped the Lord Rukmadharman,
the devotee next worshipped Mahādeva, known as Haṃsa, at Mahākāśī.
Having performed worship, he then went to the excellent Saindhava forest;
having seen and honored Hari there, he proceeded to the Kanakhala tirtha.
There, the Dānava worshipped Rudra, Kāmeśa, and Vīrabhadra.
Then he went to Girivraja, where he saw Gaṇādhipa, who has the luster of a cloud—
the god Paśupati, the lord of the world, Maheśvara.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rites, he went to Kāmarūpa;
having worshipped the three-eyed Śaśiprabha, the best of gods, together with Mṛḍānī.
He went to that most excellent sacred ford known as Mahākhyam,
and there he worshipped Mahādeva.
Thereupon, he went to see the Lord who holds the discus (Viṣṇu) on Mount Trikūṭa, the son of the king of mountains;
and having praised him with devotion, he beheld [the place] where Gajendra was liberated.
He recited the supreme and most purifying prayer.
Having stayed there for three months, the son of the lord of the Daityas, desiring to subsist on roots and fruits,
offered gold to the most excellent of Brahmins.
For he indeed went to the formidable Daṇḍaka forest.
There he beheld the lotus-eyed one, who possessed a divine great conch and bore the form of a tree, as well as his great bow.
Beneath him stood for three nights the great devotee of the Lord, the asura, sleeping on the bare ground while reciting the Sārasvata hymn.
Therefore, the Dānava went to see Hari, the remover of all sins, at Vindhya, the best of holy places that destroys all evil.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Then, having gone to Vārāṇasī and worshipped the bull-bannered God (Śiva),
and having touched the waters of the Kapilā-hrada, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice."
[241] O king of kings, having reached the difficult-to-attain tīrtha of Mārkaṇḍeya at the world-renowned confluence of the Gomatī and the Gaṅgā.
One obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
As stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: "The great Tīrtha called Kṛtaśauca is the destroyer of all sins."
Where Janārdana himself dwells as Narasiṃha.
Likewise: Vaśvāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Siddheśvara-mahālaya,
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, and similarly the one called Suvarṇa.
For these are indeed purifying places due to their proximity during both twilights:
Kālañjaravana, Śaṅkukarṇa, and Sthaleśvara.
For these are purifiers that bring about my presence, O beloved; as stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
"Gaṅgādvāra, Kurukṣetra, Narmadā, and Amarakaṇṭaka..."
The confluence of the Yamunā is meritorious, as are Vidiśā and the Vetravatī.
The Sarayū, the Kauśikī, the Vindhya, the Gaṇḍakī, and the Sarasvatī;
the holy river Candrabhāgā and likewise the river Godāvarī.
The Kāverī, the divine Gomatī, the Devikā, and likewise the Varaṇā—
these most meritorious rivers are proclaimed [as sacred] during eclipses and other such occasions.
And there are many other meritorious [occasions] that bestow merit at all times;
they are renowned as occurring during the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during the *vyatīpāta* yoga.
During a time of distress, at a lunar eclipse, at a gathering of Brahmins,
in times of great joy, at social assemblies, and when pursuing a common purpose— there, seven or five [should be invited].

"In festivals" (*saṃmodeṣu*) means during celebrations; "in assemblies" (*samājeṣu*) means in gatherings; "for a single purpose" (*ekārthe*) means when they have one common objective. When seven or five [people] are assembled, then the previously mentioned rivers are most meritorious and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) performed there grants all desires. Likewise: "Thus, on all festival days (*parvasu*) and during all the phases (*kalāsu*) of the moon."
On the third day of Vaiśākha, or on the eighth day falling on a Tuesday, [one should perform the rite].
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, during the libation for the ancestors on a Tuesday,
this should be performed by the best of the twice-born for the fulfillment of all desires.
O Sage, that man who worships Śiva and Āditya on the new moon day and during the sun’s transit becomes purified and the Blessed One is pleased with him.
Likewise:
"An eclipse during the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent; but an eclipse during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā, O great sage, is meritorious."
In the month of Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious; in Māgha, the auspicious Saṃnihitā;
in Phālguna, the one known as Varaṇā; and in Caitra, the meritorious Sarasvatī.
In Vaiśākha, the excellent river Candrabhāgā is of great merit;
in Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; and in Āṣāḍha, the river Tāpikā.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the river named Sindhu; in the month of Bhādrapada, the Gaṇḍakī;
in Āśvina, the Sarayū; and furthermore, the Narmadā is most meritorious.
O great sage, when the moon is joined with Rāhu during the Godāvarī festival of great merit,
and likewise when the sun is eclipsed by the moon, then [the time] has arrived.
Those men who drink the water of the Revā while the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu become fulfilled through contact with the waters of the Narmadā.
Those who touch and bathe therein are no longer ordinary men;
having touched it, they obtain the fruit of a hundred sacrifices, and having seen it, they obtain the fruit of the gift of a cow.

Having bathed there, one obtains a merit equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice, and by touching [the water], one gains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī; this is likewise true during an eclipse of the sun or moon, as well as during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
In this same way, the Gaṅgā is to be regarded, and likewise the Sarasvatī;
as well as whatever fruit is proclaimed for the Maṇḍala of Śivāditya.
In this regard, a person shall obtain [the fruit] here in the gathering, the mandala, and the sacrifice.

The meaning is that whatever fruit is obtained at the *maṇḍala* or sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Śiva and Āditya, one obtains that same fruit through sacrifice and worship when the disks of the moon and sun are eclipsed by Rāhu.
Whatever merit is proclaimed for being in forests or in saline wasteland (*ūṣara*) fields,
that becomes even greater here during an eclipse due to the majesty of the time.
Or, having brought water by which they may perform a bath even at home,
if it is purified with the mantra itself, their merit from that is even greater;
[this should be done] in a vessel made of metal or earth, according to one's own intention, for the sake of a worthy recipient.
One obtains blameless fruit by means of bricks, stones, or wood;
therefore, having brought earth from that very sacred bathing place for the purpose of eating, [one should use it].
Rising every morning, those best of men who play [these instruments] all become liberated from evil and freed from disease.
Or that brahmin who, having bathed there, should worship the Sun and Īśvara with offerings of fruits and flowers, shall become free from all affliction.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite with jars filled with holy water sanctified by mantras and containing fruit, he shall obtain all his desires.
This merit, which I have related as heard from the mouth of Brahmā,
shall accrue in its entirety to him who [recites it] in forests and in barren lands.
I shall describe the forests as well as the saline wastes:
Saindhava, the Daṇḍaka forest, Naimiṣa, and Kurujāṅgala.
The forest of Utpalāvarta, Jambūmārga, Puṣkara,
and the Himavat forest from Sahya— these are thus proclaimed.
And that man who should give up his life-breaths in these forests,
having become a guest in the world of Brahmā, goes to the supreme goal.
Whatever fruit is obtained at Kālikā, at the place called Śikhara, at the abode of Kālakāla, at Kālañjara, or at Mahākāla— it is indeed equal in all of them.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "At Kālañjara, at Daśārṇa, at Naimiṣa, at Kurujāṅgala,
and in the city of Vārāṇasī, the Śrāddha should be offered with great care."

Having gone there, one becomes purified; moreover, the śrāddha offering becomes inexhaustible, as do whatever recitations, oblations, austerities, meditations, or other meritorious deeds one may perform.
In the Mahābhārata:
Having plunged into the Śatadru, the Candrabhāgā, and the Vitastā garlanded with waves,
one should indeed become like a sage— free from food and free from the sense of "mine."
Whatever great rivers flow in the region of Kaśmīra,
by reaching the Indus, one who possesses virtuous conduct shall attain heaven.
Having plunged into Puṣkara, Prayāga, Naimiṣa, the waters of the ocean,
the Devikā, the Sindhu-mārga, and Svargabindu;
Seated in his celestial chariot, praised by apsarases, he awakens;
having stirred Hiraṇyabindu, he offers a reverent salutation with a disciplined mind.
The sin of one who worships Kuśeśaya, the Lord of Gods, at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vindhya, or the Nīla mountain, is purified.
Likewise, having bathed at Kanakhala, one whose sins are washed away shall go to heaven;
by touching the waters at Apāmhrada, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
A celibate student who has conquered anger, who is true to his word, and non-violent,
[should go] where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā flows toward the northern direction.
By the empowerment of Maheśvara,
the man who consecrates himself while fasting for one month beholds the deity himself.
That man who indeed plunges into that auspicious water at Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Indramārga is not born again.
Having bathed in the Mahāhrada, one who is pure and devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice,
remaining without food for a single mealtime, shall attain perfection in due course.
Having bathed at Mahāhrada on the Bhṛgutuṅga mountain,
one who is free from greed and has fasted for three nights is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having touched the waters at Kanyākūpa, sleeping on leaves and having performed the water-libations,
one gains renown among the gods and shines with glory.
Having touched the waters of the Mahāgaṅgā and likewise at Kṛttikāṅgāraka,
one who remains without food for a fortnight attains the stainless heaven.
Having touched the Vimānaka and prepared a bed of leaves,
one who has performed the water-libation attains fame among the gods and shines with glory.
Having bathed at Kiṅkiṇīkāśrama as well as at the holy abode of the Apsarases, one who moves at will is glorified in the celestial mansions.
Having reached Kālikāśrama and performed water-libations in the Vipāśā river,
a man who observes celibacy and has conquered his anger is liberated after three nights.
Having bathed at the hermitage of Kṛttikā and offered libations to the ancestors,
one who gratifies Mahādeva shall attain the stainless heaven.
Having touched the waters at Mahāsaras and fasted for three nights, a man shall abandon the fear of becoming stationary beings or bipeds.
Having bathed in the Devadāru forest, purified of sin, and performed the water-libations,
one who remains pure for seven nights attains the lineage of the gods.
At Kauśāmbī, at Kuśastamba, and likewise at Droṇadharmapada,
as well as at Prapatana in the center, one is served by hosts of Apsarases.
Having plunged into Citrakūṭa, Janasthāna, and likewise the waters of the Mandākinī while fasting,
one indeed attains royal splendor.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śyāmā, stayed there, and performed the consecration,
and having maintained composure for three periods of three nights, one should proceed to the city of the Gandharvas.
Having reached Kauśikīdvāra, a man who subsists on air alone and is free from greed ascends to heaven within twenty-one nights.
He who bathes at Mataṅgavāpī attains perfection in a single night;
he who is self-restrained and well-concentrated at Jambūmārga attains it in three months.
One attains success in a single day and night at Caitra,
but at Prabhāsa, one who is composed attains it in a single night on the new moon day.
But one succeeds, O mighty-armed one; such a man is not born again, having touched the waters at Ujjānaka and at the hermitage of Ārṣṇīṣeṇa.
Having bathed in the hermitage of Piṅgā, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, by touching the water at Kulyā and reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, one is purified.
Having fasted for three nights and remained pure, a man who touches the waters at Piṇḍāraka while staying there for one night obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having bathed at Mount Maināka and likewise performed the twilight devotions, one who is pure obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice when the night has dawned.
Having gone to Nada-Brahmasaras, adorned by the Dharmāraṇya forest,
one who is pure obtains the merit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice when the night has turned to dawn.
Having bathed at Mount Maināka and likewise performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā),
and having conquered desire for a month, one obtains the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
Having approached Kālodaka, Nandikūṭa, and likewise Uttaramānasa from a distance of a hundred yojanas, even a killer of an embryo is liberated.
Having beheld the image of Nandīśvara, one is liberated from sins;
having bathed in the Svargamārgahrada, one goes to the world of heaven.
The Himavat mountain is renowned and holy; it is the divine mountain of Śaṅkara, a mine of all jewels, and frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
A twice-born man who has mastered the Vedanta, knowing that life is transient, should renounce his body there through fasting according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped the deities there and likewise paid homage to the sages,
the perfected one shall then go to heaven, to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Whoever, having conquered desire, anger, and greed, should dwell at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
for him there would be nothing unattainable through that visitation of the ford.
Those sacred fords that are inaccessible, difficult to reach, and treacherous—
all of them, in brief, can be reached simply by the mind.
Yama says: Having bathed at Puṣkara on the full moon day of Kārttika, one is liberated from all sins;
but having bathed at Prayāga in the morning during the month of Māgha, one is released from all transgressions.
Having bathed at the banyan tree of Gayāśīrṣa on the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha while pure,
and having bathed in the waters of the Narmadā on the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa;
Likewise, having bathed on the full moon day of Caitra at Śālagrāma, on the fourteenth day at Sanaka,
and similarly on the tenth day of the bright fortnight at Puṇḍarīka;
[249] Having bathed at the *saṃnihati* on the new moon day, or likewise again at dawn,
a man who bathes for the sake of vital energy (*ojas*) is liberated from all sins.
Likewise, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha at the Yamunā,
and similarly on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha.
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada, a person is liberated from all sins.
Having bathed in that Vitastā, one is liberated from all sins;
likewise, having bathed in the waters of the Candrabhāgā on the thirteenth day of the month of Māgha or Phālguna.
Likewise on the eighth lunar day in the waters of the Revatī [river], as well as in the waters of the Revā;
on the full moon of Āṣāḍha in the waters of the Sarayū, and likewise constantly on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
Having reached the Śravaṇa asterism at any confluence whatsoever,
one should likewise spend the entire fourteenth day in the pure waters of the Devikā.
Having touched the waters of the Mahāgaṅgā, as well as at Kṛttikāṅgāraka,
on the thirteenth day of the month of Āśvayuja, and likewise at Viśālā;
Devala says:
Even the sin of killing an embryo, if committed unknowingly,
perishes through great sacrifices or by visiting sacred fords.

Now, the Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, Vipāśā, Vitastā, Kauśikī, Nandāvarī, Candrabhāgā, Rūtyalāvatī, Sindhu, Arjunīyā, Aparṇāśā, Śoṇasnāyī, Airāvatī, Pāṣāṇātīrtha, Gomatī, Gaṇḍakī, Bāhudā, Ramyā, Devikā, Godāvarī, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇī, Parṇī, Carmaṇvatī, Revatī, Bhīmā, and Rakṣuvīraṇā—these are the most meritorious great rivers.
Gaṅgādvāra, Kanakhala, Śūkara, Prayāga, and Gaṅgāsāgara are the sacred fords (tīrthas) of the Gaṅgā.
Plakṣaprasravaṇa, Vṛddhakanyāka, Sārasvata, Ādityatīrtha, Kaubera, Vaijayanta, Pṛthūdaka, Naimiśa, Vinaśana, Vaṃśodbheda, and Prabhāsa—these are the Sārasvata tīrthas.

Puṣkara, Urvaśa, Gayāśiras at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, Kurukṣetra, and Prayāga—these are the [tīrthas]. Vārāṇasī, Mahābhairava, Devadāruvana, Kedāra, Udyama, Rudramahālaya, Trastāvatāra, Chagalaṇḍa, Viṣṇuśiras, Mahākāla, Kālañjara, and Jambumārga—these are the āyatanas.
Himavān, Sahya, Vindhya, Mahendra, Hariścandra, Śataśṛṅga, Devaparvata, and Vindhyaparvata—these are the names of the mountains.

Likewise, these and other sacred regions, shrines, mountains, hermitages, and holy fords are most meritorious. By visiting them for that purpose, being disciplined by vows, fasting, and observances, and by not bathing for three days while staying there for three nights, one is liberated from all sins and becomes possessed of well-being. Regarding this, there are two verses: "Having visited the holy fords and the sacred shrines..."
A man is liberated from sin, as are Brahmins who practice austerities.
All rivers flowing to the ocean are meritorious; all excellent mountains are meritorious;
every sacred site is meritorious; and all forest hermitages are meritorious.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "By bathing in each river individually, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
however, at the confluence of these rivers, the merit is equal to that of ten gifts of cows."
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
Brahmā questions Keśava, the Lord Hari, who was situated on Mount Mandara:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace!"
In which various sacred fields, O Lord, are you to be seen by me,
and by other devotees, especially those who desire liberation, O Best of Gods?
O Lord of the World, O lotus-eyed one, I desire to hear from you those secret names and those sacred fields of yours.
"O Lord of the Gods, for the benefit of your devotees, tell me this: what mantra should a man constantly and tirelessly recite to attain a happy rebirth?"
The Blessed One said:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmā, to my secret names now;
I shall tell you truly of the sacred fields and the shrines."
One should worship Varāha at Kokāmukha, Madhusūdana at Mandāra,
Ananta at Dvīpa, and Kapila at Prabhāsa, as well as the Son of the Sun (Yama).
One should worship Vaikuṇṭha at Matsyodapāna, Nṛpāntaka at Mahendra,
Mahāviṣṇu at Ṛṣabha, and Bhūpati at Dvārakā.
One should worship the Lord of Gods at Pāṇḍisahya, the Lord of the World at Vasutuṅga,
the Great Yogi at Bhallivana, and the Sovereign of Men at Citrakūṭa.
[252] He saw Hari wearing yellow garments at Naimiṣa; Hari departing from Gayā;
and his inconceivable dwelling in asceticism at Śālagrāma and Gandhamādana.
One should worship Hṛṣīkeśa at Kubjāmraka, Payodhara at Gaṅgādvāra,
Garuḍadhvaja at Toṣalaka, and Govinda at Nāgasāhvaya.
One should know Gopāla to be in Vṛndāvana, Svayambhū in Mathurā,
Mādhava in Kedāra, and Keśava in Vārāṇasī.
At Puṣkara is the one called Puṣkara; at Dhṛṣadvatī is Dhṛṣadhvaja; at the forest of Tṛṇabindu is Vīramaṇoka; and at the ocean of the Indus is [the other].
One should worship the mighty-armed [Viṣṇu] at Kuśīvaṭa, Amṛta in the Taijasa forest,
Viśveśa at Viśākhayūpa, and Nārasiṃha in the Mahāvana.
They know Lohārgala as the destroyer of enemies, Devaśāla as Trivikrama, Puruṣottama as [the deity] in Kuśavana, and Vāmana as being in Kubjaka.
One should worship Vidyādhara at Vitastā, Dharaṇīdhara at Vārāha,
Guhya in the Devadāru forest, and Nāgaśāyin at the Kāverī.
They know Yogamūrti at Prayāga, Sundara at Payoṣṇī,
Kaumāra at Kumāratīrtha, and Hayaśīrṣa at Lauhitya.
One should know Vikrama in Ujjayinī and Caturbhuja at Liṅgasphoṭa;
by beholding Harihara on the Tuṅgabhadrā, one is liberated from sin.
One should worship Viśvarūpa at Kurukṣetra, Halāyudha at Maṇikuṇḍa,
Lokanātha at Ayodhyā, and the Lord of Rukmiṇī at Kuṇḍina.
One should know Vāsudeva at Bhāṇḍira, Sudarśana at Cakratīrtha, the Primordial One at Piṣṇupada, and Śūkara at Śūkara.
They know Brahmeśa to be at the Mānasa-tīrtha, Śyāmala at Daṇḍaka,
Nāgamokṣa at Trikūṭa, and Bhāskara at Merukūṭa.
They know Viraja to be in Puṣpabhadrā, Bāla in Cāmīkara,
Yaśaskara in Vipāśā, and Hutāśana in Māhiṣmatī.
One should worship Padmanābha in the Ocean of Milk, the eternal [Lord] in Vimala,
the bestower of auspiciousness in the Śivanadī, and Gadādhara in Gayā.
He who perceives the Supreme Self everywhere is liberated;
thus, sixty-eight names have been proclaimed by me to you.
And the meritorious fields have been specifically described;
these, O Prajāpati, are my secret names.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should constantly recite or even listen to this,
enjoys the fruit of giving away a hundred thousand cows.
Whoever, having become pure day after day, should remember these sacred fields, no evil dream shall befall him by my grace; of this there is no doubt.
The man who recites these sixty-eight names at the three times of day is liberated from all sins and rejoices in my world.
These sacred fields should be visited by men according to their ability, especially by Vaiṣṇavas; I shall now declare the liberation that results for them.
Having worshipped Hari and standing before Him while remembering Hari, especially on the day of Viṣṇu,
that man who always recites this hymn—
One attains the immortal state of Viṣṇu.
[254] Likewise, having directed this excellent hymn toward Brahmā, the Blessed Lord Hari spoke again:
"Learn from me those sacred fords (tīrthas) which they are."
The Gaṅgā is the first meritorious river, followed by the Yamunā and the Gomatī; then the Sarayū, the Sarasvatī, the Candrabhāgā, and the Carmaṇvatī.
Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Puṣkara lakes, Arbuda,
and the highly meritorious Narmadā— these are the sacred fords in the north.
The Tāpī and Payoṣṇī are two holy rivers; the Utsaṅga is a supreme sacred site (tīrtha);
and the Godāvarī is greatly meritorious everywhere, O best of the twice-born.
O Lotus-born One, there is the highly meritorious Tuṅgabhadrā,
where I dwell with affection together with Hara, honored by the sages.
The Tuṅgabhadrā and especially the Gaṅgā and Kāverī are to the south;
O Lotus-born One, I am stationed on Mount Sahya at Āmalakagrāma.
O Lord of the gods of gods, you have always been worshipped there by the name Brahmā;
indeed, many sacred fords exist there that remove all sins.
"By bathing and drinking from them, a human being is released from sin.
Having spoken thus regarding the sacred fords, Madhusūdana—
He went to Brahmā, and Brahmā also returned to his own city. Likewise,
Sūta said:
In the village of Sahyāmalaka, having propitiated the immutable Lord of the gods of gods,
seventy attained perfection along with the four-faced ones.
From the sole of his foot, a sacred ford emerged facing the west;
that became the holy Cakratīrtha, which removes the sins of men.
Having bathed at Cakratīrtha, a man is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.

O Sage, by bathing at Śaṅkhatīrtha, a man obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice; furthermore, by residing there during the pilgrimage in the month of Puṣya on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, he gains even greater merit.
O Brahmin, the water-pot of Brahmā, previously filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā, fell upon the Sahya mountain; there it became a great sacred site (tīrtha).
The sacred ford named Kuṇḍikā is located near a stone and a tree;
those sages who bathe there shall also attain perfection.
The man who, having fasted for three nights, remains there,
is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
To the north of Kuṇḍikātīrtha and to the south of Piṇḍasthāna is the Tīrtha named Ṛṇamocana; it is a supreme secret.
O Brahmin, he who, having fasted for three nights, performs a ritual bath there, is liberated from the three debts; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the śrāddha for the ancestors, that man who, according to the prescribed rule, shall offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) intended for the ancestors at the place of the cakes;
The ancestors, being fully satisfied, go to the world of the fathers; of this there is no doubt—for him who, having fasted for five nights, bathes in a sin-destroying holy place (tīrtha).
Having attained the destruction of all evil, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
indeed, he who bears a great stream there upon his head [attains that state].
Having obtained the fruit in every case, he is glorified in the vault of heaven;
so too for that devotee who performs a ritual bath at the great holy site of Dhanuṣpāta.
Having obtained the fruit of the yoga of longevity, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
by bathing at Śatavindu, a man shall go to the city of Indra.
Having bathed at the great tīrtha Sahasravindu, one shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
O best of Brahmins, so too for him who performs a bath at Varāhatīrtha on the Sahya mountain.
Having fasted for a day and night, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
and there is an excellent holy site named Ākāśagaṅgā on the Sahya mountain.
O Brahmin, a white clay has emerged, rising from the surface of the rock;
O best of the foremost of the twice-born, whatever man bathes after touching that clay, [attains merit].
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
To the south of the Lord is the holy ford named Vāgmatī-saṅgama.
The wise person who stays there for one night and bathes obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Vishnu.
O Brahmin, know that the water which has issued forth from the stainless Sahya mountain is indeed a sacred ford (tīrtha); by bathing there, one is liberated from sin.
Having bathed in these meritorious holy sites arising from the Sahya mountain,
and having offered flowers and beheld Hari;
Having abandoned evil, one should enter into Viṣṇu.
One should visit other holy fords only once, but one should visit the Gaṅgā again and again;
for the Gaṅgā embodies all holy fords, and Hari embodies all gods.
Aha! Those learned in the Vedas declare that Cakratīrtha is equal to a thousand horse-sacrifices;
those who bathe there become free from passion and are not born again.
Having bowed his head at the feet of Madhusūdana.
The Gaṅgā, Prayāga, Gayā, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and the holy sites of Kurujāṅgala and the Yamunā—
these waters of sacred fords purify one from sin over time.
But the water from the feet of the Blessed One purifies instantly.

Thus ends the section on the majesty of various sacred sites (*nānātīrthamāhātmya*) within the *Tīrthakāṇḍa* of the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, the great minister for peace and war (*mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*), son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara.
[258] 24 Now, on the great journey to the Path and so forth.
In that regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"A journey upon the Great Path (Mahāpatha) over the snow should be undertaken;
for, relying upon truth and fortitude, it bestows heaven immediately."
As long as one has not reached the worlds of Indra due to the weightiness of one's task,
who indeed would venture to cast off their body amidst the frost?
But when one, losing consciousness and giving up his life-breaths which are to be consumed by frost,
beholds the blazing fire with its flames turning clockwise;
The body of Viṣṇu as Sāṅkarṣaṇa is like a fierce fire that consumes worldly existence.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Whether one is a preeminent maintainer of the sacred fires or has entered into heroic meditation..."
Having first composed the mind, one should recite the mantra slowly.
O Agni, you are Rudra; you are the great ocean of nectar;
all the Maruts quickly went to you; you are Vāta, you are Sagara, and you are he who moves through the wind.
He, whose form is composed of bone, is casting me down.
A twice-born man who thus correctly utters this mere mantra in his mind enters the fire and goes to the world of Rudra.
[259] But fire is time; time is remembered as Rudra.
Therefore, he who enters the fire approaches Rudra.
In the Devīpurāṇa,
the Supreme Lord said:
"This form of Bhairava which has been assumed for the destruction of beings..."
O Lord of Mountains, it shall come to pass for the benefit of all beings.
Those sons of mine who have entered into that state and have been meditated upon by me—
may they become my husbands, equal to me.
Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time in that city of the king of kings,
they gradually attain the supreme and certain liberation there.
Thus was the boon granted to them by the trident-bearing God of gods:
that the sound [of their music] shall be eternally a source of joy for men who have wives.
Brahmā said: Those who, having conceived Śiva in their minds,
attain the state of Bhairava, go to the supreme abode through devotion to Rudra.
Even those who go to Bhairava out of affection, fear, greed, or curiosity, they too,
by his power, [attain] the lord of the worlds.
By practicing in the sequence of stages, those twice-born ones attain the state of Rudra;
or else, they attain the form of Bhairava, which resides in the sacred texts and is worshipped by the gods.
O mighty-armed one, having fashioned that formidable image which grants all desires—
a god with twenty-five arms, full-limbed, and worshipped by the gods— he set it forth.
One should be depicted holding a sword and a shield, while the other has his hand raised with a trident; another wears an elephant hide, and likewise, one has a wheel raised in his arm.
[260] A khaṭvāṅga, a skull-cup, a vajra, and likewise a ḍamaruka;
with such a form, his face has its lower lip bitten.
But the venerable one has a mind-nature that is jagged and possesses three eyes.
One should visualize the god Bhairava, who is worshipped by both gods and asuras,
joined by various Śivās and Śivas, and adorned with diverse ornaments.
Abounding in the splendor of fresh youth and illuminating all forms of beauty,
[he was adorned] with a dagger as his royal serpent and Vāsuki as his sacred thread.
The Kulika should be placed in the binding of the matted locks; Śaṅkhapāla, as a bracelet;
and Takṣaka and Padmarāga should be made into the ornaments of the armlets.
The two auspicious serpents Padma and Karkoṭaka, acting as anklets upon his feet—
thus one should fashion the god Bhairava, the granter of all desires.
His two gatekeepers should be fashioned with stout limbs and all auspicious marks;
they are two auspicious deities holding tridents in their hands, and the other two have the faces of an elephant and a horse.
If one performs [the rite] at the corner of the door, at the gate of the Gaṅgā, or at Bhairava, it will cause agitation, physical affliction, and many other inauspicious things.
Just as fear arises for the perpetrator due to the destruction of monasteries, wells, and so forth,
so too has this been explained to you here by way of incidental discussion, O lady of noble vows.
The two door-keepers of the deity should be depicted adorned with all ornaments, holding skull-staffs and tridents in their hands, and carrying blue lotuses and goads.
One should visualize the form of Bhairava with a half-face, accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods,
bearing the appearance of having pierced Andhaka with his trident.
Having thus prepared [the image] on cloth and worshipped the other Lord, the Supreme One, the Lord of all mantras, with red garlands, garments, and so forth; [261]
Having adorned oneself, with hands decorated by mudrās,
one should go to the God who has arisen from all the gods, the Lord of Heroes and Asuras.
Free from sorrow, fear, and delusion, having reached that truly delightful abode which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one rests in supreme bliss.
Having performed worship to the Lord of Gods, who destroys the great darkness of Gaja,
one shall ascend to the supreme station that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having meditated upon the form of Aghora, which bestows one's own will,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the fire of his mouth by means of the offering of oneself.
Those who desire supreme accomplishment should offer the divine wheel, the fire, and substances such as ghee and sesame seeds with that same [devotional] disposition.
Listen duly to that which was done by the hero Pātāṣṭaka;
how he cast himself like a moth into a blazing fire.
Then, having restrained the multitude of his wings, he made his body swift-moving, [preparing] for the flight known as *pāta* and thereafter that called *haṃsa*.
One should fly that bird named Haṃsa, which grants the fruits of the practitioner's desires;
just as a deer becomes capable of leaping over pits and the like when its form is blinded.
Likewise, when both feet are equal, that is called the *mṛgapāta* (deer-fall);
when one becomes like a pestle (*musalin*), it is the *musala* (pestle) fall, which is performed upon the mortar (*ulūkhala*).
O twice-born one, having bellowed like a bull, he shall obtain celestial chariots, banners, garlands, and the like, as well as trembling branches, bows, and humps.
One should recognize the "fall of the bull" as bestowing the fruit of the world of Śakra;
it is like a lion displaying its prowess when the lord of elephants is slain.
Thus, having assumed that state, he is considered to have gone to the lake of lions;
and having assumed a terrifying form equipped with weapons, he is freed from all affliction.
O twice-born one, one should cast that body into the fire of Śiva; that fall bestows the state of Bhairava, just as the flight of a moth or similar creature leads it to its own destruction.
In that way, all of them bestow fruits in succession upon the state of Bhairava;
their abodes are manifold and beyond counting by number.
Those who have gradually taken recourse to food and drink here,
and even those who, though perfected through initiation and other means, remain attached to the enjoyment of worldly pleasures;
Having enjoyed pleasures for a long time, they too go to the supreme state;
for even a sinful man there is freed from the distinctions of caste and stage of life.
And by the power of the God of gods,
Nandin, Kedāradeva, and likewise Rudramahālaya enjoy supreme happiness.
O tiger among gods, these four are equal to Bhairava; they bestow both worldly enjoyments and liberation, and they grant grace to all.
Even those men who go to these places, though they be evil-minded, are liberated;
they are endowed with diverse forms and bestow all desires and happiness.
And those maidens, aged sixteen and possessing full, elevated breasts,
who are diverse throughout the worlds, are enjoyed by men through their protection.
Or if women should cause [the mantras] to fall, then they consume terrible men who possess divine enjoyments and the like, who are my own forms and possess great strength.
[263] Likewise, the Gāndharva, the Brāhma, the Vāyava, and the Vāruṇa;
as well as the Vaidyādhara, the Saura, the Saindra, and the Cāndra, all remain equal.
Through their own desire, the world may fall from its state of abundance;
yet, having enjoyed according to their will, they eventually go to the supreme state.
The Lord of the gods of gods should always wear a garland made of the bones of Viṣṇu and a conch-shell belonging to Śambhu,
for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds.
Those people who worship images made of various elements, wood, or precious stones and mountains, having performed meritorious deeds, proceed to the state of Śiva.
Thus, whether in a house, on a mountain, by a river, or in a forest,
whoever fills [the space] with the Bhairava [mantra] shall obtain his desired fruit.
Having constructed these four— a leaf-hut, a flower-garden, a monastery, and a well— for Bhairava, they should be offered for the attainment of happiness.
Whatever fruit a human being obtains by giving to all the gods,
or whatever a Brahmin learned in the Vedas obtains— that fruit one may receive from Bhairava.
"He will become [the one] known as Hariścandra in ten million ways; there is no doubt about this, for he is the Self of All through all yogas.
Thus it is stated in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "He will undoubtedly become known as Hariścandra."
Because this [merit] was performed here, and because it was performed again here as it proceeded,
therefore this Bhṛgu becomes meritorious in every way throughout the world.
In this place, the man who approaches the Lord of Gods and accomplishes his purpose by leaping from the Bhṛgu cliff shall indeed go to the exceedingly radiant world of Hara.
Even one who is joined with great sins and afflicted by disease,
if he gives up his life here, shall be liberated from great fear.
Or whatever else he may desire, there is nothing here that is not primary;
it is traditionally taught that a person shall obtain all of that without delay.
In the Āditya Purāṇa,
Durvāsas said:
"By what kind of austerities and gifts do human beings behold that city?"
Of the Sun, or of Brahmā, Śambhu, Viṣṇu, or Indra—in every respect.
Bhānu said:
"Those kings devoted to righteousness who were slain for the sake of a kingdom,
those struck by fire or lightning, and those killed by lions and tigers;"
And they all reached the auspicious city of Airāvatī,
for the Blessed Lord Agni himself dwells within the mouth of the Naga.
Viṣṇu alone is established within lions, tigers, and lordly elephants;
likewise for those struck by lightning or fire, and those killed by lions and tigers.
"And those men who were slain by the *nāgas* are performers of meritorious deeds.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Lakṣmīdhara, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara and Great Minister for Peace and War (*Mahāsāṃdhivigrahika*).
The section on the Great Pilgrimage and other [tirthas] within the Tīrthakāṇḍa is completed.
Thus ends the Tīrthakāṇḍa in the Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Lakṣmīdhara.
